I can quite imagine a young preacher reading Bishop Earle's criticism in this spirit, and will not insist that he would be utterly wrong. It is only to the old that the young appear hasty, impetuous, and impulsive, and it is undoubtedly true that the bishop wrote the preceding after he had passed his prime. And this reminds me of a conversation I accidentally overheard the other day, and which I have frequently reverted to when alone, but have put on one side until I could take its lesson properly to heart. I had been to the stable to look after a favourite old pony whose health has been declining, and upon whom the lengthened severity of this winter has told almost as palpably as upon the old men and old women of my parish, many of whose vacant seats at church bear testimony to the illnesses and ailments under which they labour. To gain this stable from my door, you pass down a short garden walk which is periodically covered with the little round pebbles only obtainable at the sea-side, and, opening a small iron gate, find yourself in the churchyard. Wisely eschewing the path to the left, which would only take you to the river-side, and lead you to inspect the now neglected boathouse, which I once took such a pride in building, and turning sharply round directly you leave the garden, you reach in due course the stable standing at the end of the wall, and almost in the churchyard itself. Another and more usual mode of approach is from the village street, upon which its gates open, and up which my modest little vehicle has been so often driven. As a short cut and purely for convenience, I habitually stroll by the way first named, and thus it was I overheard the remark—for I was wrong to term it conversation—of my good and faithful man-of-all-work Stephen, to his friend and neighbour William Stubbs, who was employed in renovating the churchyard wall. Stephen was in his shirt-sleeves wringing out the piece of wash-leather with which he had been zealously cleansing and polishing some of my equine chattels and ornaments, and Mr. Stubbs looked down upon him from the top of the ladder whereon that worthy craftsman had perched himself, the better to manipulate with mortar and masonry, and generally carry out the behests of the churchwardens employing him. You will readily understand that the plashing of water on the one side, and the attrition of stone on the other, caused these cronies to raise their voices, and that as the stable door nearest my house was open, I stood at the head of the steps leading into the yard where Stephen was at work before either of them knew of my approach. Mr. Stubbs had evidently been passing a favourable criticism upon a sermon de-

IN THE VICARAGE.

livered on the preceding Sunday by the son-in-law of the gentleman in whose hands the patronage of this living lies, and who, having held a curacy (his first) in the South for some two years, is now visiting in our immediate neighbourhood, prior to starting for a lengthy Continental tour. My servant Stephen, who not unfrequently favours me with his opinion on my own compositions, had concurred in his friend's estimate, and added, in my hearing, that he 'shouldn't wonder when anything happens to the old master \[myself], if he \[the young preacher of the Sunday before] weren't brought down here.' Thus, in a succinct form, I had the speculations of a member of my household on the results of my demise. I have heard it stated of a great statesman still living, that he once hoaxed the newspapers with an account of his own death, that he might read the opinions of his contemporaries on his character and career. It may be a gratifying experiment to elicit an estimate of your public actions from the public press; but when your life is as private and retired as mine has been, there is something rather startling in hearing from the man with whom you chat every day of what shall be sown there, or pruned off here, and what will most benefit the few fields you farm,—with whom, in short, you talk over your little plans for the future freely and at length,—it is, I say, a little startling to hear that man speaking calmly, nay, cheerfully, of a contingency which will cause you to have no share in the produce of what is sown, which will make the augmented or diminished fruitfulness or beauty of your garden trees a matter of supreme indifference, and which will hand over the fields in whose fertility you take such an interest to some one you do not know, and of whose existence a few years back you never heard. And it was for the moment the more bewildering, because Stephen's tone and manner implied a continuity of interest for himself. The 'something' after the 'happening' of which another gentleman is to sit in this study, and another figure is to plead from the pulpit I have occupied so long, is a 'something' which is not to affect Stephen in any personal way. My junior by some three years and four months, it gives this good fellow a pleasant sense of superiority to speak of his master as old, and to build up little air-castles as to what will happen under the new _régime_. When I gave a warning cough, he blushed and cleared his throat with such ostentatious promptitude and manifest confusion, that I spoke to him about his wife, who has been long bed-ridden, and in other ways endeavoured to show my esteem for him to be unabated, and my self-love unmortified. If I could have made it seem that I had not heard him speaking, I should have gladly done so, but unhappily I had closed the door I found open, and retreat without noise and discovery was impossible. So I not only know that Stephen talks pleasantly of what will occur when I die, but Stephen knows I

IN THE VICARAGE.

137

know, and we constantly eye each other—for I am, alas! much alone now, and not a little dependent upon dependents—with a guilty shyness quite disproportionate to the simplicity of the incident.

And this brings me to the great question, Why do we make such a bugbear of death, that even an illiterate serving-man employs a euphuism to express it, and is remorseful, as one who has sadly erred in thinking of it at all? If Seneca could quietly ask, 'What is death but a ceasing to be what we were before? we are kindled and put out, we die daily; nature, that begot us, expels us, and a better and safer place is provided for us,' surely our faith might teach us to regard the shedding of the mortal husk—the throwing away of the casket that the gem within may shine in purer radiance—with a nearer approach to cheerful satisfaction than we do. 'Joining the majority' is not a flippant witticism, but a sober truth to grey men, such as Stephen and I, when contemplating our departure hence. I number in the churchyard over which my windows look many of my dearest friends. The partner of my life, the dear sharer of my early hopes and fears, the one sympathizing soul who knew my every mood, to whom my weaknesses and infirmities were as nothing, and with whom I lived and loved and was truly happy for the greater portion of my life, lies beneath that railed-in stone. The handsome, strong, honest, and adventurous lad who, despite my arguments and entreaties and his mother's tears, would try his fortune in a new country, and who died, we never knew how or where, but of whose demise we had but too sure evidence,—is not his name inscribed on the same memorial tablet? and does not his spirit seem to hover near? Is there, indeed, a single portion of the familiar ground wherein I hope to sleep which has not its own special lesson, from the far corner where lies the old pensioner, over whose earthly remains I read the burial service but last week, to the stately tomb of a magnate of the Middle Ages, which looked as old and time-worn when I first beheld it as now? I have seen in the long years which at one moment form so interminable a retrospect, and at another seem to compress themselves into a span—the years in which I have become husband, father, and widower—every variety of character carried to the house appointed for all. Surely the great lessons of natural equality and mutual dependence are impressed here in the most forcible of practical homilies! The quiet scene before me has so frequently pointed the moral I wish to convey, has so often been laid privately to heart, that it is strange poor Stephen's hapless speculations should have had weight with me at all. Amongst others, did not that learned Dr. Donne, of whom Dryden said, with a compliment savouring of hyperbole, that he 'was the greatest wit, though not the greatest poet of our nation,'—did not he write on the old strain in a fashion I cannot hope to equal? and does not common

IN THE VICARAGE.

sense and reason, even apart from revelation, teach us that, as has been tersely put by Swift, “it is impossible that anything so natural, so necessary, and so universal as death should ever have been designed by Providence as an evil to mankind?” Yet, despite the accumulated wisdom of centuries, despite thought, speech, writing, advancing civilisation, and widely spreading knowledge, we have only arrived at this: a servant talks of his master’s dissolution as a casualty which may or will “happen,” and that master, who, by vocation, temperament, and habitual tone of mind, should be permanently fitted for the calm contemplation of the topic, is almost shocked that it should be talked of at all. What a pitiful commentary it makes upon the teacher and taught! The good Dr. Donne I was about to quote just now reminds us that “death comes equally to all, and makes us all equal when it comes,”—an undeniable truism, which both Stephen and I may lay to heart. “The ashes of an oak in a chimney,” continues he, “are no epitaph of that, to tell me how high or how large that was; it tells me not what flocks it sheltered while it stood, nor what it hurt when it fell. The dust of great persons’ graves is speechless too; it says nothing, it distinguishes nothing. As soon the dust of a wretch whom thou wouldst not, as of a prince thou couldst not, look upon, will trouble thine eyes if the wind blow it thither; and when a whirlwind hath blown the dust of a churchyard into the church, and the man sweeps out the dust of the church into the churchyard, who will undertake to sift those dusts again, and to pronounce,—This is the patrician, this is the noble flower; and this the yeoman, this the plebeian bran?” We have here the stoical form of consolation. It is the puerility of human honours, rather than the sublime calm of the grave, which stands out most prominently after the perusal of such a passage as this. But we who have affections fixed beyond the tomb, who have bidden a temporary farewell to father, mother, brothers, sisters, friends, wife, and children, and who are patiently waiting our summons to join them, take higher ground. The more sand which has passed through the hourglass of life, the more clearly are we able to see through the empty glass; and while our youth and manhood may be viewed as testimonies to the mercy and lovingkindness of God, our future—its duration and destiny—should be, and we will hope is, left with the same confidence in His hands as if, in very truth, his attributes as our Father were never absent from our thoughts. It is, however, the want of an active and all-pervading consciousness of this omniscience and omnipresence which makes such speeches as poor Stephen’s strike harshly on the ear. Let us but feel, and keep firm hold of the great truth, that what we call death is really but the getting rid of an encumbrance, the shedding of a skin, the emancipation of the clay-bound spirit, and we shall neither talk of its “happening,” as if it were an

IN THE VICARAGE.

The room in which these rambling moralizings are put to paper is filled with what a furniture dealer would stigmatize as rubbish, and which, when the time comes for their being dispersed by auction, or divided among heirs, will never again win the consideration and esteem they have accorded to them now. Partly by the process of drifting, partly by natural selection, article after article which has done its duty in other parts of my house, and at different periods of my life, has at length settled down here as an appropriate resting-place after the labours it has undergone. My study is, in short, an asylum for deserving chairs, tables, and knickknacks, which are either altogether past work, or require to have it gently apportioned to their present capabilities. It pleases me to think that I thus in some fashion award a pension or a sinecure post to those who have served me well; and though my stern friend and doctor, Mr. Hardhead, laughs at the conceit as childish, it is surely as harmless to preserve tenderly things endeared to you by many a past association as it was to cart off, as he did, an old work-table of his dead mother's, and a clock which has been in his family for a century, and after including them, by private arrangement with the auctioneer, in the effects of poor Mrs. Sturdy, then offered for sale, boasting publicly that he cleared £2 18s. by the transaction. Selling your own household gods, parting with the sofa whereon she who is gone reclined during her last illness, changing chairs because they have grown shabby, or tables because they are old-fashioned, is to me domestic sacrilege. I don't believe in the heart or affections of a man who could do this, unless I give up all belief in his strength of head too. There have been mad kings, and others who have celebrated their own obsequies; and it is only on the ground of some joint being wanted in the intellectual armour that one can pardon either a man or woman who deliberately destroys reminiscences which at once soften and humble the heart. If Cowper be right, and—

'The fond attachment to the well-known place\
Whence first we started into life's long race\
Maintains its hold with such unfailing sway,\
We feel it o'en in age, and at our latest day,'

be sure that every item recalling it to the mind should be treasured with the tenderest care. This battered old desk, for example, with its once green cloth stained with a bluish-black by age and ill-usage, its wooden framework dotted with initial letters, and with a rude caricature of what seems to be a monkey in gown and bands, with its dim and mouldy-looking brass adornments—can there be a less attractive

IN THE VICARAGE.

desk, _per se_, in the world? The boy to whom I presented a prize for good writing the other day at the National School would assuredly sneer at it; while my new housemaid, who is of a literary turn, and has been accused by Stephen of answering conundrums in the _Halfpenny Guide_, would as certainly refuse to indite a line on its crazy surface. Yet it speaks to me of schoolboy pride, of youthful hopes and fears, manly struggles, successes, and trials, of long and earnest communings with my own soul, and of anxious, humble endeavours to give the result of those communings to the dear friends entrusted to my care. When this dark and murky cloth was new, a surreptitious letter was written on it complaining of school discipline, and earnestly praying to be sent to sea. Ah! the number of idle plaints and foolish wishes it has helped me to form and to repent of since that time! The other letter so carefully composed, so laboriously altered and improved, the letter written and re-written and sealed with a trembling hand, the letter which had for answer permission to “come and talk” was the letter which bound one heart to me through a wearily long engagement, through years of subsequent happiness, through sickness and sorrow, through toilings and joys, even unto death. The letters written on this desk, too, from that queer little room in a learned old city, a little room looking upon a bit of grass held to be sacred by all the orthodox as much as ever cow was by pious Hindoo—have they no story? Mixed up and intermingled in hazy fashion with the acknowledgments of remittances, the invitations to drink wine—port and sherry, with, at rare intervals, a bottle of claret, to which the liquid now sold under its name is but a thin potation indeed,—the exercises and copyings, the lengthy crossed epistles beginning “My own,” and ending “Ever most fondly,”—mixed with all these comes the offer of that appointment abroad, the acceptance of which would have altered the tenor of my life as completely as if my foolish school-lad wish had been granted, and I had been shipped off as cabin boy in the next outward bound. Bronzed, and pensioned with a possibly diseased liver, and yellow, hairy face, I should perhaps be at this moment debating over an odd trick, or eating curry in a London club; or, more likely still, should be lying quietly and forgotten in some Eastern cemetery, where my bones would bleach and moulder under an Oriental sun. The cogitations, the counsel-seeking, the advice asked, and the diverse resolutions taken, when the offer of that appointment came! Surely my friends were kept in ignorance of the loadstone holding me to dear old England, and that wealth and honours and distinction were as nothing in my sight if their purchase involved separation from her,—_Her_,—or they would never have argued so bravely, or insisted so eagerly on my seeing my own interests with their eyes. I know the pain, not to say indignation, my refusal caused. I remember the bitter little

IN THE VICARAGE.

speeches of unsympathizing relatives—the unpleasant prophecies and depreciating comments of family friends,—and recalling with gratitude the career of modest enjoyment and I hope quiet usefulness it has been given me to pursue, I thank God for inspiring me with the resolution to run counter to advice and act on the dictates of my own heart. And without inculcating a spirit of rebellion in the young, or encouraging that overweening self-confidence which is one of the vices of the age, I would still say that in the great crises of life all men of mental stamina must think and act for themselves. The counsel of friends, if followed, would invariably lead you into doing what they themselves would do under similar circumstances. If men were all made on the same pattern, like forks and spoons, this would answer admirably; but after allowing for differences of temperament, of disposition, and of gifts, I incline to the opinion that the only valuable counsel in matters of grave moment is that held between ourselves and God.

But the changes this desk typifies to me are legion, and it is difficult indeed to credit that the sober, chastened man now writing so placidly can ever have thrown his energies into trifles, or been almost as deeply interested in some affair of the moment as he now imagines he is on the great business of life. That writer knew human nature who said, 'As we advance from youth to middle age, a new field of action opens, and a different character is required. The flow of gay, impetuous spirits begins to subside; life gradually assumes a graver cast; the mind a more sedate and thoughtful turn. The attention is now transferred from pleasure to interest; that is, to pleasure diffused over a wider extent and measured by a larger scale. Formerly, the enjoyment of the present moment occupied the whole attention. Now, no action terminates ultimately in itself, but refers to some more distant aim. Wealth and power, the instruments of lasting gratification, are now coveted more than any single pleasure; prudence and foresight lay their plans; industry carries on its patient efforts; activity pushes forward; address winds around; here, an enemy overcome; there, a rival to be displaced; competition warms; and the strife of the world thickens on every side.' Happy are they whose lines have been cast in pleasant places, who are spared the bustle and turmoil of great cities, and whose way of life is sufficiently elevated to be free from the miserable shifts and sordid cares of poverty, while it is too lowly and insignificant to excite envy or provoke anger. The day comes when the love and esteem of your fellows, and the consciousness of having played your part, if not brilliantly, at least honestly, is of more importance than noisier and more pretentious triumphs. This is what the journey I am making round my room leads me to declare, as I note item after item and remember the people they have seen. That old rocking-chair, which

in course of time had its cane seat replaced by wood, and became hard to the sitter, and unpopular in the nursery in consequence, tells of that halcyon, half-mysterious time when, in all the pride of first paternity, I held a warm and breathing bundle of lace and long clothes in my arms, and listened lovingly to—even while I made a show of deprecating—the enthusiastic encomiums of the nurse and such of her village gossips as were assembled to do honour to the parson's boy. The serious cogitations when the time for christening him approached, the private deliberations as to who should be asked to accept sponsorial honours, the dread of offending there, the innocently prudential wish to propitiate here, the long, and, at the time, intensely interesting discussions as to what his names should be, the infantile ailments to which he became a prey, our terrified astonishment when he persisted in becoming black in the face without, as the monthly nurse's successor feelingly remarked, 'rhyme or reason,' and our indignation at the doctor's indifferent manner when informed of the novel and complicated malady under which our darling suffered—are all brought to mind by that old rocking-chair. The ceremony known in the uncouth jargon of the district as 'wetting t' bairn's head,' and which consisted of a number of crones and superannuated peasants bringing votive offerings to the cradle, and being supplied with gratuitous stimulants in return; the first unassisted toddle from mother's to father's arms; the first attempt at articulation, and the powerful effort of imagination which declared it to be my name; the first walk, the first school, the first parting!—ah me! how vista after vista of human interest opens out when we once give memory play! Beyond that chair, and hanging from the wall against which fishing-rod and a long array of substantial walking-sticks are reared, is a leathern telescope-case and strap, purchased long before I had any thought of rocking-chairs, and which brings to mind a certain reading party in Wales, before the Continent was such a glib possibility as railway and steamboat have made it, and when even pedestrianism at home was rather an exceptional than a common pastime, but when we read doggedly, and walked bravely, and were as blithe and hopeful as all lads ought to be. For it is in the next few years, or sometimes months, that we are under the influence of the factitious gloom I instanced just now. The first taste of the responsibilities of life, the first discovery that we have prescribed duties to perform and defined relations with our fellows to preserve, almost always acts as a corrective to high spirits, and not unfrequently throws the young worker into the opposite extreme. But before we have donned harness, and when we feel all the dignity of manhood without its cares, the mere consciousness of life suffices to make us merry and light of heart. A very clever clergyman of our own time, from whom I differ on many points

You loved when all was young.'

Surely we have in these two verses given to us, in simple, tender fashion, the philosophy of life. Even the late Mr. Thackeray, whose week-day preachings were not so remarkable for their tenderness to frailty as for the iron truth with which they branded sin, made one of his characters, a bankrupt, braggart, cheating, lying Irishman, declare that he always felt more affectionate when he was in trouble. This scoundrel had robbed his mother, and was habitually guilty of a thousand petty and degrading sins ; but the chastening hands of sorrow and of time exerted their usual influence, even over a nature coarse and bad as his, and the longing for some one to whom his good as well as evil qualities were known was the touch of nature connecting him, though at a long interval, with honesty and repute. Depend upon it, when the regal beauty, whose infinite variety age could not wither nor custom stale, looked back regretfully to her life in Egypt, and dwelt upon its wit, its dalliance, and its strife, her yearning for the face she “loved when all was young” ran through and tinted with a still more sombre hue the bitter contrast between the present and the past. The faces of most of the dear friends the contents of this little room bring before me have not been gazed on save by the mind’s eye for years. Many of them have gone into the house appointed for all living. Neither the history nor present surroundings of others are known to me ; yet they all speak with an eloquence fiction could not reach, and leave me with a softened and not unpleasing melancholy at my heart. “All the days of my

And now, dear reader—dear to me in proportion to the interest you feel in these hints and revelations of my inner life,—let me for the moment say farewell. It has been said that if any man would truthfully set down, and in simple language, his private history, he would add an interesting and instructive book to the library of mankind. It can only be on similar grounds that such prosings as these can be acceptable at all. I have even heard of people who think it wrong for any one to write about themselves, and of others who think it wrong for a clergyman to publish at all. These latter critics consider men of my cloth as sermon-preaching machines, and regard the production of aught more secular as subversive of the laws of order and the fitness of things. Others again would have you believe—as if the soul and heart could be always in a state of tension—that because you smile at trifles, take a sympathetic interest in men's pursuits, and even view their errors with something of Christian toleration, you have no right to write seriously or think tenderly out of canonicals. But what Montgomery happily termed, in his 'Pelican Island,'—

'Labour, the symbol of men's punishment,

is so sweet to the accustomed hand, that I suppose we penmen would continue to weave our ideas into words, even if we were certain of censure and averted looks as the penalty of publication. It pleases me to think that several of those who know and love me will easily recognize the writer of the foregoing, and that from study to stable, and from ivy-covered porch to churchyard, I shall be accompanied by at least some readers who will recognize familiar ground, and appreciate the feeling under which this essay was penned. We read that when Nabal was very drunken his heart was merry within him; but that the next morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal, his heart died within him and he became as a stone. Happily for such of us as have drunk the wine of life, and who have before us only its lees, our hearts need neither die within us nor become cold. Our days for boisterous merriment are over, but if we have not forsaken the fountains of living water to hew out broken cisterns that can hold no water, our impulses are as tender, and our joyful faith stronger and more pure than when half intoxicated with the sweet scents, bright hues, and smiling faces besetting us in the morning of life. And this sums up the contrast I promised myself

Taking the hint, I slowly fold up the closely covered sheets of paper, throw down my pen, and, followed by the snoring little terrier at my feet, pass up the quiet stairs and through the dark and slumbering house to rest.

# ON THE WATCH-TOWER.

# I.

WATCHMAN, what of the night?\
The enemy's camp-fires blaze:\
Over plain and valley, a falcon's flight,\
I see the lines of lurid light\
Veil'd by a smoky haze.

# II.

There's the flash of a signal-fire!\
And lo! through the midnight black,\
The stir of a multitude, moving nigher—\
And the terrible escalade grows higher,\
As our sleepless foes attack.

# III.

Watchman, what of the night?\
That peril has pass'd away:\
But still be ready for truth to fight,—\
Though the morning star in the East shines bright,\
We are not safe till day.

# IV.

Still must this lonely tower\
By my patient feet be trod,\
Till the utter defeat of Satan's power,\
When the siege is raised at the sunrise hour\
By the angel hosts of God.

# MAY-DAY.

BY THE REV. I. R. VERNON, M.A.

MAY-DAY! The glow of the mere word! “It is not always May;” no indeed, nor when May comes is it always just what we expected it to be. The May-day of the poets and the May-day of ordinary experience are held now-a-days to be two distinct things. “May has set in with its usual severity.” This has been a jesting saying; and, indeed, the bitter east wind does often blight the trust of the confiding primroses, and white-clad pear trees, and rose-robed peach espaliers, and silver-arrayed cherry boughs; driving mortified mankind back to warm under-waistcoats, and winter socks, and linsey-woolsey gowns. Ah, those old Mays,—so we talk, ever fancying the past and the future (especially the past) better than the present. Those old Mays, they were different, we think, from those that come to us now. And truly we must not venture to affirm that we can often match with reality the following exquisite description of the old ideal May:—

“All the land in flowery squares,
Beneath a broad and equal blowing wind,
Smelt of the coming summer, as one huge cloud,
Drew downward; but all else of heaven was pure
Up to the sun, and May from verge to verge,
And May with me from head to heel. And now,
As though 't were yesterday, as though it were
The hour just flown, that morn with all its sound
(For those old Mays had thrice the life of these)
Rings in mine ears. The steer forgot to graze,
And, where the hedgerow cuts the pathway, stood,
Leaning his horns into the neighbouring field,
And lowing to his fellows. From the woods
Came voices of the well-contented doves;
The lark could scarce get out his notes for joy,
But shook his song together as he near'd
His happy home, the ground. To left and right
The cuckoo told his name to all the hills;
The mellow ousei fluted in the elm;
The redcap whistled; and the nightingale
Sang loud, as though he were the bird of day.”

There! but that sounds almost more like June than May now-a-days. It makes one feel inclined to lean upon a stile and enjoy for an hour or two the mere fact of living; that feeling—

“When life is sweet, we know not why,”
and hearts, even in their autumn, become spring-like with the spring.

148

MAY-DAY.

However, we do sometimes have a May-day of the ideal kind, and at worst, _some_ fair straggling days mostly come into the month to redeem its title to our love. And such an ideal May-day shall be in my mind while I put down my few thoughts on the May.

May is pre-eminently the month of the return of the flowers, the eloquent flowers, that have so much to teach to those who listen to them with the key of God's revelation in the heart,—

'Consider the lilies of the field.'

These are the words of the Great Teacher, and truly how sweet and resting a lesson—if we would but learn it and lull our cares to sleep—did He teach to His true followers when He spoke those words!

'Live for to-day! to-morrow's light\
To-morrow's cares shall bring to sight;\
Go, sleep like closing flowers at night,\
And heaven thy morn will bless.'

Flowers, _preacher_ flowers—they have been thus called by a heavenly-minded divine and poet. Hear him in his garden:—

'And flowers were preachers, and (still stranger) drew\
From their own life and course\
The lore they would enforce;\
And sound their doctrine was, and every precept true.'

And the hedge pulpits of May are thick with these preachers, and the garden beds so thronged with them that you would, at first sight, have fancied them the congregation rather, bright in their silks and satins. And though all speak together their voices do not clash, and there is no confusion; and though they never leave off preaching, yet no one ever tires of their sermons. You may find in their speaking, sentiment, poetry, morality; but with all these, and above all these, if you will listen, you will hear them declare the glory of God, and show His handiwork.

May-day! What a May meeting of these gentle, and loving, and tender preachers assembles together on that day! And how suggestive this thought of their holding a May meeting will seem to be, if we dwell on it and expand it! For have not they their missions to the heathen? In the dark lands they are part of God's witness, and God has left no shore without some of these quiet, eloquent little missionaries; you find them hard at work before you already, in even every land to which you may go. They have also their home missions, which they zealously and industriously fulfil; they preach in buildings and in the open air; they neglect no nook of the country, and here and there you are pretty sure of finding one or two of these additional curates labouring lovingly and sweetly, and giving

MAY-DAY.

149

real and effectual pastoral aid in the close and dark lanes of the crowded city. Sweet preachers, with so many tender, and cheering, and soothing, and loving lessons to impart, now God has interpreted to us those teachings!

I have a pleasant recollection of these lovely and loving May meetings, as taking place every year, on May the 1st, in the old home in which I was a boy. Let me recall them to my mind ere I even take my seat among the great congregation of my readers, to listen to the May-day sermon of the flowers.

There was a good space of gravel before the front door in that old home, entered upon through wide, dark gates, crested with eagles on the posts; entered upon, yet further in, through two old chestnut trees, that held arms, as though for the game of oranges and lemons, for all who passed through. Through these dark gates and up towards those chestnut trees, at an early hour of the morning, flitted sundry minute stragglers; now two or three with a garland; now a solitary waif, bearing a stick crested with a small bunch of cowslips, \&c. But all these were sternly bidden by our watchful and implacable servant to retire. For her orders were to direct all the candidates for pence to come, at a certain hour, together.

You should have seen them streaming in when that certain hour came. In clusters and in units, single spies and in battalions, bearing from the merest handful at the top of a stick to the largest and stateliest garland. Truly our front gravel walk was littered with limp cowslips, faded lilac, and dying hyacinths, for the rest of the day after the children had gone.

And then there was the dear Father in the dining-room, watching beamingly and genially from the window till the children should have all assembled, his pile of halfpence crammed into a brown holland bag, and possibly a fourpenny piece or two, or even a sixpence, lurking in his mind and pocket for any very extra large and noble garland. In they swarmed and in they straggled, until at last they were drawn up in front in a half-circle like a fallen rainbow. A fair sight: young bright faces and fresh spring flowers, both abundant and well matched. A fair sight, when we came out on to the steps under the porch,—the May meeting of the preacher flowers was complete, and heaps of delegates had flocked from the towns and cities, well as from the rural districts; I mean, of course, from the gardens, as well as from the woods and lanes. There were many speeches delivered (indeed, those left on the gravel kept preaching on to me, as they lay a-dying in their freshness and beauty); but since the sentiments were not expressed in words, I do not think that the young bright faces ever sobered into a listening seriousness, and only one or two of the elders heeded the silent eloquence. The children were chiefly concerned, I believe, with the exciting distribution of pence;

MAY-DAY.

Well, I have described the May meetings; it remains now to give a sample of the speeches or the sermon of the flowers, one suitable for the May.

'Wondrous truths, and manifold as wondrous,\
God hath written in the stars above;\
But not less in the bright flowerets under us\
Stands the revelation of His love.'

Let us take, then, the thought arising so naturally from the crowded thronging of the angel flowers out of the bare earth in this month of May—a thought also already in our mind from the Easter season which comes to us hand-in-hand with the May,—I mean the thought of the _Resurrection of the Body_. And it is important to dwell upon this truth (which, though the flowers could never have taught us, they yet come in sweetly to illustrate and confirm), because it is wonderful how in popular sermons, and popular religious books, and common conversation it becomes—unconsciously and for want of thought—slurred over, or ignored and left out altogether. And yet it is a doctrine full of comfort, full of beauty, full of truth. It is pre-eminently a _Christian_ doctrine, the doctrine which was inconceivable to the clever Greeks on Mars' Hill, though among them, no doubt, were those who held that doctrine of the _immortality of the soul_ which Plato had reasoned out so well before. 'But how are the dead raised up? and with what BODY do they come?' That was a question with them, an incredulous, wondering question, for a long time. And we all know how St. Paul answered it, by the simile of the small perishing grain, and the tall, fair new growth that sprang from the ruins of the old. _Resurrection_; that word alone, even, can of course mean nothing less than the resurrection of the _body_. For surely no Christian, at least, would doubt that the _soul_ is already alive, indeed, has never died.

And how much these preacher flowers have to say on the subject of the resurrection! It will be only difficult to compress their teaching into anything like limits, and to deal, in short space, on this fellowship of the Easter season with the time of May. I did not mention, just now, that I have actually heard a sermon in church preached by these preacher flowers—very innocently, and so simply, and sweetly, and unaffectedly, that the most stern advocate of entire plainness and simplicity would yet have listened graciously to their pleading, and have loved to see them where they were. For it was the custom, in a little secluded country parish that I knew, for all the school children, on Easter eve, to go out into the woods and lanes

MAY-DAY.

151

and fields, and to take toll at the cottage gardens, and thus to collect great quantities of flowers. Then they all laboured busily to tie them into little bunches,—hundreds of bunches; and then these were placed in many washing-tubs in an inch depth of water. All along the open sittings in the church, holes were drilled; into these, pegs were stuck, and so, on the Sunday morning, it was easy to fix on every peg its little bright bunch of flowers—chiefly yellow primroses—on the dark oak. And when you came into church on Easter morning, how sweet a sight awaited you! Lines crossing lines, and all of _risen_ flowers—not an evergreen admitted among them. So that the preachers were there already, and the whole church seemed to cry out, as you entered, “It is Easter day! Christ is risen from the dead! Look at our resurrection, and rejoice, O fleeting race of dying men!” The church was always crowded on that day, and there seemed something touching, and that stirred strong, though tender emotion, within the heart, as I rose to preach among the still congregation of the people, and the voiceful congregation of the flowers. I felt an unwillingness to disturb their silent eloquent sermon. I shrank from obtruding my weak utterances upon what I almost felt to be God’s own words, perfect, and simple, and sublime, the only thing on earth that seems untainted by the fall; born of earth, but so unstained by it as to seem to have come to us straight from heaven. Yes, the flowers seemed to me to be always God’s very words, and all I could do seemed to be just to endeavour to interpret them.

For how easy is it to imagine the earth in the winter-time to be one vast and bare and melancholy churchyard! Bulbs, and fibres, and all kinds of roots and seeds,—each lies, as it were, in its grave, brown, unattractive, and as though dead, seemingly indeed little else than the ground which closes it in. But the May has come, and the spring angel has called them; and lo! how the innumerable multitudes have started from their graves!—not dark and dull and earthy, as they lay in them, but transformed into angelic beauty, exquisitely lovely, endlessly various. Regard that rich spike of that dark hyacinth; compare with it the lilac, and with this the early rose, and with all these a million others as different, and each with its share, its degree of beauty. How astounding, how infinite the variety! how absolute the perfection! how surprising the transformation! how fraught are all these with sweet heavenly lessons!

Let us turn our thoughts now to the churchyard through which we passed to church—ay, to the whole face of the world, which is but one vast cemetery. The millions of bodies—among them the one or two that we love so much—lie dark, and changed, and mouldering, closed in by the earth, or become a part of it now. The soul is not dead—this we know,—but the body? shall we behold that again, that which was once so familiar to our eyes? Shall the naked soul

The written words of God have answered our question; and the blossoming words of God have for ever taken up the chorus, with their million million voices and tones. The body rises, it rises the same body, but oh, how different! As different as the tall golden sceptre of the wheat, or the drooping rain of the oat, or the tasselled, waving spike of the barley, from the brown rotting grain that was laid in the mould; as different as the tall angel-lily, or the “deep tulips dashed with fiery dew,” or the scarlet sword of the gladiolus, or the clustering white of the yellow-eyed narcissus,—as different as all these are from the sluggish, unpromising bulb. As different as the thick-petalled scented magnolia, or the fragrant white masses of the May, or the dim, faint depths of the crowded lilac, from the buried creeping fibres of the dark roots that spread underground. As different as the freaked gold of the rare-scented wallflower, or the “darling blue” of the speedwell, or the delicate diversity of the balsam, or the quilled precision of the aster,—as wonderfully different, I say, as are these from the little lifeless seeds that we lowered into the ground, crumbling the fine mould over them—earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust. The same, then, but oh, _how different!_

And we have the warrant of Holy Writ for this illustration. I am but trying to go on with the song of which St. Paul gave the keynote, in that famous 15th chapter of the 1st Corinthians. And, mind you, one little nugget of Bible-gold can be beaten out, oh, into miles of gold-leaf by the thoughtful mind and loving heart.

And notice,—The glory of the resurrection compared with our homeliness in this brief life, may be, indeed, well hinted to us by this comparison of the flower-angel that springs from the homely bulb, or seed, or bunch of fibres. But another thought, another head of this resurrection sermon of the preacher flowers, is suggested to us now. The _germ_ of that ethereal beauty, which bursts from the plain ground out of the bulb, _had already been placed_ in that bulb by its Maker _ere you laid it in the garden bed_. And now do you see? The _germ_ of the _heavenly beauty_ must have been, by God’s Spirit, placed in this poor earthly heart of ours before the perishing body was planted in God’s garden that surrounds His house; the germ, I say, must have been formed there, in this life of discipline, if ever a radiant shape of glory is to burst from the wintry earth when the great Easter-time and the great Spring-time come, for the last need that shall call them, hand in hand into this garden of God. There will be, alas! many and many a rotten bulb on that day; but, thank God, many a one also that through the long winter was not dead, but only sleeping. Ah! let us watch and pray, and use every means of grace, in order that God’s Spirit may be forming such a germ

To recur to the head of the different and infinitely various beauty in flowers. There are many lessons to be learnt from this. One,—How endless, infinite, inexhaustible, are God's thoughts of beauty! for these flowers, be it remembered, are but embodied thoughts of God's mind; and under the single head, 'FLOWERS,' in but one speck in His systems, how astounding the variety of exquisite ideas! Now go higher, and just peep, on the tiptoe of thought, at what may be included under the head—PLANETS. And go out into the warm May night, and look up at that gauze scarf of heaven, the Milky Way, and catch one far glimpse at the mighty marvels that may be classed under the awful head—SYSTEMS. And then go back into your small sphere of work again, and never fear but that there will be employment enough for the most active and untiring mind and body throughout the great Ages of Eternity.

Another lesson—How good God is to give us this variety of beauty! How kind! A little pale, monotonous blossom would have, no doubt, sufficed for mere _use_, in developing seeds and fruits. But our Father has provided not merely _necessaries_, but _luxuries_ even, for His fallen children. What a proof of His kindness! what an earnest, again, of the beauty and delight of the _unfallen_ world!

A third thought comes under the head of this _variety_ in the flowers—a thought that fits in well with the subject of their Easter sermon and May-day speeches. These infinitely diverse, yet always beautiful flowers will serve to explain to us how there can be degrees in heaven, and yet all be satisfied there. Ask you, How can one be said to be _perfectly_ happy if there is above him a yet higher degree of happiness to which he cannot attain? These flowers, I say, make it all clear to us. For is not the humble daisy perfect? and yet who would not say that the rose has a higher, nobler perfection?

We shall rise, all who fall asleep in Jesus—we shall rise like the flowers, each beautiful, each perfect _in his degree_. From the little green weed-flower, which _is_ yet a flower, to the speedwell, and the forget-me-not, and the daffodil, and the heart's-ease, and the chestnut bloom, and the garden flowers, and the hothouse flowers, there will be an infinite gradation and variety, but all will be in their degree perfect. There will be no jealousy, no discontent, and that for this very reason, that each has _its own perfection_. The gradation is not, I mean, from cankered rosebuds, up through more or less of imperfection, to the perfect rose; but the violet has attained to its own proper perfection, just as the lily has to hers; and the little celandine may gleam up brightly from the grass, all the more happy because above it opens the distinct and different beauty of the rose. Ay, even amongst the roses themselves how vast the variety! and among

This world, let us ever remember, is the nursery-ground. Here the gardener has us under His care. He has made us, He gives us all that we are, or can be. But He has made us plants with will and reason—according to our use of His care, according to our watchfulness and prayer, and use of means provided, shall our culture progress, and the next year, after death's winter—the year, I mean, of eternity—find us flowers for the meadows, or for the palace-rooms of heaven. And while yet in that nursery (we are taught on the best authority) the degenerate vine may develop into the good vine, the tares into wheat, under that husbandry, and the fig tree, long barren, blossom and bear at last; also, what was a mere wild, single flower may be by that Gardener developed into the rich, rare double blossom.

Earth is God's garden, then, under God's care; a garden of immortal beings as well as of perishing flowers; and the undying growth may learn much from the innocent, fair flowers that fall by its side. To the worldling they tell but of evanescence and failing hopes; to the earnest Christian they seem God's crowding promises, as they edge his path with their sorrowful, sweet eyes. Sorrowful, I say, or rather grave, for nothing lovely in this fallen world but makes us sad with a foreboding and a recollection of something that is not, but that was, and is, in a higher degree, to be yet. Just as we remember, in days of childhood, the sorrowful yet yearning eyes of a sister when we were in disgrace; so, I fancy, the angels and the flowers look upon this fallen world, that will not, though it might, be reconciled to its God.

Earth is God's garden, mostly under the winter of death. And what shall we say as to the resurrection of the bulbs and roots that rotted in the ground? for we did not pursue any analogy for them. Yet an analogy there is, ready to our hand, if not from the _flowers_, at any rate from vegetation. Ugly fungi and damp lichen and charnel mould are the loathsome growth that start up after the _first resurrection_ of the spring is over, and when the damp days of autumn have come: this is the only second life of the rotten, wasted bulbs. Sad, suggestive thought! But we will not dwell upon it, only hint it in a May-day paper.

And now, have we not had some profitable and eke loving speeches at this our May meeting of the preacher flowers? Have they not preached to us a sermon well fitted for the Easter season? Hear, then, its end. The loveliness of soul and body to which we look forward was purchased for us by our dear Lord. From Christ the germ must come here; from Christ must the perfection be derived hereafter. In Adam all die; in Christ must all be made alive. When

# THE HOLY LAND.

“THE East” is the one quarter in which the hopes and aspirations of the world centre. The Jew still gazes thitherward in expectation of his Messiah; the Moslem sees there the spot where all that was mortal will undergo judgment; and the Christian beholds there the fulfilment of prophecy, the solace for present trial, the assurance of future life.

Mr. Hepworth Dixon is one of the latest travellers who brings us news from that land which is the true link which binds this world to the next. In his “Holy Land,” a book full of the brightest word-pictures, broad speculation, and deep philosophy, we have his varied experiences of that quarter of the world where gods have clashed with gods, and where the mystery of the one God and one Lord was revealed to man.

Syria, the home of the chosen people, to whom was imparted the knowledge of the true God, has ever been “the prolific soil of creeds.” Mr. Dixon points out how Phœnicia lent her gods to Egypt, Egypt to Greece, and Greece to Rome, “so that when Venus and Jupiter returned to Galilee in the wake of Cæsar, they were only coming home to their parent soil.” The shores and valleys seem to teem with rival deities, as these are enumerated in an eloquent passage, in which the author observes that “the Jews, the Christians, and the Moslems trace back their faith to these Syrian shores, on which there has always been, as there is even now, an abounding nursery of religious creeds. In the days of Herod the Great as many deities sought for supremacy in Galilee as fight in the Lebanon now; Ashtoreth over the Sidonians, Molech over the Syrians, Isis over the Egyptians, Dagon over the Philistines, Manah over the Ishmaelites, Artemis over the Greeks, Jupiter over the Romans.” Mr. Dixon is of opinion, that if any man ever existed who could have fused these diverse peoples into one nation, making fellow-citizens of the Jew and the Greek, Herod the Great was the man. How he might have succeeded, but why he also failed, is shown in a brilliant portrait-character of a man who is masterly etched in a few words, as being “by birth an Arab, by profession a Jew, by necessity a Roman, and by culture and by choice a Greek.” The measure in which Herod was each of them, not by turns, but at once, is admirably well put. “An Arab as Napoleon was a Corsican; a Jew as Henri Quatre was a Catholic; a Roman as Mohammed Ali

Nevertheless—with all his art, all his ability, all his power, all his craft, cunning, and expedients, all his triumphs in war and in peace, all his pagan courtesy, all his orthodox zeal—Herod disappointed and alienated all parties. His political genius was not equal to the task of converting Syria into a nation on the principles of a cultured and a liberal Greek; and his personal life, as Mr. Dixon remarks, 'was such as to estrange from him the sympathies of all good and honest men.' After describing this personal life, and the darkest shades in the character of this lustful and cruel king, and depicting the shade with as much power as he paints the light and glory with beauty, such as only a master hand can give to the work, Mr. Dixon sums up the case between Herod and his accusers and defenders alike in these eloquent words:—'Genius, valour, courtesy, eloquence, and taste had come to nothing, to worse than nothing, in Herod's hands. He had crushed the nobles, but he had not raised the multitude. In fighting against the intolerant spirit of the Oral Law he had toiled to a noble end; but the means to that end were beyond his reach, and perhaps beyond his conception. The way to unite a crowd of hostile sects into one people is not by pandering to every passion and delusion in its turn, but by kindling in the whole body of rivals a new spiritual passion hot enough to consume the old. Herod provided games, rites, comedies, architecture, for a society too much corrupted ever to become a nation except by being born afresh. To become one in heart, Jew and Greek required, not old shows, but a new spiritual life. But this new life of the Spirit is a gift which kings and governors have not to give.' It seems to us impossible that a case so boundless in its bearings could be described, examined, and explained with more terseness, perspicuity, and truth than it is here by Mr. Dixon. It is strange that around the cradle of the blessed Prince of Peace there should be no peace; that in the once abiding-place of the chosen people there should be no distinct people; that when the old law and the new dispensation were proclaimed and enshrined, there should be no law, or what is the same, no observance of it. Tents and towers, convents and mosques, but no race, no people, no law. 'In the province of Galilee,' says our traveller, 'there are perhaps as many gods as in the time of Herod the Great.' Mr. Dixon looks out from the hill of Nazareth, and in that noble landscape counts the habitations of Christian, Jew, and Moslem, 'each sect as intolerant of the other as, in the apostolic times, an Arab was of a Greek, a Samaritan of a Jew.' Is there peace more to the North, where Druse assails Maronite, and Maronite repulses the Druse; and where, hated by both, dwells 'that sect of the Ansayreh, whose obscene rites no Frank has yet been suffered to see, and live.' Dixon marks, not without lamenting, the strife and division that prevail everywhere. 'Men who herd goats detest their brethren who till the ground, as if the quarrel of Cain and Abel had become an inheritance of the tent and field.' As of old, and foretold, every man's hand is raised against his brother. It is almost with a despairing tone that Mr. Dixon sums up the sad testimony by saying, 'The charities and affinities which, in Europe, soften men's hearts, are here unknown. Love of country and pride of race are phrases which convey no meaning to a Syrian ear. In Syria there are now no Syrians, nothing but hostile races and rival sects. The very name of Syria,' he adds, 'is unknown to the natives,' being the delusion of a Greek sailor, from whom it descended to the makers of books and maps.

Then, again, as God had a sacred name which no Jew dared pronounce, as Rome had an appellation different from that of Rome, which no religious and patriotic Roman would presume to utter in more than bated breath, scarcely a whisper, so there seems to have been a name for that holy place which the Greeks called 'Nazareth,' and which has not been delivered down, by tradition, to man. Yet, before the name of Nazareth was given to it, the village was there, between the sunny hill and bubbling fountain, and shepherds, craftsmen, and vine-dressers were in its street, its fields, and its synagogue; the place was, indeed, as humble as it was lovely; but it was to become one of the most remarkable places in the history of the world and of men. Yet, of what came to be called Nazareth, 'no poet, no ruler, no historian of Israel had ever yet taken note.' In the days of Rachel, in those of Ruth, ere there was tower on the hill, or camp had been pitched in the valley, no one could have surmised 'that one who would become dearer to the fancies of men than either Ruth or Rachel' would hallow it for ever. 'The magistrate of Siphoris,' as Mr. Dixon remarks, '_must_ have known the village name, but the hamlet was never mentioned by the Jewish scribes.' It is assuredly in the utmost degree remarkable that 'in the Bible, in the Talmud, in the writings of Josephus, we search in vain for any records of this sacred place.' The old inhabitants, husbandmen, and oil-pressers lived secluded in the lanes and in the fields about this hamlet, far away 'from the bright Greek cities and the busy Roman roads.' That Nazareth once possessed an Arabic or a Hebrew name we cannot doubt; but we are ignorant of that name, 'except,' as the author remarks, 'in its Hellenic form.'

picturesque ability. Herod the Great comes from his hands like a colossal statue from the hands of a sculptor; and the Syrian Pacha, or the shuffling Jew, stands before us, under his presentment, an almost living photograph. But the chief abiding-place of the Jew will excite the greatest interest.

The sanctity of Jerusalem is probably the prevailing sentiment with every pilgrim who gazes on it for the first time. It is a sanctity which men of very opposite faiths unite in acknowledging, for it is the shrine to which many opposite inspirations are directed. Actions committed at Jerusalem, according to Medjired Din, whether they be for good or evil, go for a thousand times the same actions committed in any other place. More hearts have beat tumultuously or throbbed deliciously, there has been more chastening tears or hysterical laughter, more impatiently tender gazing forward along the road that leads directly to the City of Cities, than along any other portion of the earth's broad way; and yet the vicinity is not touched by beauty. A winding road traverses the rocky limestone, and the waste and stones increase as the city is approached. A bramble in a cliff, an olive in a hollow, may salute the eyes now and again, but with that exception there is no vegetation deserving the name. 'Rock, white and blinding; rock, broken into fragments; rock, burnt into powder, stretches before you and behind. At length, when the long reach of water, twining gloriously rugged and picturesque round the base of cathedral, synagogue, and mosque, appears in sight, the eye clings fondly to the figure of a single palm, shooting gracefully up from a garden in the city, near the Jaffa gate; and on the right, in a deep, natural trough, to an olive plantation, in the midst of which nestles the Convent of the Cross. The aspect of the land is stern and desolate, and the great city itself seems to spring from the centre of a rolling plateau of stones and graves.'

It is scarcely necessary for us to say that the city of to-day, while it preserves many relics of the older cities that have occupied the same site, is, in its details and appearance, essentially different from them all. The fashion of kings rarely changes in the East; but Jerusalem has suffered mutation, for the spoiler has been there often, the Saviour but once.

The glories of the old city exist only in its memories. It is in itself desolate; and though its traditions survive, the scenes of their action are hotly disputed; the streets were always nameless, though the Bakers' quarter derived a name from the vocation carried on there. The Dolorous Way and the Street of David are born only of the tender remembrance or the affectionate pride of Christians. To the native race they are unknown. Yes; the desolation that was prophesied has descended on the most renowned of the cities of the East. Her streets are unpaved; the rock on which the city rests pierces here

THE HOLY LAND.

and there through the soil, as if it would fain split it into wider destruction. Fragments of the old glory only impede the path of the wayfarer, or serve to remind him of irrecoverable splendour and irretrievable ruin. Down each lane runs an open sewer, in which is every abomination, offensive to sense and menacing to life, festering and waiting for the tardy cleansing rains. Terrible remedies have sometimes been applied for the cure of terrible evils, arising from this horrible condition of the Holy City. More than once, when it has been choked with filth and threatened with pestilence, “the gates are said to have been opened in the night, for the hyenas to enter and devour the waste, a means of escape from the abomination which would be used more frequently, were the inhabitants not more terrified by the chance of a visit from the Adouan than by fear of the plague.”

But the highly picturesque springs from the deep destruction around, and the ruin and irregularity which present themselves at every turn. Artists and nature abhor straight lines, and there are none in the Holy City. Waving outlines, angles that are almost impossible, and broken surfaces, with the Greek glories of Herod mingled with the Saracenic glories of Saladin, are before him who gazes with a mixture of sorrow and admiration. In the vaults of a ruined palace the Arab plies some trade; in the cellars of a once great hall the Hebrew lazily follows some unprofitable vocation; coffee-house keepers establish themselves in the first floor of a house which is the crypt of a church; and braziers, barbers, corn-chandlers, and tanners divide the fallen Hospice of the Knights Templars with tenants who have converted other parts of the ruins, adjacent to the Holy Sepulchre, into baths and bazaars.

Much of the beauty that now exists, and some that lies scarred and in ruin, is not a relic of the Hebrew time. Mr. Dixon reminds his readers that “none of the beautiful towers and cupolas which adorn the modern city existed in the time of Annas. Jerusalem owes that beautiful feature, first to the Byzantines, next to the Saracens. A Hebrew roof was flat, having a screen of open tiles going round the ledge, at once to prevent children from falling off, and women from being seen. No belfry broke the sky-line; no minaret reared its graceful form into the air. The style of all Jewish building was tame and flat.” Yet it had magnificence of aspect, which may be ascribed, as Mr. Dixon suggests, with much probability, “mainly to its rocks, its ravines, and its walls, to the heaving ground on which it stood, to the splendour of Pilate’s palace on Mount Zion, and to the gold and marble of the temple front.”

The first church that was erected over the Holy Sepulchre was the work of Constantine. That and several of its successors were destroyed by Oriental sects or tyrants. For a thousand years the sepulchre and the church have been in the keeping of the Mahomedans, who hold Him, whose mortality there established the warrant of immortality, in higher respect than we are made to believe in our books of elementary instruction. 'By the disciples of this Arabian creed,' says Mr. Dixon, 'the Holy Sepulchre has been kept, on the whole, and with rare exceptions, open, free, and safe.'

There is much there, however, that will not edify a pilgrim, however ready he may be to yield to the influences of the place, and to the spirit which belongs to the vicinity and all within its limits. In the very doorway, a squad of Turkish soldiers are in possession of the church and its treasure. Some are on duty, some idling; none are acting unbecomingly, but there is much seeming unbecomingness in their very presence there, and there is still more in the condition of that over which they are supposed to keep watch and ward. Mr. Dixon says that in three or four days the pilgrim becomes reconciled to the Turkish guard, as a minor evil. 'A little experience of life in the Rotunda, as it may be seen from dawn to sunset,' suggests to the traveller's mind some explanation of this great mystery,—Why has Providence, in its wisdom, taken from our care the custody of our most sacred shrines? This tremendous question he thus discusses:—

'It is not because we are feeble. It is not because we are poor. It is not because we are distant and lukewarm. The masters of Delhi and Algiers might become the masters of Jerusalem in a single week, if it depended only on the assertion of physical power. But we are weak in the spiritual charities of brotherhood and forbearance. Among the crowds who gather in this porch, and worship under this dome, there are twenty rivals, and not two brothers. A pilgrim from one country believes the pilgrim from another country to be a heretic and a scoundrel, a deserter from the true Church, a denier of the true God. The monk of Mount Gareb scowls on the monk of Mount Zion as on a man who is hurrying to his bed of everlasting fire. What a Catholic peasant of Connemara thinks of a Presbyterian tradesman in Derry is something tolerant and fraternal compared with the bitterness of heart in which a Spanish padre speaks of a Greek, an Armenian pastor of a Copt. With each it is a shrug and a curse. Every friar in Jerusalem imagines that his Christian neighbour is damned beyond hope of mercy, being worse, far worse, than a knighted Moslem, an abandoned Jew. A Turk has no better light. A Jew has been cursed with a heart of stone; but what excuse can a Christian pastor imagine for a brother who has had his choice, and has wickedly selected an impure creed? . . . It is in this fierce spirit—a Galilean, not a Christian spirit—that we judge each other at the tomb of Christ. Greek meets Nestorian, Latin encounters Copt, on a spot which each professes to revere, asserting that his brother is not his

Hence, our only salutation is a scowl of hate, our worship is a scuffle, which requires the presence of negroes and Bashi-Bazouks to prevent it from degenerating into a daily fight.'

To those who have seen, in camp churches, how the Roman Catholic soldiers march out, and their Protestant comrades march in—how these are succeeded, perhaps preceded, by the Presbyterians, and how all things are done decently and in order, the following passages will not bring matter for pleasant comparison :—

'Each sect has a right to its turn of service before the shrine—a service of chants and candles, much clouding of incense, much blazing of flambeaux, much glamour of incantation in ancient and mystic tongues—making a scene as wild as the bronzed and picturesque men whom it appears to kindle into flame. The Copts, say, are standing before the shrine long before they have finished their service of sixty minutes, the Armenians have gathered in numbers round the choir, not to join in the prayers and genuflexions, but to hum profane airs, to hiss the Coptic priests, to jabber and jest and sneer at the morning prayer. The singers repay them in frowns and curses. As the hour draws nigh for these Copts to cease, the men who should be their brethren begin to rear and push, one side trying to remain a second of time beyond their right, the other side elbowing them away a second before they are bound to retire. To steal one moment from the false church is held to be a victory for the truth. Often these priests and worshippers come to blows; but on the very first cry of an attack—an affair of candles, crooks, and crucifixes—the Turkish guard is under arms and on the spot; and, unless blood has been drawn, in which case the church is cleared and locked up, the ferocious rivals are allowed to complete their hymns and prayers under the protection of a line of Moslem matchlocks. Each party in their struggle looks on the Turkish soldiers as its allies against the others; and it may be said, in plainer words, that among the Greek and Armenian Christians of Judea, many would not scruple to join the Dervishes and Fakeers in cutting every Latin throat in Jerusalem.'

These facts, as Mr. Dixon thinks, reply to the query, why Christians are not thought worthy of holding the guardianship of the one shrine of universal Christendom. The Moslem admits freely every one who desires to kneel and pray there. Mr. Dixon asks if there would be equal freedom under the guardianship of any single sect? 'Would the Russ divide his privilege of grace with a Frank? Would the Greek permit the Pope to kneel at his holy shrine? Would the Chaldean tolerate the presence of either an English Quaker or an American evangelical near the tomb? No one believes it, no one imagines it.' But what each would fain have for himself and co-believers, all might feel pride in maintaining, and all might joyfully contribute towards such maintenance. But what are the facts? The great dome over the Sepulchre, which should be, above all other domes, a work of marble and gold, 'is a wreck. The plaster is falling from the wall; the metal has been stolen from the roof; the paint has either been washed away by the rain or scorched away by the sun; and the showers of winter come rattling through the rents.

Any day, any hour, this magnificent tomb may be destroyed by its crumbling canopy of stone and lead.' This condition is a consequence, not of priestly jealousies, but of political feelings. The springs of these vices are traced by Mr. Dixon to European cabinets, each sovereign of which would fain hold the keys and lock out all but his own co-worshippers. The evangelist who lived long in the world after his Master had departed from it perhaps foresaw something of what would arise. He strove to obviate the consequences in the sole legacy which he bequeathed to the Christian world, in the imperishable but faintly heeded words, 'Little children, love one another.' Mr. Dixon sums up this great question by remarking that 'so long, perhaps, as we Christians have so little of Christianity as to forget that we are brothers, the guardianship of the Holy Sepulchre will be left with the more liberal and impartial Turk.'

Such is the Christian aspect, such the Christian prospect, in the land which we hold to be, above all others, holy. With regard to the Jewish aspect and prospect, these, too, do not tend to encouragement. The Jew waits and waits, folds his hands, eschews work, hates the outer world, lives on its alms, is never cheery or industrious, whether he be native born or sent hither from cheery and industrious climes. He is altogether a delusion and a snare to those excellent Christians in those very climes, who think to restore the Jews by sending them to Jerusalem, and supporting them there by alms which suffice to keep them idle. As for the Jew possessing the land on which he will not even work, it is slipping away from him into the possession of the busy, far-seeing, land-loving Greek. The Greek priors in the chief convents are the great barons of Palestine. The Latin monks are only exiles, some of them criminals, longing to get home again; but the Greeks are—some native, others willingly resident—ingratiating themselves with the people, learning the language, supple and insinuating, adding acre to acre, winning the respect of the Bedouins, and mastering the country and the people.

In Jerusalem, as in other parts of the Holy Land, the traditions which fix the scenes where events of great moment or of surpassing interest have occurred are for the most part exceedingly trustworthy. What Tischendorf calls 'demands on our faith' are, indeed, made upon the traveller long before his eyes reach the dim outline of the sacred city. Common, every-summer tourists will remember that at Loch, on the Rhine, there is a perpendicular rock; a panoplied knight is said to have ridden full tilt up the face of it. In proof of the fact they exhibit the saddle. So here in Jaffa. Travellers in the ancient days were told that Andromeda was bound to the rock, exposed to the mortal assault of a sea-dragon, and rescued by Perseus. The skeleton, or some portion of the skeleton of the monster was shown at Rome in support of the legend.

Mandeville turns the legend inside out, like the New Zealand version of Hero and Leander, and alludes to a rib, forty feet long, as that of an antediluvian giant who assaulted the daughter of Cepheus. Sir John also saw the marks of the rings by which the chains had been fastened to the rocks. Some persons have seen in this legend a perversion of the story of the deliverance of Jonah from the whale. But the whole fable is cleared up when we remember that Neptune in his rage drowned the country, that he sent the sea monster to which Andromeda was to be sacrificed, and that Perseus, who rescued her, came on the wings of a favouring wind. We read in these volumes that Jaffa is the most dangerous port in the world. 'A steamer may now and then stand off the town, a mile or more from the rocks, but she will only come thus near when the winds are low and the waters calm. A puff of storm from the west or south warns the sailors away from this perilous coast, and for week after week of bad weather the place is cut off from communication with the world.' Even in moderate weather to land at Jaffa savours of peril. 'As we near that wall of rock, one of the dirtiest bits of reef in the world, the crests of foam break high above its top, and cover it from our sight. Hot and blinding glares the sun; the slit is about twelve yards wide, and to miss it as we rode through the breakers in our tiny shell would be instant death.' The slit is the niche in which Andromeda was—in which Andromeda, Jaffa, still is—rock-bound. When the monster sea is shrieking and tossing at her there is danger, but when Perseus, on favouring air, advances and changes the monster itself into rock, that is, when the sea subsides and the rock is visible above the comparatively calm waters, Andromeda is 'safe,' and Jaffa accessible to all comers from over the ocean.

At Ramla the Mahomedan raises a demand on faith in the same way that Christian tradition establishes it. Under a column lie the forty faithful companions of the founder of Islam. Beneath a tower sleep the forty martyrs of Sebaste, who have given their name to that beneath which they sleep. Between Ramla and Jerusalem is the 'Latrûn' of the Franks, interpreted by Dr. Richardson the 'Den of Thieves.' Mr. Dixon, however, seems to accept the signification assigned by early Christian monks. 'The new name of Latrûn, completely superseding that of Modin, comes from Disma, the penitent thief, who is said to have been a bandit on this very road, lying in wait for merchants in the Bab-el-Wady, where, hiding behind rocks and pouncing upon unarmed men, he spoiled them of their goods, and sometimes took away their lives. By a habit of the language and the people such a hero was almost certain to give his name to the place in which he lived. Modin became Latrûn . . . as Kuryet-el-Enab, Village of Vines, has become in our own day Abu Gosh.' This is an excellent illustration of the vein of truth

Near Wady Aly is a square block which Mr. Dixon takes for a Crusader's fort, and the Arabs call 'Deir Eyub;' but 'why such a building should be called 'Job's Convent' there is not a soul to tell.'

It is otherwise with the pillar set above Rachel's grave near Bethlehem. The memorial stones, upwards of 3,000 years old, are still there, 'protected by Moslem piety, beneath a Saracenic dome, covering that which, in the eyes of every Jew, is the most sacred dust in the Holy Land.' It is otherwise with a far more important locality connected with ever-sunny and smiling Bethlehem, where many of the young men are, as David was, bright-haired and fair-complexioned, and where the young girls are full of innocence, beauty, and laughter, as if happiness and refinement were the possession of the Bethlehemite Christians for ever;—we allude to the place of the Nativity.

Protestant writers, without denying, have doubted the genuineness of all the so-called places. In the majority of cases the doubt has no foundation. Least of all, as Mr. Dixon shows, is there resting-place for scepticism with regard to the inn and stable where Christ was born. Around the Khan of Bethlehem the bands of Johanan raged during the ten days that Jeremiah was praying to the Lord. A khan, or inn, was one of those places sacred to hospitality, which might, indeed, fall into ruin, but the site of which was not likely to be ever occupied by a meaner edifice. The inn of Joseph and Mary was, therefore, that of Jeremiah; it had been the house of Chimham, and probably that of David and of Ruth. Tracing back, all this is presumable, at least; coming in the direction of our own era, what follows is undoubted.

The house of Chimham was known by his name five centuries after his death. The birthplace of Jesus was a holy legacy and memory to Christians; and an Oriental, like Justin Martyr, who knew the place, could find nothing but what was in agreement with the manners and customs of the country then, and are not opposed to them even now. In less than a century after Justin, the Empress Helena visited a site, the tradition connected with which could not have departed from memory; a knowledge of the site of the Khan of Bethlehem, the cave of the Nativity being still close to it, must have
