The wells, the springs, and the fountains, things that do not perish, or which, perishing, leave unmistakable traces of their being in all after times, have been great aids in the identification of many localities which, perhaps, could not have been ascertained but for the 'bearings' thus furnished.

To Capernaum, next, certainly, to Jerusalem, the mind turns with a certain fond interest; for Jesus loved that abiding-place before He came to denounce it as ungrateful. He dwelt in it for a season with four of His disciples, cured the possessed man, made the withered hand whole, and gave health to Peter's wife's mother and to the man shaken with palsy. His crowning miracle there was the raising of Jairus's daughter from the dead. Notwithstanding these miracles, there are no demands on our faith in localities here, since no localities are pointed out as the scene where they were enacted. This is to be accounted for by the fact that the city has ceased to exist, and men are at issue as to its very site. Mr. Dixon will be found to have set this question, as he has done that of the site of Cana, at rest; but we refer our readers to the text which discusses it in these volumes. We confine ourselves to the statement that the author is disposed to recognize the site of Caphar-na-Hum (Capernaum) in Tell Hum, a mound of ruins on the west bank of the lake of Gennesareth. But, with regard to the miracles performed there, no demand is made on our faith. There are bearings given by old writers, whereby man may reach Shiloh, Ebal, and Jacob's Well. The Eastern and Western Churches have preserved the memory of the sites of scriptural events; of the Annunciation, the Nativity, the Baptism, the Last Supper, the Agony in the Garden, of all the solemn events that followed, even to that of the Ascension, the site of which is the axis, so to speak, of the faith of all who believe in the resurrection through Christ. But these churches have left the memory of the scene where Christ made whole the centurion's servant, where dwelt the good nobleman whose son He had restored, and of the scene of other miracles we have previously recorded, to perish with the city. 'The churches are dumb;' and there is no other record of the scene of the miracles and sermons at Capernaum.

It is not quite the same at Nazareth; yet few are the demands there made on the traveller's faith. There is no tradition delivered to, or forced on the traveller, as to the synagogue, or the locality of the synagogue, in which Christ read the text, which _He_ explained as being applicable to Himself. 'No synagogue of the time of Christ is

Manners and customs have changed in so small a degree in these districts, that the life, morals, and buildings of a thousand or two thousand years ago are, with small modifications, those of the present hour. The biggest ruin in Bethany is said to be that of the house in which Lazarus lived and Jesus lodged. If it be not so, it is certainly the ruin of a house which resembled that of Lazarus, and the likeness of which may be seen around; for in Syria there is little mutation: as Abraham encamped and David built, so now do Arabs pitch the same tents and Pachas erect palaces. At table and in the mart, at home or in the field, all is done nearly in accordance with the old law of custom; 'a fact which renders the daily life of Palestine a continual illustration of the sacred text.' We collect from Mr. Dixon, that Esau still eats his pottage, but without selling his birthright for it; and that the sons of Rechab keep their lofty scorn of wine, planting, and living in houses. Job's plough is still at work, asses and kine tread the seed into the ground, the olives are shaken from the boughs as in Isaiah's time, the trees are grafted as in the days of St. Paul, and in the like old fashion does a Syrian build, and 'a Syrian house is a stone tent, just as the temple was a marble tent.' The _lewan_, or archway, in front of the Syrian house, is the old opening or doorway of the Arab tent. Beneath this lewan the whole family sleeps till the chill weather comes down upon the land, when the members of the household creep into one of the little rooms connected with the lewan, 'closing the doorway with a mat, just as their fathers closed the tabernacle entrance with a veil.' In such a house, many of which exist—and many might be built out of the ruins which encumber the ground—Lazarus was established, Mary and Martha lived, and 'Jesus, on His visits to the Holy City, lodged.'

If the house of Lazarus may not be indisputably identified, it is otherwise with the inn or khan where the good Samaritan sojourned and Jesus found shelter on the way between Jerusalem and Jericho. On the very spot where that khan would be established stands a pile of ruins, in which all the parts of a noble Syrian inn are easily traceable. The Arabs still find refuge in the wreck of courts, archway, and walls of Khan Houdjar; and there is a demand on our faith that is not to be gainsayed, when for this pile, halfway between Jerusalem and Jericho, we are told that this _must_ necessarily have been the Samaritan's inn. For the true interpretation of the word _Bethany_, we must refer our readers to some of the most interesting pages in Mr. Dixon's volumes.

Between the old Pacha and the new in this country the difference is extreme. The orthodox old chief knew that paradise was for him alone, since he alone professed the true faith. He did not mortify his senses here, and he looked forward for greater powers of enjoyment hereafter. He had a contempt for all Frank knowledge, a hatred for all Frank professors, a proud ignorance of and indifference for all Frank geography. He had occasionally a little passing curiosity in matters of Frank politics, scornfully admired, in spite of himself, Frank firearms, and with cheerful resignation quaffed champagne,—for the same reason that the Newgate ordinary drank punch, because it is a liquor nowhere spoken against in his Scripture. The old Pacha spoke no language but his own, wore no garments but those of the flowing fashion of his forefathers, for many generations, and carried no heart beneath them influenced by milder principles than those which encouraged him in brutality to woman and cruelty to man.

The new Pacha is altogether of a different quality. He has seen Paris and London; he has heard “La Gazza Ladra,” and has nodded to Mario. He is as familiar with French novels as with Eastern odalisques. He can read the English papers with more ease than he can the Arabic of the Koran. He is as tightly buttoned up as any well-clad Frank in Frangistan; and though he has not adopted our hideous head-pieces, he has discarded all that was graceful and useful in his own. In short, a modern Turkish Pacha, between the East and the West, is very like the legendary coffin of the prophet, which hangs between heaven and earth, without precisely belonging to either. He camps in the valley of Nazareth, but believes only in Mahomed; like Cabouli, Pacha of Said, who is poet, scholar, and soldier, “one of those new statesmen of Islam, who play whist and read papers, and aim at being good Moslems in faith and practice, while they are perfect Franks in culture and in speech.” Mr. Dixon can only call to mind three Englishmen who may be said to know more about Syria, Persia, and Arabia, than Cabouli knows about England, Germany, and France. These three are “Layard, Rawlinson, and Strangford.”

We think that, possibly, this list might be increased; but, generally speaking, we doubt if, in these later days, the Turk is not as well instructed in Western geography and history as an Englishman of corresponding rank is in the geography and history of the East. The well-bred Turk of the present century is not puzzled as to whether London be in England or England in London, and how both stand with regard to Ireland and Scotland, which he does not take for capital cities. He is conversant with maps and the instruction they convey. We do not know how it might be with any dozen educated young Turks questioned on British topography; but we

“Benighted heathens!” Nay, let us be modest, and more civil. Cabouli is not an exceptional individual. The habit of searching into the policy and manners of Western Europe is not confined to a few men of rank and genius in the Ottoman Empire. We are quite assured that Mr. Dixon is good authority for such an assertion. He asks if any man has ever seen a Pasha of Belgrade in the living flesh? Such a dignitary is as unlike the Pasha of other days as that Pasha was unlike his histrionic presentment in the opera which had the siege of Belgrade for a subject. Bright and shrewd intelligence, and a wary outlook into Western arts, are among the characteristics which Mr. Dixon detected in many a Turkish officer of inferior grade. As to pashas and begs, whom he encountered in Turkey, Syria, Egypt, and the Islands, the author’s testimony of them is, that in nearly every one, he found “a man of gentle manners, of fair information, of unfailing courtesy.” Nearly all could converse in French or English; some, in addition, had colloquial practice of Russian and German, and few were ignorant of Greek. All these languages, it is to be remembered, are foreign to them. They all knew Turkish, of course, “and most of them read Arabic and Persian, the languages of the Koran and Ferdousi.” Mr. Dixon asks, “Do the best men in our service beat them much?” We ask, “Do any similar number of men, in similar service in England, equal them?” It would be difficult to find a score or so of English colonels or generals who are royal lieutenants in distant British possessions, who, even if they could speak French without that _exasperating_ British accent which is so

afflicting to every well-tuned ear, are able, moreover, to make themselves understood in two or three other continental languages, and could read Hebrew and British-Saxon, the languages of the Bible and of Cædmon.

With all the changes which have come over the Turkish character, externally and internally, the swarthy Turk is not washed white. Mr. Dixon vouches for the fact that he “has not ceased to be plump and languid and poetical, to smoke overmuch, to love colour and pomp, to hold his head high in the world.” But, on the other hand, “he has pretty well ceased to buy slaves and eunuchs, to pride himself on his ignorance, to contemn the rest of mankind as infidels and dogs;” and he adds that “Cabouli Pasha is a Turk of this better school.” Such men are as the salt of a nation. It may be beyond their power to restore the nation to young life and vigour, but not beyond their ability to keep it from decay, death, and corruption.

Here we must close Mr. Dixon’s attractive volumes. They are far above being merely a book of travels. They tell the old story of the Holy Land on the spot. Under the shadow of Jerusalem the author explains past and present, and paints the probable future. This is so ably effected, that we seem to be rather accompanying the traveller and sharing his experiences, than perusing the details far away from the scene of action. There is, in short, not a class of readers to whom these volumes may not be heartily recommended.

# OUR NAVVIES.

It is gratifying to know that so much is being done in these days for the working people. The upper classes, as they are called, are interesting themselves in the lower. The old stupid barriers that separated betwixt the two are being broken down. It is not thought beneath the dignity of wealth and rank to be conscious of the existence of the poor and lowly: and the best in the land are striving to do their duty by their less fortunate and favoured brethren.

Among the honoured names of those who have done much for the social and spiritual amelioration of working men, that of Miss Marsh occupies a prominent and conspicuous place. In her deeply interesting little books, “English Hearts and English Hands,” and “Light for the Line,” she shows us how much can be achieved by patience and perseverance, by judgment and good sense. The roughest and most reckless of the race can be humanized and Christianized, and from the least promising fields for benevolent exertion, by the grace of God, the richest harvests may be reaped.

In the following little narrative of what has happened within my own experience, I desire to furnish my readers with an account of the efforts made by certain good people among a large number of railway navvies who have been living temporarily among them, the way they set to work, and the result of their labours. I need hardly say that they can confirm all that Miss Marsh and others like her have stated, and that the man or woman who works conscientiously and energetically, even among the most brutalized, shall be well repaid, and shall not “run in vain, neither labour in vain.”

In the spring of 1863, a railway was begun to be made in our neighbourhood—let us call it Lemorskiel, for the sake of distinction. About a hundred men, chiefly Irish, but with a sprinkling of English and Scotch, were imported and set to the works. These were subsequently increased to near three hundred, at which number they have remained, with little alteration, up to the completion of the line.

I need hardly say that their advent was not hailed with much delight. The quiet, steady old inhabitants were in a flutter of fear—“They are a terrible set,” they would say, “these wild navvies. They are utterly lawless. They care for neither God nor man. Shocking stories of what they will dare and do are abroad. We shall have an awful time of it. We shall be assaulted on the roads, rifled of our money, beaten, and perhaps killed. Our houses will be broken into

OUR NAVVIES.

on dark nights with crowbars and pickaxes, and our goods and chattels carried off before our eyes; while on 'pay-days' and red-letter days the whole neighbourhood will be disturbed with bacchanalian revelry, and men maddened with drink and ranging the country-side will make decent and honest people quake.' The letting loose among them of the inmates of Bedlam or Wombwell's menagerie would have been looked upon as the lesser evil of the two. 'What is to be done?' was the excited inquiry. 'How shall the lawless and turbulent spirits be kept in order? We must have a tremendous force of police to overawe them with the majesty of law. The great men at the head of affairs must be appealed to to bestir themselves, or none of us by day or night will be safe.'

All such fears turned out, I may say at once, to be perfectly groundless. Our navvies had no resemblance to wild beasts, either in outward ferocity of look or inward disposition and character. We found them in the long-run a good deal like other men, open to any good influences brought to bear on them, and wonderfully alive to kindness. In reference to the way of dealing with Irish navvies, to keep them in order, from molesting others or fighting among themselves, I would say, in passing, that the very worst that can be conceived is that of an overawing force of police. A sufficiently numerous force to do any good can never be obtained; and what were two or three among as many hundreds? In the case of a 'row' they would be utterly powerless. But let them muster in a mighty army, our rough friends are not in the least overawed by any number of stiff blue coats and queen-headed batons. So far, indeed, from that being so, the very sight of a policeman, or posse of policemen, irritates and excites them, and becomes the signal for a fierce and sanguinary onslaught. It is analogous to the presenting a red cloth to a turkey-cock or a bull. If you want to infuriate the turkey-cock or the bull, out with your red rag and wave it; if you want to infuriate an Irish navy, especially if he has been applying for a stimulus to the 'crather,' present before him a 'charlie.' He hates the very sight of him; not, by the way, that he is ever much troubled with the sight of that gallant officer, even when especially appointed to attend and supervise him. I rather think there is some truth in the widespread belief that when anything is actually required to be done, as in the case of a fight or a 'row,' the majesty of law, in the person of its supporters, is usually seen 'skedaddling' in the direction of dignified security, _i.e._, in a direction the very furthest removed from difficulty and danger. This being so, I should recommend the country to save its money, and limit its army of policemen;—among the class I have come to know, at least, there are better ways of establishing and maintaining order and peace.

With this view it fell to my lot to go among and make acquaintance with them, to ascertain what sort of persons they really were, and what arrangement would best suit them. Two things I soon discovered, first, that the great majority were not accustomed to go to any place of worship at all; and secondly, that they had no suitable clothes in which to do so if they were. I could not, therefore, ask or expect them to come to the parish church. Apart from their having no suitable dress in which to appear there, I do not think that the sort of preaching delivered in the hearing of the regular congregation assembling there—a congregation composed to a large extent of the upper classes,—would have been at all suitable or edifying for them. A very simple and familiar style of address is what they appreciate most and understand best—a style in which copious use is made of homely illustrations and narratives of events,—a style happily defined by a clerical friend as “pithy, pointed, plain.” But the want of becoming dress was an insuperable obstacle to their coming to the parish church. No doubt, “the rich and poor should meet together” there; and there is no more pleasant sight than to look round on a Sunday morning on such a congregation gathered indiscriminately from all ranks, and sitting without distinction side by side with each other in the house of prayer. Class distinction in God’s house and before the Supreme Majesty may well be laid aside and forgotten. In His eye there is neither rich nor poor, noble nor beggar, great nor small, but all are alike, on the same plane and platform. Still, as we all know, there is nothing about which persons in humble circumstances are more dainty than this—that they shall be like their neighbours when they go to church, well-dressed, as they say in Scotland, in “Sunday braws,” neat, tidy, and clean. And long may that feeling survive; it indicates a certain most becoming respect for God’s day and house. The worship of God, as it is addressed _to_ a Spirit, is to be conducted _in_ spirit, but external things are not to be overlooked. They may be, and often are, the outward indices of inward feeling, and the very garments men put upon their bodies become a sign of that better spiritual raiment which should clothe and adorn their souls.

But, in truth, our poor friends, with rare exceptions, seemed never to think of religion in any shape at all. Living a careless, wandering life, now here, now there, a month or two in one place, and again a month or two in another, with none to care for them, none the least interested in their welfare, either temporal or spiritual, they had got into a seared and utterly oblivious state about all religious concerns. Not half a dozen had Bibles; not half a dozen ever thought of saying a prayer. To them, in another sense than the

OUR NAVVIES.

We resolved, therefore, to erect a wooden building that should, in the first instance, answer the purpose of a chapel, in which to hold Sunday service. Afterwards it was used, as I shall explain, as a reading and lecture room on week-days, and for about nine months as an eating room, where, at a very cheap rate, a poor fellow could get a capital breakfast, dinner, and supper, well cooked and neatly served. In about a fortnight this erection was complete. It consisted of a rough shed formed of broad deal boards overlapping each other, and nailed tightly together. The roof was composed of common 'sarking,' covered with felt paper, well tarred and impervious to rain. It was supplied inside with one long table running down the centre, and a number of rough, strong forms, on which the men could sit. At one end there was a small platform, table, and chair, which did for preacher or lecturer, as the case might be. It could hold comfortably about 240. My Sunday service was held in the interval between the hours of divine service in the parish church. The first day, unfortunately, was a day of drenching rain and tempest; still there was a fair turn-out, considering all things—there were upwards of sixty present. Through the kindness of a certain Bible Society, I was able to make a present of a Bible to each navy then present, and to many others who afterwards attended the service. I may here say that I invariably took with me the beadle of the parish church, and a good singer to lead the music, that everything might be done 'decently and in order.' I likewise systematically preached in full canonicals, and always with as much care and preparation as though I were to address my regular congregation, in order that the poor fellows who had not clothes to come to church might not think that they were having in any respect an inferior service, as not worth anything better. I think clergymen cannot be too careful in these small matters. We are all influenced by little outside details, and the class of whom I am writing are sensitively alive to anything that savours of indifference or contempt. One rule I laid down at the first, and, except on one or two occasions, rigidly adhered to; that rule was to admit to my service none except such as were dressed in working clothes. The necessity of this rule was proved by the exceptional occasions to which I have referred. On these occasions some of the well-to-do people resident in the neighbourhood, anxious to see how the service was conducted, were foolishly admitted in their Sunday clothes, presenting a painful contrast to the poor fellows who had no dress but their every-day mud-soiled moleskins. It nearly ruined the whole undertaking. Going up one Sunday afternoon as usual to preach, I found but a very scant audience. There were a

OUR NAVVIES.

175

good many well-dressed persons present, but only two men in their working clothes. On inquiry I found that 'a feeling,' as they expressed it, had got abroad among them in reference to the admission of those who were better dressed than themselves, and, as they were ashamed to appear alongside such, they were going to keep away altogether. I hastened, of course, to remedy the evil. I thereafter rigidly excluded every person not dressed in working clothes, and in a few Sundays our numbers were as large as ever.

A very considerable proportion of the men were Irish and Roman Catholic, and of course would not attend the ministrations of a Protestant clergyman. Now and then a stray individual would come to my service with a companion, but as a class I could not get them to attend. I am glad to say, however, that their spiritual interests were not neglected, as a priest of their own church occasionally visited them, and used his influence for their good. Indeed, in his own way, this priest was a most useful fellow-labourer, and I did what I could to assist him in his work. Perhaps some may think that as a Protestant minister I went too far in this respect, for I gave him up my little chapel to hold service for his flock on Sunday mornings. Shortly after I had begun my own service he sent me a message through the contractor, desiring to know if he might have the use of it for that purpose. In spite of the grave looks of some, and the bigoted expostulations of others, I at once acceded to his request, my only stipulation being that his service should always be held at such an hour as not to interfere with mine, and with such an interval between that our respective congregations should not be brought into contact, either in meeting or dismissing. I know the horror people have of popery; I know the opinion they entertain of the priesthood; that the former is pernicious, root and branch, source and stream, centre and circumference; and the latter all designing and deceitful, devils in disguise, wolves in sheep's clothing. Whether such views be exaggerated and untrue, a libel and a caricature, I care not to inquire. I am a good Protestant and staunch supporter of the National Church, holding the Roman Catholic creed to be equally contrary to Scripture and to reason; but at the same time I hold that there are many excellent men, both among the laity and clergy of that deluded 'body,' that it is better to be a good papist than a bad Protestant; and that, notwithstanding all its errors and faults, a man may yet be saved in the bosom of the Church of Rome. Look at my position! I had tried to get the Irish navvies to come to my meeting, and they would not. Surely, then, it was better that they should have some spiritual superintendence than none; a priest whom they would respect and listen to than a minister whom they might respect, indeed, but would never listen to. When subsequently discussing the matter, one of my detractors assured me that the Roman

OUR NAVVIES.

Catholic priest would not have done the same by me and my congregation. Well, I cannot answer as to that; he might or might not; but whether or no, surely it was my duty to set an example of Christian kindness and liberality. Are we to do evil because others would do evil to us? I have yet to learn that this is the spirit of true Protestant Christianity. The priest was welcome, therefore, to the chapel, and he got it accordingly. To relieve anxiety on the part of the good people who fancy that all Romish priests are more or less diabolical, I may state that I have frequently seen our priest, and he had _no horns_!

When the summer had gone past, and the long, dark nights were beginning to set in, our next object was to supply the poor fellows with the means of rational enjoyment, and keep them away from the ensnaring allurements of the neighbouring taproom. Their 'bothies,' or places of lodging, were close and confined almost beyond belief, and the bright light and warmth, to say nothing of the alcoholic pleasures, of the 'tap' were too great to be resisted. Two things are unspeakably attractive to an Irish navvie; these are, abundance of light and abundance of heat. He luxuriates in just sitting in a room where there are lots of bright lamps and a good roaring fire. It is to him a terrestrial paradise. Add a little of the 'crather,' and he wants no more. How well the proprietors of our 'gin-palaces' understand this idiosyncrasy on the part of the frequenters of those 'hells!' See how they have them lit up with gold and paint, and all ablaze with countless lights from glittering crystal chandeliers. That glow and sparkle, they know, is worth to them hundreds of pounds a year. It appeals to the eye as never fatal syren voice to the ear, luring many a passer-by who but for that had gone untempted on his way.

Not forgetting these important facts, we turned our chapel on week-nights into a reading-room, and in order to make it as attractive as possible, we had it brightly lit up with photogene (not paraffine, which is abominable) lamps and a great blazing fire, at which you might have 'roasted a bullock.' This room was given in charge to a man whose duty it was to open it every evening at six and shut it at ten o'clock, and to keep the lamps always well trimmed and the fire piled with coals. But the warmth and light of the place were not the only attractions. The room was supplied with all the daily papers, books from the parish library, draft-boards, and the game of curling. Some kind friends sent also a large number of illustrated papers, which seemed to interest and amuse the men exceedingly. No liquor except water was allowed to be drunk, but the poor fellows were allowed to smoke their pipes and laugh and chat as much as they pleased. Nor did they fail to avail themselves of their privileges. Here, in one corner, you would see

OUR NAVVIES.

177

a knot of six or seven gathered round a comrade who, with more learning than themselves, was reading aloud to them the last news in the papers, or some interesting passage from a book. There, in another, sitting by the fire and puffing forth volumes of smoke, ten or a dozen others would be chatting and laughing pleasantly together, or listening to some 'traveller's tale' of heroic adventure which one of their number was relating, usually himself the centre-piece of the tale round which the glory clung. Elsewhere, seated at table, two and two, with corrugated brows, and many scratchings of the head, and fierce glaring at the boards, others might be seen in earnest rivalry, waging silent battles and winning bloodless victories, at drafts, or more noisily in the distance at the exciting game of in-door curling. It was altogether a pleasant sight to see, as, now with one thing and now another, the cheerful night wore on.

Once a week, every Friday evening, we organized a special entertainment for the men, consisting of readings, concerts, lectures with experiments, dissolving views, and the like. On these occasions the room was crowded, and the appreciation of the audience was demonstratively enthusiastic. Music had special charms for them, and we arranged that it should enter as a large element into all the entertainments. No entertainment would have been complete without several songs. Of these the comic and the sentimental seemed most in favour. No humour came amiss, and no sentiment could be too strong. Various ladies and gentlemen in the neighbourhood played and sung on these occasions, giving unfeigned delight to their auditors. But among themselves there were not a few who exhibited great powers, not only of singing, but acting and reciting, and who would have 'made a figure,' with a little cultivation, on the stage and in the concert-room. One man in particular exhibited quite a genius for comic singing. He was a fine, decent young fellow of about five-and-twenty, and, which is rare with one gifted with his peculiar talent and temperament, as steady and sober as a judge.

On these Friday nights I carefully abstained from mixing religion in any shape or form with the entertainment, beyond a single word now and then when opportunity offered, pointing out the baneful results of a reckless life, and the beneficial results of a thrifty and prudent one. There always appears to me a monstrous incongruity in any attempt—as evidenced in the sort of speeches too often indulged in by clergymen at those strange kind of meetings, called _soirées_, where tea and teaching are sought to be combined—to blend the sacred with the secular, what is funny with what is holy, the most solemn matters that can engage the mind with frivolous jesting and unseasonable mirth. There is a time for everything; and everything should be done in its fitting time and turn,

OUR NAVVIES.

“decently, and in order.” I know nothing that so shocks one’s sense of decorum, one’s idea of the fitness of things, as listening, as I have sometimes had the misfortune to do, to a reverend buffoon preaching and punning in the same breath, passing from grave to gay, from the mournful to the mirthful, from what should awe into silent reverence and holy dread into what provokes laughter and dissipates seriousness, without a moment’s interval, without a thought or care.

But I had another reason as well for my abstinence from religious teaching on such occasions. Had I not been scrupulous in this respect I should have shut out the poor Catholics from their enjoyment. Indeed, very early in the history of our undertaking I had a hint of this, after more had been said at one meeting on religious matters than I quite approved. Suspicion was created that, under cover of an attempt to amuse, we meant to proselytize. I soon put that right, however; I told them that if they wanted preaching they must come to my Sunday service, as on Friday nights we were simply going to provide for them something that should interest and amuse. Fun is a grand end—a grand _means_ to an end. I hold, with that sensible Scotch judge, in his manly address to the Social Science Congress at Edinburgh, that if men laughed more they would be better. The stupid old idea, that to be good men must be always grave, is not to be tolerated now. Let such a monstrous and miserable caricature of the requirements of our holy religion be put down at once and for ever.

And how did the undertaking succeed, it will be asked, as an antidote to the taproom, and a means of keeping the men straight? Why, simply beyond all expectation. Though we had living here, all through a dark winter, some three hundred of the roughest and generally most lawless class of the community—the wandering Arabs and Ishmaelites of civilization,—we have had no disturbance of any kind. No houses have been broken into; no property has been made away with; no attempt to injure or insult a single soul has been known. At any hour of the day or night you might pass along the roads without danger or remark; and as a lady, who saw much of them, truly said, if you went to have a look at the works, the men “behaved like perfect gentlemen.” They would touch their caps, and offer a rough but strong hand to help you across a plank or cutting, and were ever pleased with a kind word or salutation. But more than this, they were kept sober, wonderfully so, considering their habits and temptations, and the “tap” was all but beat off the field. They were the few and not the many who frequented its dangerous and degrading shades. When I think how our navvies conducted themselves before any efforts were made in our neighbourhood on their behalf, and how they conducted themselves after, the result is equally

OUR NAVVIES.

179

surprising and satisfactory. On the 'pay' preceding our efforts, I myself saw as many as a hundred drunken men, fighting, swearing, making night hideous on the public road. One month from that date, on the very next 'pay,' there was not a single drunken man to be seen in the whole neighbourhood, and the majority returned to their work again sober, decent, and steady. Of course, it was not all as it should be—it was not to be expected. It is to be confessed that although no men got drunk in our neighbourhood, some dozen or so, but only a dozen or so, went a few miles off to the surrounding villages, and exceeded there. But, after all, what was that compared with previous excesses? Out of three hundred men it was a small minority; and even in their case there shone out a certain sense of respect and regard for those who were interesting themselves on their behalf, in their retiring out of sight and going elsewhere when they were going to give themselves to drink. Nor was this an isolated instance of an exceptional 'pay.' The same good conduct was systematically observed at every succeeding 'pay.' Now and then, when strangers were imported, and before they had come under the humanizing influence brought to bear on the others, a small 'row' would occur, but such a thing was very exceptional, and was soon put down. The mass behaved themselves like rational and responsible men, and not like ruffians or brute beasts, as they commonly get the credit of doing.

Well, this, I think, was something. Are there any disappointed with the results? I know there are some who demand great things, and we may have been too content with small. I know also that there are those—I have had to stand the brunt of their questionings and the annoyance of their dissatisfaction,—who will apply a religious test, and inquire how many recognizable conversions have been effected; how many of our rough friends have been made Christians; how many can truly now be numbered among the disciples of our Lord. 'The kingdom of heaven cometh not with observation;' and I am not prepared to say, as I should not be warranted in saying, sitting in judgment on the consciences of my brethren, who are and who are not true followers of Christ. That lies betwixt a man and his Maker, and not betwixt a man and his minister. I humbly conceive that those who are always trumpeting conversions would act more wisely if they held their peace, and that that kind of arithmetic so much in vogue in some quarters, numbering the saints and balancing them against the sinners, is unspeakably objectionable and revolting, and flagrantly opposed to the whole scope and spirit of the word of God. Not long since I had occasion to visit, quite accidentally, a family of strangers. It consisted of three sour and ill-natured old spinsters. The conversation turned upon the clergy—'What do you think of So-and-so?' one of them asked. 'Well,' I said, 'I

believe, from all I hear, that he is a good man and a capital preacher.” “Yes; but is he a man of God?” was the next question. “I have no doubt he is,” I replied. “But has he ‘the root of the matter’ in him?” was further urged. These questions, which seemed to be stereotyped ones in the family, and were put with singular asperity and suspicion, were repeated with regard to three or four distinguished clergymen who would be ornaments to any church. I could stand it no longer. “Madam,” I said at last to the one who had just ceased speaking, “these are things with which neither you nor I have anything to do. I take it these men would not be what they are, nor do what they do, if they were not men of God, if they had not ‘the root of the matter’ in them. I cannot believe that they are vile shams and impostors, discharging duties that demand, that will only exist along with a true discipleship. Let us leave them alone, therefore, if you please, and look homewards and inwards on ourselves: have we ‘the root of the matter’ in us? That question is vastly more important to you and me than any of these others.” And so with our navvies. I cannot speak positively as to conversions. I trust and hope that not a few have turned to Christ for salvation, and are living under the influence of His blessed religion. “Man looketh on the outward appearance;” God only can, and God only has the right to look inward on the heart. Let us curb, therefore, an unholy, as it is a vain, curiosity. This only would I say, that if a steady and upright outward life is any index of a renewed and regenerated inward nature, we may entertain a good hope that on not a few of these rough and horny-handed labourers who have been working on our railway a blessed and saving change has passed.

In working out our scheme we had one or two special difficulties to overcome deserving of notice. First of all, the class of labourers on railways, those who are distinctively called _navvies_, _i. e._, persons not bred to a craft or trade, but fit only to wheel, and pick, and shovel, are as a rule strangely migratory and unsettled in their way of life. They don’t like to stay long in one place. Whenever they have made a little money by work, off they go elsewhere. They have no forecast or prudence about them. Such a thing as laying up for a rainy day is all but unknown among them. The moment they get money, it burns a hole in their pocket till it is spent. Amusement to them is what they call “going on the spree.” Hence, after every “pay,” more or fewer would leave the neighbourhood, go off to the large towns to enjoy themselves, and then beg their way through the country to some place where another job was to be had, probably a couple of hundred miles away. This, of course, involved the infusion of more or fewer strangers to take their place every month, and these, it is obvious to see, coming fresh and lawless among the others, produced no good effect. It requires a little time to make any

OUR NAVVIES.

181

impression. Men are not moulded and disciplined all at once. There was consequently always more or less a beginning at the beginning over and over again. When anything disorderly occurred, it was invariably done by some of the new hands, so that if we could only have kept the same men from first to last our work would have been easier and far more complete.

Again, it is impossible to conceive, unless you have been actually brought face to face with it, the all but brutalized condition of mind in which these poor fellows were sunk. No one seems, as a rule, to take the smallest interest in them. To be knocked about the world, here, there, everywhere, the recipients of more kicks than kindness, in too many cases they have sunk down to the position of mere beasts of burden, 'hewers of wood and drawers of water.' Nor is this all. Feeling themselves, if not cast off by the better classes, at least separated from them by a wide and bridgeless gulf, they harbour in their hearts no very friendly feelings towards them. Those, therefore, who desire to interest themselves on their behalf have great difficulties to contend against. Their very interest, new and unused, is viewed at first with suspicion. The poor neglected wretch, neglected so long, imagines you have some selfish motive in what you do, so that at the beginning one is apt to be repelled even in one's best intentions.

In conclusion, however, let me say this:—If you persevere you are sure to succeed. Let no one be down-hearted or despairing because baffled at the outset by unforeseen obstacles, or because the expected harvest does not speedily follow the careful and diligent sowing. Success in the end is certain. The roughest, sternest natures will thaw at last beneath the sunshine of true kindness. Make the most brutalized sensible that you have no interested or selfish motive actuating you,—that you desire to be their friend,—that it is with a view to ameliorate their condition that you have come among them, and though the night, the winter, last long, the dawn, the summer, will glow out at last. Their hearts will soften towards you. You will discover that they are not insensible to kindness. In respecting you they will come to respect themselves, and, by God's help, in a shorter time than you could have anticipated, you will see the fruits of your labours—you will see how much can be done where so little could be hoped.

Of course, it will cost some trouble, and constant trouble. But, then, what good or great work was ever accomplished without trouble? And how great soever it be, you will have many things to stimulate and cheer you on. You will have the consciousness of doing your duty, and the inward gratification _that_ never fails to yield. You will have the kind and liberal assistance of kind and liberal friends—for a scheme or effort that is really good only requires to be set before men to secure their hearty co-operation and help. # THROUGH THE FURNACE.

_Look the first._

MARTHA'S STORY.

## CHAPTER V.

### LAWRENCE ANNESLEY'S TRIAL.

We did not separate until four o'clock, when my cousin and his companions returned to the little village, where they had left Miss Annesley's pony carriage, while Sophy and I walked homewards across the grassy downs; but before we parted the Aylmers insisted upon our promising to dine at Colethorpe with my uncle on an early day.

Of course Sophy and I talked of our new acquaintance. We, who so rarely saw a strange face, had a great deal to say about these three faces—all rich in character and individuality.

'And how do you like Bernard's friend, Sophy?' I asked, when we had fully discussed the manners and dresses of the two ladies.

My sister smiled, and shrugged her shoulders with a careless gesture. I discovered afterwards that the tone which Lawrence Annesley took about himself was a tone that other people assumed almost unconsciously when they spoke of him—half contemptuous, half good-natured.

'I don't think any one could _dislike_ him,' answered Sophy; 'he has a way of talking that sounds almost wicked, but one sees at once that words have not the same value for him as for other people. And then, after being shocked, one begins to be amused by him. Yes, I really think I like him, Patty; he is so very good-tempered.'

'Good-looking too?'

'Yes, I suppose he is good-looking. But I think it is the expression of his face that is so agreeable;—such a bright, boyish look, and so full of variety.'

Ah me! a little shivering pain thrilled through my heart as my sister said this. 'So full of variety!' I knew now the secret of the shadowy likeness between those two faces,—it was the changeful expression, the want of earnestness, the lack of that one steady look which takes its light from within and not from without; the look of a man or woman who holds in himself or herself the power to

THROUGH THE FURNACE.

resolve, the strength to persevere, and needs no factitious force, no influence or help from without, to induce constancy and sustain effort. Imagine the difference between the face of a John Bunyan, who could write a 'Pilgrim's Progress' within the walls of his prison, and the face of a George Morland, painting in a sponging-house, and sending his pictures wet to the pawnbroker.

My uncle was pleased to hear of our day at Rixmount, and my sister, who had the sweetest pleading ways that ever beguiled a man to sacrifice his inclination to the pleasure of others, very speedily induced her darling uncle Geoffrey to appoint an early day for our dinner at Colethorpe.

'If you knew how fond they are of Bernard, I'm sure you'd wish to please them,' she said; and that last argument subdued my uncle.

I have no need to dwell upon our day at Colethorpe. It was very pleasant, as a first visit to a fine old house full of objects of art, and inhabited by agreeable people, is always likely to be. My sister was in very high spirits, pleased with everything she saw, and winning admiration of which she was as innocently unconscious as the Sir Peter Lely portraits which we looked at in the dining-room. My uncle was deeply moved by the affection for Bernard which Lawrence demonstrated in almost every word; and in the course of the evening Lady Annesley, who was, I thought, very superior to her husband in judgment and intellect, entered with my uncle into a serious discussion of her son's prospects. I heard nothing of this conversation, for all the younger members of the party were gathered round the piano. Laurence played exquisitely: now a scrap of a Beethoven sonata, now a fragment of Mozart, then an air of Rossini's, with a few brilliant variations, in the last of which he was sure to break down, and turn to us to declare, laughingly, that when a composer _will_ go off into seven flats and double arpeggios that look like fireworks, he can't be surprised if a fellow makes a mess of him.

Yes, we had a very pleasant evening. Sophy sang. She had a sweet soprano voice, silvery and clear as crystal,—a voice that sounded like dropping water in any little cadence which the timid singer ventured to attempt. But she was not a fine singer. She had the most delicious repertoire of old ballads, and I thought the Annesleys would never be tired of hearing her. My cousin Bernard sat near the piano, watching her and listening to her with an almost regretful look on his face. I could not help fancying that if such a feeling as envy could live for a moment in that noble heart, my cousin might feel the pang as he saw Lawrence Annesley's sympathy with Sophy's love of music, for this was the one missing link in the chain of union between Bernard and his affianced wife. was not artistic. No music moved him deeply, no splendour of colour, no grace of form thrilled him with the solemn wonder, the profound delight, which your true artist can feel in the faintest flush of rose-colour on the edge of a cloud, the commonest weed whose tendrils wind about a fallen column.

The result of my uncle's conversation with Lady Annesley was a decision in which Lawrence very readily acquiesced. He was to take a lodging at Sandycoast, and was to read steadily with Bernard before going back to Oxford to try for his degree. The rectory would be almost his home, my uncle said, and Bernard promised to be the severest taskmaster who ever made a drudge of his pupil.

'That's the sort of thing,' exclaimed Mr. Annesley, gaily; 'you can't be too hard upon me, Bernard. Wasn't it Coleridge who hired an Irish labourer to hold him tight when he wanted to go into a chemist's shop and buy opium? That's what _I_ want. If flogging wasn't a humiliating process when practised upon an individual of seven-and-twenty—unless he happens to be one of the defenders of his country,—I think a judicious application of the cane would be very efficacious in my case. _I'm_ ready to do anything in the world if anybody else will make me do it. I dare say there's motive power of some kind in me, if a superior being will have the goodness to set it going; but you can't ask me to be engine and driver at the same time. Did you ever hear of a horse winning the Derby without a jockey to ride him? or do you suppose Oliver Goldsmith would have finished the 'Vicar of Wakefield' if he hadn't owed money to his landlady?'

Lady Annesley put her hand softly on her son's shoulder,—

'But for _my_ sake, Lawrence! Are not my earnest wishes any inducement?'

'My dear mother,' returned the young man, eagerly, 'if you were starving I'd do a new translation of the 'Iliad,' and besiege the emporiums of the London publishers until I made some one buy it of me. But, you see, you're _not_ starving, and however low we may be in the world, we have not come to bread and water yet. When we _do_ come to bread and water, I'll show you what energy is.'

His mother smiled fondly at him. I think she was as much pleased with this nonsensical talk as if her son had been a Theodore Hook or a Sydney Smith. Perhaps this was Lawrence Annesley's chief misfortune. It was impossible for any one to be angry with him. Reproachful looks melted into smiles, stern remonstrances broke down into laughter, when Laurence was the subject of them. If life could have been nothing more than an innocent holiday, a village merry-making—simple, and genial, and bright, and natural, as the rustic festival in Mr. Frith's delicious picture,—who among the holiday-makers would have been gayer than Lawrence? But then life is not a holiday, and a man cannot live after his own fashion,

doing neither good nor harm to his fellow-creatures. If he does no good, it is terribly probable that he will do very great harm. We are not told that the tares were bad or poisonous in their nature; they were only useless weeds, beautiful, perhaps, as weeds so often are; but they were utterly intolerable to the Creator of an harmonious universe.

Lawrence Annesley drove over to Sandycoast with his two sisters for a grand inspection of certain lodgings, which had been selected by me as likely to suit the young man during his residence in our town. Bernard had returned to us by this time, and the Colethorpe party were to dine at the rectory, after the investigation of the apartments. What a merry day we had in the quiet old town, where there was so little material for gaiety! The vivacious brightness of Lawrence Annesley's nature needed no such material. There was no field so barren that he could not find flowers within its boundary. How shall I ever explain the influence which this young man exercised over almost every creature with whom he came in contact? Ah, rare gift of fascination! infinitely more irresistible than beauty, more subtle than intellectual power; wonderful attribute, which is born with the man who possesses it, and which no refinements of education can impart. I look back upon the story of the past, so plain and easy to read now that it lies all before me like an open book, and I see how precious a gift this power of fascination is to the man who holds it. I have read the stories of many men and women so gifted, and I fancy that this dangerous attribute never yet went along with high principles or incorruptible honour. But ah, how difficult to resist the enchantment! how impossible not to be dazzled by the glamour! I had selected three sets of apartments, any one of which I thought likely to suit Mr. Annesley, and we made a merry pilgrimage from one to the other. The rooms were all more or less low and dark, and more or less pervaded by strange beams and ghastly-looking hooks, to say nothing of abnormal cupboards; and there were more corners in some of the apartments than were consistent with any geometrical figure I had ever encountered in my study of the elements of Euclid; for Sandycoast is a very old town, and the quaint, low-roofed parlours, in which prim Puritan households assembled together in the days of the Long Parliament, are the same rooms which tradesmen's wives decorate to-day with starched muslin curtains, and fly-cages made of glass beads.

I could not be otherwise than pleased by Lawrence Annesley's manner to the simple women who were so anxious to secure him as a tenant. He was charmed with everything. The mysterious old cupboards, he said, were deliciously romantic, suggestive of innumerable ghastly and agreeable stories.

'I know all about _that_ cupboard,' he cried, pointing to a door

He can't do anything _less_ than three times, you know, because he is a ghost, and it's his nature to, as Dr. Watts observes; and then by this time I shall have plucked up my spirits, and I shall begin to question him politely; but he will rise from his chair, point to that hook in the beam up there, again three times, and melt away through the cupboard door. Of course after this I shall sit up for him, and by the time I have seen him three times familiarity will have bred contempt, and on the third occasion we shall make ourselves quite comfortable together, and he will tell me the story of his wrongs, ask me to avenge his murder, which I shall certainly do if convenient, and tell me where to find a hat-full of hidden money—rose nobles, no spade guineas I suppose,—which I shall most decidedly appropriate on the earliest opportunity.'

With another lodging Mr. Annesley declared himself enraptured, on the ground of the likeness which the low, dark little sitting-room bore to the cabin of a ship.

'One day I shall fancy myself Columbus sailing steadily over unknown seas towards the Western world. Another day I shall be Raleigh, brooding, dark and despondent, over a broken life,—the Golconda of my dreams fading further and further away from me as I roam this trackless ocean; while a stubborn, pig-headed tyrant, and death and ruin are waiting for me at home. Oh, I most decidedly _must_ live here.'

I was grieved to find that Mr. Annesley said this sort of thing to all my three candidates; and as I knew he could not occupy three lodgings at once, I felt that two expectant landladies must be inevitably disappointed. But I had little time for serious reflections upon any subject that day. Lawrence Annesley's vivacity was contagious, and perhaps our party was one of the gayest that had ever perambulated the narrow streets of Sandycoast. Mr. Lester and his daughter had been invited to meet the Annesleys, and our dinner went off as pleasantly as our morning excursion. My uncle sat very quietly at the head of his table, pleased with the pleasure of his guests. Lawrence and his sisters and the Lesters had so much to say about modern art and modern literature, things that were worth seeing or reading, and things that were utterly abominable and only to be looked at as amusing practical jokes in the way of painting or authorship—London sights and amusements, London people, popular concerts, fashionable flower-shows, that we simple country people were content to listen almost as reverentially as Mr. Primrose's daughters listened to the fine ladies from town. Lawrence fascinated the banker as he had fascinated the three landladies. His vivacity never approached impertinence; his fun might lapse into nonsense, but it never degenerated into buffoonery. There was a caressing softness in his manner, so reverential to superior age, so pleasantly familiar to inferior rank, and I scarcely wondered that he should be what he was—the spoiled pet of a household, the useless darling of a fond mother and admiring sisters.

He came to Sandycoast early in the following week, and established himself in the parlour, 'where the delightful pig-tailed phantom lived,' as he told Sophy and me. My uncle Geoffrey, himself the gentlest and quietest of men, was pleased with his son's rattle-brained friend. He would have opened his doors freely to welcome any friend of Bernard's choosing, however distasteful the choice might have been to himself; but he opened his heart to Lawrence Annesley, and before the first fortnight of his much talked-of 'coaching' came to a close, the baronet's son seemed to have taken his place amongst us as another son and another cousin. The common feeling which is so natural in these cases arose in all our minds, and we began to wonder how we had ever lived without him.

In the mean while the reading seemed to go on in real earnest. Bernard had a powerful influence over his friend, and Lawrence appeared tolerably resigned to his labours, but he confided all his troubles to Sophy and me; and he spent his evenings in the rectory drawing-room, playing to Sophy, or listening to Sophy's singing, or sitting at the centre table—a country rector's drawing-room was a very simple apartment in those days, and a table in the centre of it

He was always eager to do us some service or other, and he was always impetuously anxious to begin any task which bore no relation to the purpose of his life. He was like a man who, with every wish to reach a certain city, yet cannot be induced to walk straight upon the high road that leads to it, but will frisk away across the meadows, and lose himself in the woods, and waste more labour on climbing hills and scouring moorlands, for the sake of a sprig of heather or a trembling harebell, than would have served to carry him easily to his destination. I am sorry for him when I remember the talent he wasted on pencil sketches that our housemaid used to light the fire, and idly scribbled epigrams which had no meaning when the worthless incident that furnished the theme was twelve hours old.

Our evenings in that dear rectory drawing-room were very pleasant. Perhaps there is no one who enjoys a calmer peace than the woman who has put aside all hope of happiness, and who has wrestled with and vanquished the foul unbelieving spirit which men call despair. At this time I was very happy—happy in the love and confidence of an idolized sister, happy in the affectionate friendship of my cousin and my cousin's friends. Oh, how completely the old pain was lulled to rest! how entirely the old fever had worn itself out! The past was little more than a twelvemonth old, and I already could afford to look back and smile at its pale ghost. Yes, this was a happy pause in my life, and I shudder when I remember the day upon which the face of a new care first showed itself to me.

When did I first find my sister's confidence slipping away from me? When did I first see her eyelids droop under my gaze? When did I first find that there was one corner of her innocent mind into which I could not penetrate?

I think it was when the stubble-fields were still yellow in the autumn sunlight that I first saw something that was new to me in my sister's face. The happy light had not faded, but it was a very fitful light now,—even brighter than of old, perhaps, when it did shine, but oh, so transient! My darling had some secret cause for unhappiness. I questioned her one night, when, going up into her room to fetch a book, I found her standing alone by the window, with her forehead resting against the glass, looking out into the moonlit garden. I took her in my arms, and for the first time questioned her about the change which I had watched so anxiously. My darling hid her face upon my breast, and sobbed as if her heart was broken.

'My dearest Sophy, my own darling girl, what is this hidden grief?'

'No, no!' she exclaimed, eagerly, 'it is not grief. I am _not_

'But you used to be the gayest of the gay, Sophy,' I said, sadly. The cruel truth had begun to dawn upon me. A host of trifling incidents, so insignificant when considered separately, strung themselves together like a necklace of beads. I began to understand why in our little family party two people had changed so much of late. I began to understand how it was that Lawrence Annesley's vivacity had degenerated into a spasmodic kind of gaiety that came by fits and starts, and was broken by long intervals of melancholy; and why it was that my sister's silvery laughter no longer pealed a merry accompaniment to his boyish sallies. And my cousin Bernard loved her so dearly, with such a chivalrous confidence in her purity and truth, that to doubt her was an impossibility. For him there could be no pause between the perfect happiness of believing her true and the horror of knowing her to be false. No purgatory of doubt, but a sudden fall from heaven to hell. Had she never loved him, then? I asked myself. Surely if she had once loved him she must have loved him always. Was there any man upon earth who could steal a woman's heart away from Bernard Champion?

These thoughts were in my mind as I stood with my sister's slender figure folded in my arms, while I tried to soothe her agitation.

'Darling,' I said, 'there is no grief which cannot be conquered by Heaven's help. There is no sorrow which cannot be transformed into a blessing if we accept it meekly. No one ever yet went through this world without some encounter with pain and trouble. Remember this, darling, and believe me, however bitter your sorrow seems to you just now, you may live it down, and be able to look back upon it with a smile.'

She clung closer to me, and her sobs were less passionate now.

'Talk to me like that, Patty,' she cried; 'talk to me like that. Ah, if you knew how good I feel when you are talking! I think I am capable of holding to the right, but not by myself,—I am so weak and helpless. When I hear Bernard speak my soul seems to float up into some higher region, and I want to leave the world, and I could give up all my life to heaven; but when we come out of church I drop back to earth again, and I am only a helpless, unhappy creature.'

'My darling, you have so little cause to be unhappy.'

'Oh, not for my own sake,' she murmured, 'not for my own sake, but for—'

It needed no more than this to tell me the story which I had so nearly guessed already. Ah, well, the wisdom that comes too late is very useless; but I fancy now that I ought to have divined at the very first that these two bright young creatures could scarcely help loving each other, any more than two roses growing on the same stem can help meeting when the summer wind blows them together.

'My darling,' I said to my sister, as she looked up pleadingly in my face, 'with God's help I will try to save you from a great dishonour. You are Bernard's promised wife, and it would be a sorrowful thing if that promise should ever be broken.'

Sophy looked indignantly at me.

'You mean that, if I were not engaged to Bernard, Mr. Annesley would be a bad husband for me?' she asked.

'He could never be what Bernard will be to you. Oh, Sophy, Sophy, can you for a moment forget the parable we hear so often about the rock and the sand?'

'You think that Lawrence would be fickle?'

'Not fickle, perhaps, but unstable. Just now you called yourself helpless; believe me, Sophy, you were created to be the wife of such a man as Bernard. My darling, for pity's sake be true to him, and to yourself.'

Her transient anger had passed away; but oh, how much that anger had revealed! She was ready to humiliate herself to the very dust, but she rebelled against a disapproving word if it applied to _him_.

'I want you to help me, Patty,' she murmured, imploringly; 'I can do anything if you will help me.'

'And I will, dear, with all my heart and soul.'

'Bernard must never know.'

'He never shall.'

'Is—is he down-stairs?'

I knew by her timid, faltering tones that she meant Lawrence Annesley.

'He has been talking, then?'

It went to my heart, as the common phrase goes, to hear my sister talk like this. But it has been one of the errors of my life to be too self-reliant, and I fancied that if I took this matter in hand and went to work seriously, I could speedily bring things right. I had a plan of action formed in my head already, and in the mean time I affected to speak lightly of Lawrence Annesley's folly.

'My darling girl,' I said, 'if every pretty woman were to break her heart because one man is weak enough or dishonourable enough to fall in love with her after she is engaged to be married to another, the pretty women would almost all be heart-broken. What has happened to you is the commonest thing in the world, and you have only to hold steadfast in your faith to the man you love. Mr. Annesley's wounds will heal very speedily when he loses sight of my darling's sweet face. The sorrow that would kill Bernard would pass lightly over Laurence's sunshiny spirit. You won't come down-stairs again to-night, dear, I suppose? No, your eyes might look red. Go to bed, and rest. Don't call yourself helpless, my darling; Heaven will always help you to do right.'

She said that she would not go to bed just then, she would sit up reading until I returned to her. She followed me out into the corridor, and stood leaning against the ponderous, old-fashioned banisters at the head of the staircase. I guessed that she would stand there until Lawrence Annesley left the house, when she would be able to hear his voice in the hall below. I knew too well now that she had never loved Bernard, but I still hoped that she would learn to love him. Ah me! how sad to think that the rich treasure of this good man's love should only be a burden to her! But then I comforted myself with the thought of her youth.

'She is only a foolish child as yet,' I said to myself. 'She will love him and understand him by-and-bye.'

I went back to the drawing-room: my uncle Geoffrey and Bernard were playing backgammon at a little table near the fire; Lawrence Annesley was sitting at the centre table with a gold pencil-case in his hand, scribbling random dots and lines upon a sheet of note-paper. He looked up at me as I entered the room, and looked beyond me into the hall, as if expecting to see Sophy following me. I saw his look of disappointment as I shut the door, and though I was so angry and indignant with him, my heart bled for him just then: there was such a yearning tenderness in the hazel eyes, such a deep melancholy in the face that had once been so bright.

'Is your sister ill, Miss Champion?' he asked.

Bernard looked up from his game.

'Oh no, she has only a headache. But I advised her not to

Lawrence Annesley sighed, a very faint, half-suppressed sigh, that was heard by no one but myself. I could not help being sorry for him, just as one is sorry for a child to whose frivolous fancy all the happiness in the world seems concentrated in one beautiful toy. I did not set a higher value on his love than on the child's fancy, but I was sorry for him nevertheless. Once, and once only, I thought,—

'Ah, if Bernard had only chosen me for his wife, what a happiness it would have been for us to watch over and cherish these two bright, loving creatures!'

But then I remembered how indispensable the oak is to the fragile parasite mistletoe; and how that beautiful clinging ivy, which can climb to the topmost pinnacle of a cathedral tower, having the sturdy wall to cling to, left to itself can only grovel helplessly upon the ground. I remembered this as I knelt by my little bed that night and prayed for strength to help my sister to do right. But though I prayed so long and fervently, I know now that my sin was over-confidence in myself, and I fancy that this is a sin that plays a very important part in the story of all our lives. It seems so easy to do right, so almost impossible that we should do wrong, until the hour of trial comes, and we discover all at once what weak creatures we are.

I slept very little all through that night, and once in the stillness I heard my sister sobbing softly to herself. She did not know that I heard her, and I thought it better that she should not know.

'Ah, my poor darling,' I said to myself, 'you are fighting your first battle.'

I thought very much of the past few months as I lay awake that night. Was it strange that this unhappy love should have arisen between Lawrence and my sister? I looked back and saw how much we had been together; how much all Sophy's tastes and fancies, her talents and accomplishments, harmonized with his—how little with my cousin Bernard's more solid attributes and infinitely wider learning. I looked back and saw that my sister's promised husband had been her guide, instructor, friend, but never her companion. That sweet intimacy of association which constitutes perfect companionship can scarcely arise where there is no equality. The very qualities which raised my cousin above his plighted wife removed him further away from her. Esteem, affection, veneration, all these she could feel for the man whose nature seemed so nearly perfect; but my sister's heart had been won too surely by the boyish lover who had spent idle days wandering in the corn-fields, and blackberry-hunting

My sister went down-stairs with me the next morning, and knelt in her old place by my side during prayers. She was a little paler than usual, but very calm and self-possessed. She had promised to trust in my help with Lawrence, and to cling steadfastly to the right. There was no fear that Bernard's chivalrous trust in her would be shaken by any passing change in her manner; and I thought it much better that she should meet him, and even Lawrence Annesley, as usual, than that she should shut herself in her room to brood upon her foolish sorrow.

'What is it but a child's caprice,' I said to myself again and again,—'the airiest dream, which will have vanished away a week after Lawrence has left us?'

This was my hope. I counted on the speedy departure of Bernard's friend. _His_ friend could not be a dishonourable man, and it was to Lawrence Annesley's honour that I meant to appeal.

He came in soon after breakfast, looking oh so different from his old self! He came in just as Bernard was putting on his hat preparatory to starting on his daily rounds. I saw Lawrence's face through the open door, as I stood at the bookcase in the dining-room, and I heard them talking in the hall.

'You're looking fagged, my boy,' Bernard said, kindly. 'Well, well, that's only to be expected, for I've worked you very hard, and you've stuck to business nobly. There's no fear of the degree this time, and your mother will be proud of you yet.'

Lawrence did not respond very heartily to this hopeful speech.

'You're a good fellow, Bernard,' he muttered, 'and I wish to Heaven I were like you. But I'm an incongruous wretch in an incongruous world, and I feel sometimes as if the best thing my best friend could do for me would be to show me the quickest way out of it.'

'Lawrence!'

'Oh yes, I know it sounds horrible blasphemy! but do you think Simon Peter would have been sorry to lie down and make an end of it then and there when the cock crowed for the third time, and he remembered that he saw the Divine face looking at him with pensive reproachfulness? I suppose it's the common error of a weak nature to think death the speediest and easiest escape out of temptation and sin.'

Bernard looked at his friend's face with an earnest, questioning gaze.

'Lawrence! what is the matter?'

'Oh, nothing! I've heard that my great-grandmother, on my mother's side, died mad. The family failing crops up now and then. Dear old Bernard, go out, and, 'like the sun, your daily round of labour run.' I'll go into the study and do a morning's hard reading. I've stuck pretty closely to my work for the last few weeks, eh, dear boy?'

'Better than I ever knew you stick to anything.'

'Hard work is your only physic for a mind diseased. I can cry, 'Get thee behind me, Satan,' upon the threshold of yonder study; but it is not so easy to shut the door upon the fiend,—he has such a trick of creeping through key-holes. Dear Bernard, don't look at me so uneasily; I mean to work well and honestly to-day, and you shall have reason to approve of my labours.'

He went into the study and shut the door. Bernard left the house almost immediately, and half an hour afterwards my uncle also went out. Sophy was in the drawing-room sitting before the piano, practising, as she said, but the fingers very often strayed idly over the notes, while the pretty head drooped wearily. Oh, how sad, how pitiful it seems that there must be so much wasted love in this world! like the wonderful blossoms that flourish and fade in the trackless depths of South American forests, where no mortal eye can behold their brightness. But the eyes of the Immortal look down upon those forest flowers, and it may be that the angels have compassion upon sorrowful earthly loves. I loitered about the dining-room, dusting the bookshelves and the pretty knickknacks on the chimney-piece; and then, when I had quite made up my mind what I had to do and what I had to say, I went to the door of the study and knocked softly.

I waited, but there was no answer. I knocked again, and waited again, but there was still no answer, so I opened the door and went in. Lawrence Annesley was sitting with his back towards me as I entered the room. The table was piled ever so high with big volumes—some open, some shut. There was a Greek lexicon lying on the floor, and I saw the Hebrew characters in an open book by the young man's elbow; but he was leaning forward idly on his desk, sketching pen-and-ink heads upon a sheet of foolscap, and I saw that almost all the heads were profile likenesses of my sister.

He did not hear me even when I opened the door behind him. He was not aware of my presence until I called him by his name. When I did so, he rose hastily, pushed a sheet of blotting-paper across the wet pen-and-ink sketches, and turned to me with his old winning smile. He was pale one minute, and flushed the next; but in all his trouble and confusion the easy grace, the indefinable fascination of his manner, never deserted him.

'My dear Miss Champion, you—you startled me just a little, and you come upon me in the nick of time to discover what a pitiful wretch I am; but I _have_ been reading really hard this morning. Only, you see, when a fellow's thoughts wander, it's not much use for him to keep his eyes upon the page. If I were only like Bernard!—but then I might just as well wish I were eight feet high! My mother has made a mistake, Miss Champion, and I am not fit for the Church. I shall give up the struggle—a man who doesn't know when he is beaten must be a consummate idiot—and they must get me a commission in the line. I should think any kind of man would do for India. Put a calico helmet on his head, a sword in his hand, and a couple of pistols in his belt, and there he is. But to plant a poor, weak, unstable sinner in a pulpit, and bid him teach better men to be good, seems to be little short of an insult to Heaven. But I won't bore you, Miss Champion; you want something—a book, I suppose? Can I get you any particular volume?'

He put his foot on the little mahogany ladder as he spoke.

'No, thank you, Mr. Annesley; I did not come for a book. I want to speak to you, if you will let me, very seriously.'

I saw his frank smile change to a look of alarm; but he drew a chair towards the fire and asked me to be seated. I sat down, and then for the first time I felt how very difficult it was to approach the subject of which I wished to speak. I knew so little, I was so entirely in the dark as to what had transpired between Lawrence and my sister. Had he told her of his love and his unhappiness, or had she only guessed his secret? I had scrupulously avoided probing Sophy's wounds too deeply. I had more than one reason for this reticence; I did not wish to distress my darling, nor did I wish to make much of her trouble. I hoped that, by judicious management, this mountain of sorrow might be made to dwindle into the veriest molehill. But now that I wanted to speak to Lawrence Annesley, how was I to begin? While I sat trying to make up my mind on this point and staring absently at the fire—it was late autumn now, and the days were dull and chilly—Lawrence saved me all uncertainty by dashing impetuously into the subject of my trouble. Is it possible to be dishonourable and yet candid, false and yet frank? Surely many things are possible for a weak soul that is strongly tempted. I know that Lawrence Annesley did act falsely and dishonourably, but I believe the natural impulses of his mind leaned towards frankness and candour.

I told him—in broken words, for his passionate earnestness had affected me to tears,—I told him that I was truly sorry for him, that I trusted in his honour, and that by the help of that and the grace of Heaven, all things might be brought right.

He turned to me eagerly, with a faint glimmer of hope in his pallid face.

'Tell me what to do,' he cried, 'and I will do it, for her sake. Oh, Miss Champion, I have been so happy in this house, and so utterly miserable. It seems almost hard to believe that the same place can hold so much sorrow and so much joy; it seems difficult to understand how I can have lived through so much anguish, so much delight, within the few months that have gone by since I first saw your sister's face. Is it very wicked in me to love her? Am I very wicked because I have brown hair and brown eyes? I could change the colour of my hair and eyes quite as easily as I could avoid loving Sophia Champion. You will say I am base and dishonourable because I told her of my love. Was it _I_ who told her? Was there not something in me stronger than myself which _would_ speak that day when Sophy and I lost you in Boden Wood, and waited alone for you a quarter of an hour by the rustic gate that opens on the road? If we had not lost you I should not have spoken. If we had not waited alone for you, the irresistible temptation to speak might never have come upon me.'

He had told her, then! I tried to tell him how base he had been, but the words would not come. I was so sorry for him. Presently he went on again—impetuously, passionately. He was walking up and down the room as he spoke.

'She had seen the change in me, though Heaven knows I had tried hard to be a callous, noisy wretch, what Oliver Goldsmith calls an agreeable rattle.
