she looked at me? Shall I ever forget the tender mournfulness of her voice as she asked me if there was not some hidden trouble weighing on my mind? And then the demon took possession of me, and I told her all the miserable truth,—told her that I loved her with all the strength of a weak man's passionate heart; told her that, in defiance of honour, with base treason against friendship, I loved her, and must continue to love her until the day of my death.'

'And she heard you to the end?'

'She could not do less than hear me; for the torrent, once set free, rushed on too fast for hindrance. Her face was turned from me. If it were her nature to be angry, she would have been angry with me, I have no doubt. I knew how despicable I must seem to her. But she is the living spirit of pity and tenderness. She was silent while I spoke; and before she could reprove me you joined us, and all was over. The sin had been sinned. But I am not quite a hardened reprobate; so shame and repentance followed close upon the heels of guilt.'

As he stood before me speaking thus, with his hair thrown loosely from his forehead, his eyes sparkling with a feverish light, the awful question of man's responsibility arose in my mind. To what degree was this man accountable, this man in whose nature there seemed some inherent weakness? But then I remembered the sacred promise that, with _every_ temptation, however hard, however bitter, shall be given a way of escape. The strong man may wrestle with Satan, and hold his ground as conqueror of the field; and the man who is too weak for the contest may flee to a fortress, beneath whose holy shelter the fiend dare not pursue him.

'Dear Mr. Annesley,' I said, 'to my mind your proper course seems so very plain. Your presence in this house, in this place, is a treason against Bernard, and can only distress my sister. If you leave Sandycoast—'

'Leave her, never to see her again, or only to see her when she is Bernard's wife! Oh, Miss Champion! I am a selfish and wicked creature. I wish to Heaven I could die before your sister's wedding day.'

He covered his face with his hands, and burst into tears. For the first time in my life I saw that most cruel spectacle, a man weeping. To us, tears seem so natural that they are almost sweet; but to _them_ how bitter! What a wide distance between Mary Magdalene, raining penitent tears upon her Master's feet, and the drops of blood which He shed in the garden of Gethsemane!

I tried to comfort Lawrence Annesley, and, poorly as I pleaded the cause of right, I won from him a promise that he would leave Sandycoast immediately. His habits had always been more or less erratic,

'And you will start at once—to-day?'

I was nervously anxious that his departure should take place immediately, for I saw that he had no idea of the real state of my foolish darling's heart. I did not want him to discover what I knew too well. I did not want him to know that his fatal love had found an echo in my sister's breast.

'To-day,' he said, piteously; 'you are very hard upon me, Miss Champion. Oh yes!' he added, in answer to my look, 'I know you are acting for the best, but the best _is_ very hard sometimes. Well, I'll go to-day, since it must be so. What is it the poet says? 'Better to die by sudden shock!' I have been mouldering 'piece-meal on the rock' for the last month or two. Two months! my love is only two months old. Two little months seem to hold all the history of my life. And I have wondered at a young mother's anguish for the death of a two months old baby! It seems so small a thing to lose a treasure we have held for so brief a span. Yes, I will go to-day; but I must see her, Miss Champion. You will let me see your sister before I go? In your presence, of course. I only want to hold her hand in mine just long enough to say, 'God bless you, and good-bye.' You can't refuse me as much as that.'

Could I refuse him so small a favour, when he had promised to obey me? I pointed to his desk.

'Will you write a letter to Bernard,' I said, 'announcing this sudden change in your plans, or will you wait to see him? He spoke of going some distance to-day, and I don't think he will be home until dinner-time. If you could avoid seeing him it might be better, perhaps.'

'Infinitely better. I can't look him in the face. Those calm gray eyes of his torture me with their earnest truthfulness. Yes, it will be much better for me to go at once. I will run back to my lodgings, pack a portmanteau, and leave Sandycoast by the London coach: it passes through the town at a quarter to three. And now take me to your sister. When a man is going to be hanged, his gaolers generally give him whatever he pleases to eat for his last breakfast. I have bowed my head before the justice of your sentence, Miss Champion, and I am going very meekly to my execution. Be as pitiful to me as the warders are to the poor condemned wretch in Newgate. Let me see your sister. Let me have one little word from Sophy's lips to sweeten the bitterness of my doom.'

Sophy had left the piano, and was standing by one of the windows, looking out at the falling leaves drifting in the autumn wind, as hopelessly and despondently as I had seen her look out upon the cold moonlight and the black shadows of the swaying branches on the grass.

She started at the sound of our footsteps, and looked round. The pale face flushed and then grew pale again. Her lips faltered a faint 'Good morning, Mr. Annesley,' and then she turned to the piano, and began nervously shifting the loose music that lay scattered upon it.

'I have come to wish you good-bye, Miss Sophy,' Lawrence said, going straight up to her; 'you will shake hands before I go, won't you? And if I made a fool or a brute of myself the other day, you will try to forgive me, I hope. You will find it very easy to forget me.'

I felt how foolishly my sanction had been granted for such an interview as this. My sister looked at Lawrence Annesley with a piteous, half-bewildered expression.

'You are going,' she murmured, 'you are going so soon? To-day?—Oh, Patty, is it true?'

She turned to me to-day as she had turned to me always in the little troubles of her childhood—the transient vexations of her happy girlhood,—and to-day I could give her neither help nor comfort.

'Yes, Miss Sophy, I am going away,' Lawrence answered, with a defiant recklessness which was the poorest sham that ever disguised passionate sorrow. 'When a fellow finds that he is unfitted for one career, he had better try another. Holy mother Church will acknowledge no such reprobate son as I; but mother Country is a liberal matron, and she cares very little what vagabonds she takes to her gory arms. When you hear of me next, Miss Sophy, I hope it will be at the head of a Sepoy regiment; and if you ever hear of me after that, God grant it may be in the list of the killed.'

And this was how he kept his promise to me.

'Mr. Annesley—'

Before I could utter the indignant protest that rose to my lips I was interrupted by my sister's despairing cry.

'Oh, Lawrence, Lawrence, you are breaking my heart!'

In the next moment he was on his knees at her feet, covering her trembling hands with his passionate kisses. 'My darling, my own dearest girl, if I thought that my wretched life could have a feather's weight in your mind, I could endure a thousand years of the weariest existence that ever a hopeless wretch dragged miserably to its joyless close. Oh, Sophy, Sophy, I love you so dearly, and I hate myself so

My sister looked at me. O, tender blue eyes, so unspeakably sad, so piteously entreating, shall I ever live long enough to forget that look? Can I comfort myself, remembering the sorrow that came of that day's work, by the knowledge that I did what I thought was best?

'It is very good of you to say that, Lawrence,' Sophy began presently. She had been crying, but had dried her tears, and spoke in a low, steady voice, that was sorrowfully earnest in its tone. 'I am sorry that any unhappiness should have come out of our friendship, but I know and feel that it is best for you to go away. Bernard is so good, and my uncle; I owe them both so much, that to break my promise, or to be forgetful of their love, would be a sin that Heaven would punish in me, and that could only bring remorse and sorrow upon you. But oh, Mr. Annesley, if my wishes really have any weight with you, I entreat you not to abandon your intention of entering the Church. I heard Lady Annesley speak to you about that subject, and it seems very foolish of me to ask what your mother has already asked you.'

'I will do anything for your sake.'

'Patty,' cried my sister, 'tell him what he ought to do.'

'Let him remember that Bernard Champion is his best and truest friend,' I answered.

'She is right,' cried Lawrence, 'she is right, and you are an angel. Good-bye, and God bless you. I think that was what I promised to say, Miss Champion.'

He wrung my hand, and in the next moment the door closed upon him. And then there came the resonant bang of the outer door, and we knew that he had left us.

Sophy threw herself sobbing into my arms.

'Oh, Patty, I love him so dearly—so dearly.'

## CHAPTER VI.

### THE EVE OF THE WEDDING.

AFTER Lawrence Annesley left us all was very quiet in our dear old home—a happy home, as it seemed, for Bernard's trusting love made a sunshine of its own; and if my sister's manner had lost its girlish buoyancy, its almost childish gaiety, those who loved her best recognized an improvement in the change which elevated the light-hearted

girl into the thoughtful woman. I alone knew the secret of this transformation. I alone knew that the thoughtful shadow on my sister's face had been cast by the dark storm-cloud of a first sorrow. Yes, her first sorrow. Her life till Laurence Annesley's coming had been all happiness. I pitied her so much when I remembered this, and how ill-fitted she was to sustain the burden of a hidden grief. She was very gentle, very patient; but I knew that she suffered. The sweet confidence of sisterhood which had so long united us perished in the hour of Laurence Annesley's departure. I think she would have been glad to talk to me of him, and of her trouble, but I gave her no opportunity of approaching the subject. I have fancied sometimes that the name she loved was hovering on her lips, and that something in my face chilled her trusting heart, and kept her silent.

My sin lay in this foolish confidence in my own power to set things right. How much wiser it would have been to let my darling speak! how much wiser to have told Bernard Champion the bitter truth that my sister's heart had never been his! It would have been the TRUTH; and I know now that the bitterest truth is infinitely better than the sweetest falsehood. I was very foolish. My love for my cousin was only a poor helpless woman's love, after all. I was like a mother who has not the courage to give her idolized child the one medicine which can cure his malady, because the draught is nauseous. My mind often wavered. I have sometimes shaped the very words that should announce to Bernard the ship-wreck of his hopes; but one deeply tender look in my cousin's eyes, as he watched Sophy sitting at her work in the lamplight; one low tone of his voice, softening so unconsciously as he spoke to her, would change the whole current of my thought, and I could not strike the blow which must shatter the fairy edifice of his dreams.

I knew the heroic element in my cousin's nature, and I felt very certain that if he had been aware that Sophy's heart had never been his, if he had fancied that her happiness was involved in a release from her engagement to him, he would have set her free without a murmur, and would have trodden onward, serene and unflinching, upon the path which he had elected to tread, leaving all the flowers that had adorned it far behind him: broken-hearted, it might be, but not broken-spirited.

Knowing this, and blindly trusting in my own judgment, I set my face resolutely against any allusion to the past. To me Bernard Champion seemed the grandest and noblest of mankind, and I believed that my sister must eventually learn to love him as he deserved to be loved. I fancied her his happy wife, looking back with a smile to the brief fancy of her foolish girlhood, the transient dream in which Laurence Annesley's image occupied the chief place. I could not

think that this weak and unstable Lawrence had, in a few months, inspired an affection that could endure against the devotion of such a man as my cousin, and I was very proud when I thought how my diplomacy had secured the retreat of Bernard's rival and the future happiness of my sister. I did not know that diplomacy never yet achieved any success which might not have been better won by unflinching truthfulness. I had gone to work like a surgeon, who tries by the use of medicines to effect a cure which can only be accomplished thoroughly by the knife; and I discovered very speedily the shallowness of my fancied wisdom. Lawrence Annesley's sudden departure had caused little sensation in our household.

'I am very sorry,' Bernard said, after reading the letter which his friend had left, 'I am deeply and truly sorry, but I am not surprised. Perhaps it is better so. The army rejects a recruit whose limbs are feeble, or whose lungs are unsound; but the church militant has received soldiers as little fitted for the holy fight as a poor maimed creature, limping between crutches, is to be the captain of a grenadier regiment.'

The days drifted slowly by us. The last leaves fell in our sheltered garden, above which quaint gabled roofs and ivy-covered chimneys loomed dark against the autumn sky. How often I have watched my sister Sophy pacing up and down in the shadow of the garden wall, with the withered leaves blowing round her as she walked! There was no confidence between us now. At first she had seemed anxious to talk to me of Lawrence Annesley, but little by little the frank simplicity of her girlhood vanished quite away, and she was a woman now, with a woman's power to guard the secrets of her heart.

Sometimes I was pleased to think of the change, believing that it was the beginning of a new phase in my darling's life, and that the grave stillness of her manner was only the serious thoughtfulness which was suitable to a woman who was to be Bernard Champion's wife. Sometimes a cold chill crept through my heart, and I would have given, ah! so much, to have my sister sitting at my feet in our favourite window, with a heap of open books scattered round her, and her bright childish face looking up at me out of a mass of tumbled hair. And in the meanwhile our quiet life crept on until it was Christmas-time once more, and Bernard and Sophy had been engaged exactly a year. My uncle was the first to talk about the marriage. The bishop of the diocese had been always his warm friend, and many rumours of Bernard's very unusual talents had reached him within the last year; thus it was expected that my cousin would very speedily exchange his curacy at Sandycoast for a wider field of action.

'The change may come when we least expect it,' said my uncle,

“and I want Bernard to carry a wife away with him when he leaves his father’s house. Patty and I can get on very well by ourselves. There are silly people who think May marriages unlucky. I suppose we must defer to the popular prejudice, and marry our young couple in April.”

This is how it was settled. Sophy made no attempt to oppose my uncle’s decision. Bernard had consulted his father’s pleasure in this important matter with a reverential tenderness.

“If my happiness alone had been concerned, I should have tried to carry my bride away with me last April instead of next April,” he said to Sophy by-and-bye, when my uncle Geoffrey had left the room, “but the state of my father’s health hindered me from taking any step that might distress him. I was loath to hasten any breaking up of the old home. Our marriage has been the favourite scheme of his life, darling, and I wanted the planning of it to be entirely his own. I shall take my young wife from my father’s hands next April, as I took her from him thirteen years ago, when she was a sleepy little girl, worn out by a long journey, and disinclined to be tormented by the demonstrative affection of an overgrown schoolboy.”

My sister looked up at her lover with a sweet earnestness in her eyes.

“I will try to be a good wife, Bernard,” she said, very gently; “I will try to be worthy of your love and confidence. If it were only for my uncle Geoffrey’s sake, I——”

Whatever words she had meant to speak died away upon her lips, and she burst into tears. I knew that in all her life she had never been more truthful than at that moment. I fancied that the good cause had triumphed, and that Lawrence Annesley was forgotten. I left the lovers alone in the winter twilight, sitting by the same hearth before which Sophy had told me what Bernard had said to her in St. Augustine’s Church exactly a year ago. How I smiled, remembering my own folly, and the anguish in my heart, as I listened to my darling’s confession! and yet how sharply the old pain came back to me even while I smiled! But the battle had been fought and the victory won, and I was now really and truly what Bernard had once called me, his “sisterly cousin.” cousin.'

I was very happy for some time after this, very confident in the happiness of the future. Only one thing disturbed the serenity of my mind, and that was my sister’s reserve. The old trustfulness, that childish candour, were quite gone. Do what I would, I could not win my darling to talk of her future life. Whenever I approached that subject she answered me in almost the same words—the words she had spoken to Bernard on the day I have been writing about. She would try to be a good wife, she told me; she hoped to make her cousin happy. Her dearest wish was that she might be truly worthy of her uncle Geoffrey’s love.

All that was frivolous in her nature seemed to have vanished with the childish gaiety which had once made her bewitching. She was more serious now than I, who had once seemed twenty years her senior. The religious duties which had once been performed a little carelessly, now absorbed almost all her life. The charitable works which had once been accomplished by Bernard and me were now shared by her, and she seemed never to know weariness or disgust. My cousin contemplated this change with a proud delight, a happiness which was only disturbed by a shade of anxiety about our darling's health. The beautiful face was paler than of old, and upon two or three occasions Sophy had betrayed hysterical symptoms which could only arise from weakness.

Bernard remonstrated with her many times upon her untiring devotion to painful labours; she spent too much of her life in sick-rooms, he told her; she walked too far in the course of the day.

'Darling, you must remember that your usefulness depends as much upon your power to help in the good work as on your will. If your health were to give way, these people to whom you have made yourself so dear would lose the comfort of your visits, the advantage of your counsel.'

'I want to do my duty, Bernard; I want to be what a rector's wife should be.'

'I am deeply touched when I hear you say that. I have loved you ever since I have been capable of loving anything, and I have learnt to be proud of you lately. But a rector's wife should not be an overworked invalid. There is all a long life of usefulness before you, I pray Heaven, my dear, and we must not use up your strength in a twelvemonth.'

My uncle Geoffrey gave me a cheque for a sum which I considered very large, to be employed in the purchase of my sister's trousseau; but in this matter, as in everything else, I found it impossible to engage Sophy's attention, or to arouse any of the girlish delight in trifles which had once been her chief characteristic. We went together several times to the county town, and spent long days in drapers' shops, selecting ribbons and turning over pretty dresses, with the agreeable consciousness of having a great deal of money to spend; but my sister might have been the most strong-minded of women for any enjoyment she derived out of a position which to the ordinary feminine mind is as delightful as it is important.

She was very gentle; all the old loving, clinging ways made her charming still—but the joyousness was gone. I did not know whether I ought to be glad or sorry to see her so much improved, as my uncle and Bernard said,—almost improved away from herself, as I thought; but I know that I very often found myself feeling sorry.

In all this time there had been very little talk of Lawrence Annesley, and I hoped, and even believed, that my sister had forgotten him. Now and then, when my cousin mentioned his friend's name, I had seen Sophy's cheek grow a shade paler, but it was only natural that she should be a little disturbed by any allusion to the man whose folly had so ruffled the even current of her happy life. I knew now how much better it would have been if I had encouraged her to talk freely of him; for then at least I should have had her complete confidence. It seemed to have been offered to me, and rejected. Now I dared not mention Lawrence Annesley's name. I dared not even ask if the old wound was quite healed, lest in doing so I should set it bleeding afresh.

So things went on until a month before the day that had been fixed for the wedding, and in the cold, windy March weather Sophy and I went upon our separate duties through the gusty streets, in the winding lanes and straggling outskirts of the town, while a couple of merry work-girls sat at a big table in our own pretty room, almost snowed up in many-coloured cuttings of silk and muslin.

Bernard was very happy. I think he was too hard a worker to find any leisure for those nervous doubts and fears which might have beset an ordinary lover. And then the characteristic of his mind was an unbounded trustfulness in the truth and honour of those he dearly loved. He was very happy, and he believed implicitly in the love of the woman who had promised to be his wife.

From the time of Lawrence Annesley's departure from Sandycoast until this bleak and bitter March we had only heard of him once, and then indirectly. He had never written to Bernard, and on more than one occasion my cousin expressed some wonderment at this silence.

'If anything that Lawrence might do could surprise me, I should be surprised at having had no letter from him in all these months. He has found some new hobby, I dare say, which absorbs him entirely for the moment. I rode over to Colethorpe the other day, and Lady Annesley told me she had last heard of him from Germany. She has abandoned all hope of the Church now, and seems almost resigned to the idea that her darling is to be an aimless idler for the rest of his life.'

It was one day early in March that my cousin said this, and it was within a week of this time when Sophy and I left the rectory together to pay a round of visits amongst our poor. We parted after going a little way, agreeing to meet at a cottage on the Rixborough Road at three o'clock,—the cottage of a widow who was Sophy's pensioner and chief favourite, and who almost idolized my sister. I finished my own work at half-past two, and arrived at Mrs. Burslam's cottage before three.

I found the widow full of my sister's praises; but she distressed me very much by remarking the change in Sophy's appearance during the past six months.

'If I did not know how happy the dear young lady is in her home, I should almost fancy there was some secret grief weighing on her mind,' said Mrs. Burslam, who was rather a sentimental person, and prided herself a good deal upon having seen better days; and then she went on to expatiate on my cousin Bernard's goodness, and on the changes which were to take place so soon at the rectory. I waited for some time, talking over the widow's little troubles. She had a son who was a reckless, ne'er-do-well young man, and about whom it was her chief delight to talk.

'I talk a deal to Miss Sophy about him,' Mrs. Burslam said, 'and she seems to take such an interest like, that it's a world of comfort to me to talk to her. I show her his letters sometimes, for he can write quite beautiful letters, always full of love and kindness, and such hopefulness for the future; but the hopefulness never comes to anything. And yet he was such a talented lad, that folks used to take no end of notice of him in my native place. But there he has been for the last ten years trying to get a living here, and trying to get a living there, and never keeping at anything, and never long out of trouble. First he was apprenticed to a cabinet-maker; but though he seemed to have quite a talent for turning and such like, he didn't keep to the cabinet-making; and then the rector of my native place got him recommended as a clerk to a lawyer, but he got tired of that very soon; and after that he almost broke my heart by going and 'listing as a soldier, and had to be bought off by a subscription which some charitable ladies set on foot; and so he goes on, never doing anything really wicked, but never doing any good, until my mind seems almost worn out with anxiety about him. I tell Miss Sophy all about the poor boy, you know, Miss Champion, and she has such kind, sympathizing ways, that I always feel happier in my mind after talking to her.'

I could not help thinking that my sister Sophy might see some parallel between the widow's ne'er-do-well son and Lawrence Annesley. As the time drew nearer and nearer to the date of my darling's wedding day I found myself growing more and more doubtful as to whether I had acted wisely when I fancied myself so very wise. I was made a little anxious this afternoon by Sophy's unpunctuality. I waited an hour, and then a little longer, and then a little longer again, reading to the widow, though I fear my mind wandered sadly from the sacred pages, whose words of comfort were so much sweeter than anything I could say. uneasy about my sister, and my eyes strayed away to the face of the little Dutch clock in the corner much oftener than they should have done. Sophy had never so broken an appointment with me before, and I was really quite alarmed when the clock struck five, and I got up to go away, having only just time enough to hurry home for our six o'clock dinner.

I had not left the cottage very far behind me when I saw my sister coming towards me across the marshy common land that skirted one side of the high road, and stretched away towards the sea. I was surprised to see her coming from this direction, as the straggling cottages thinly scattered along the coast were tenanted by rough fishermen and their families, whose names were not amongst the list of my sister's charges.

As she came closer to me I saw that she was deadly pale, and that she had been crying. She must have been crying a great deal, for her eyelids were red and swollen. I could see this though she wore a veil over her face, and kept it turned away from me whenever she could.

'Sophy,' I exclaimed, 'where have you been? You don't know how much anxiety you have caused me!'

'I am very sorry you have been anxious, dear. I did not know it was so late until I heard St. Augustine's clock strike just now. I left my watch at home.'

'You have been down by the sea?'

'Yes.'

'You have been seeing some of Bernard's people, I suppose?'

We called the fishermen and their families Bernard's people, for they had been a hopelessly benighted set until very lately, in spite of my uncle's efforts to reform them, and my cousin had worked wonders in this unpromising field.

My sister did not answer me. We were walking homewards side by side.

'My darling,' I said, 'something has distressed you. Why did you go amongst those people down there? You know it is against Bernard's wish that you should visit them. You have been annoyed—insulted, perhaps, by some of them.'

'Oh, no, no!'

'But you have been agitated by something, Sophy. You have seen some one who is very unhappy, perhaps. Is that it?'

'Yes.'

'Some one who is ill—dying? What is it, Sophy? We can help them a little, I dare say, whatever it is.'

'You can't help the person I have seen,' my sister cried, passionately, turning towards me for a moment flushed and angry. 'Why do you tease me so, Patty? Can't you see that something has made me unhappy, and that I only want to be let alone?'

THROUGH THE FURNACE.

209

After this we walked homewards in complete silence. I was quite mystified by my sister's manner, and very much disturbed by it, but I said nothing; and when we were in our own room, changing our dresses for dinner, my darling came suddenly to me, and put her arms round my neck.

'Forgive me, Patty,' she said,—'forgive me, dear, for being so ill-tempered just now. I have been so tired to-day—so tired by the unhappiness I have seen; and I—' She broke down, and sobbed hysterically, with her head lying upon my shoulder. I comforted her as well as I could, and in a very few minutes she was quite calm.

We were so hurried in getting ready to go down-stairs, that I had no time to observe my sister. At dinner she was silent and thoughtful; and when questioned anxiously by Bernard, she told him she was tired. After dinner my cousin went into the study to prepare his sermon, and my sister seated herself in the dusky corner where our piano always stood. She sat before the instrument all the evening, playing soft, pensive melodies from Mozart's sonatas, while my uncle Geoffrey dozed in his arm-chair.

I was very busy during the rest of that week and during the whole of the next, for I had all the arrangements for the wedding on my hands, as well as the preparation of my sister's trousseau, in which it seemed so impossible to inspire her with any interest; and I had enough to do in writing letters, superintending household matters, and directing the two young workwomen who were making Sophy's dresses.

Thus it happened that during this time I saw very little of my sister, who spent the greater part of her time out of doors, visiting amongst her poor, and doing my duties as well as her own. Bernard was away during this week, the last but one before the wedding. A new curate had come already to take his place at Sandycoast, and my cousin was absent on a visit to the scene of his future labours.

I had nearly completed all my work by the end of the week, but there were so many little things still wanting for the completion of the trousseau, that I decided on going to our county town for one final day's shopping. I begged Sophy to go with me, but she declined. She had so much to do in Sandycoast; she had such a horror of a long tiresome day spent in drapers' shops; and then all of a sudden she implored me to put off my journey altogether. The things were of no consequence, she said; she did not care for them, she did not want them; it was only a matter of a few ribbons and collars, more or less.

'I don't care for the finery, Patty,' she cried, impetuously; 'the very sight of it makes me unhappy. There seems so much sorrow in the world, that all this fuss about dresses and bonnets is a kind of wickedness. Don't go, Patty. Stop with me to-day, and let us

She pleaded with me, and all her old winning ways returned for the moment to make her irresistible. How could I be deaf to her entreaties? How could I understand her so little as not to perceive some hidden depth of feeling beneath her childish pleading? I was so dull and short-sighted, and had such a foolish pride in my responsible position, that I would not consent to anything that was likely to militate against the perfection of my sister's bridal outfit.

'You don't know how many things are wanted, Sophy,' I said. 'Half the dresses are unfinished for want of a yard or two of fringe, or lace, or ribbon, and I have to match ever so many things.'

'Can't you get the things in Sandycoast?'

'In Sandycoast! Why, Sophy, you must be mad to ask such a question. Come, darling, put on your bonnet and come with me, or else let me go by myself. I shall lose the coach if you don't take care.'

'You must do as you like, Patty. It is very, very good of you to take so much trouble about my dresses; but it seems such wasted trouble. What does Bernard care about silks and laces, and fringes and trimmings? If I can be his true and affectionate wife, he will care very little to see me finely dressed.'

The tears came into her eyes as she spoke; and she turned her face to the window, and stood there looking out.

'My darling Sophy,' I said, as I tied my bonnet before the glass, 'you seem to forget the solemn nature of my responsibilities. My uncle Geoffrey has entrusted me with the spending of his money, and I mean to achieve a success that will satisfy him; and I mean Bernard to be the happy husband of the best dressed wife in his parish. I don't mean the most expensively dressed, but the most elegantly and appropriately. I have poetic theories regarding the wardrobe of a young rector's wife;—such delicate silks, Sophy; pearly grays; and lavenders, with the faintest peachy bloom, like the lilac tinge of an evening sky between the rosy western clouds and a newly risen moon; and pale green glacé, as soft and tender as the first young leaves on the hawthorn bushes; _organdie_ muslins scattered with snowdrops and violets, and snowy white cambric morning dresses, with tiny rosebuds or miniature sprigs of lilac. Everything pale, and pure, and spring-like. And I don't think it is at all wicked to spend Uncle Geoffrey's money in pretty dresses, Sophy, for it pleases him that you should be prettily dressed: and people must live, you know; and the Spitalfields weavers prosper by the requirements of well-dressed women.'

I talked all this nonsense while I was putting on my bonnet and shawl. My spirits were very high that morning, for I took a kind of

'And that day once past, I shall be able to laugh at the recollection of your folly, Lawrence Annesley,' thought I, 'though it has given me so much trouble during the last six months.'

I enjoyed my long day's shopping in the bustling old country town. I suppose there must be something peculiarly delightful in the spending of money, for I know I felt an intense pleasure in the purchase of those bright and delicate things, which were so out of all harmony with my own plain face and clumsy figure. It was late in the afternoon when I left the busy High Street to make my way to the coach office, and it was quite dusk when I arrived at Sandycoast.

My cousin Bernard was expected home in the course of that day, and I looked forward to a pleasant evening in the cosy drawing-room. He would have so much to tell us about the new home of which he was so soon to take possession, I thought; and surely Sophy's spirits would regain some of their old buoyancy, and her face would light up with the old sunshine when she contemplated new duties in a wider sphere of usefulness. I looked forward to that evening with a vivid idea of its enjoyment, which I fancy one seldom has except about a happiness which is never to be realized, or at any rate not to be realized as we fancy it. I went home in the lumbering old coach, and sat almost up to my eyes in light, fragile parcels.

The coach dropped me at the rectory, and the servant who opened the door for me, and received all my delicate packages, told me that my cousin Bernard had returned and was in the dining-room. I was hurrying to welcome him, when I found the responsibility of my packages a hindrance to my doing so.

'We must get these parcels safely stowed away up-stairs before we can do anything, Susan,' I said. 'I suppose Miss Sophy is in the dining-room?'

'No, Miss; I think she must be up-stairs in her own room.'

'But doesn't my sister know that Mr. Bernard has come home?'

'I think not, Miss. I was just going up to her when the flyman knocked.'

The bell rang at this moment, and Susan ran to open the door.

A boy handed her a letter; 'For Mr. Champion,' he said, and walked away immediately.

'It's for Mr. Bernard, I think, Miss,' the girl said, holding up the letter as she stood under the lamp, which burned very dimly, for there was no such thing as gas in St. Augustine's Rectory. 'Such a thick letter, Miss,' she exclaimed.

She went into the dining-room to deliver it. I heard my cousin's

deep voice talking to his father. A flood of light streamed out into the hall through the half-opened door. I collected my parcels as best I could, and hurried up-stairs. I was tired and hungry, but I forgot all material requirements in the thought of Bernard's return.

My sister was not in her room. Did the familiar chamber look especially blank and empty that night because of her absence? I know I fancied that it looked so. The fire had gone out, and that alone gives a dreary aspect to any room. The housemaid had followed close behind me with a candle and a second cargo of my parcels.

'Miss Sophy must be in the drawing-room, Susan. Go and tell her that Mr. Bernard has come home,' I said, as the girl left me.

Would my cousin be wounded by Sophy's coldness? I wondered. Had I been the lover, so soon to become a husband, I should have fancied it very strange that my promised bride should fail to listen for my coming and fly to meet me when I came. I was grieved that my sister should be so apathetic; and I found myself musing, as I smoothed my hair before the glass, upon what a marvellous and incomprehensible thing this love is, which comes to no two people alike. I arranged my hair and dress very hurriedly, and then ran down-stairs; but before I reached the hall I heard a sound which froze my heart with a sudden terror such as I had never felt before in all my life. It was the sound of a groan and a heavy fall, and then I heard my uncle's voice calling, 'Martha! Martha! Some one! Come, come. My boy is dying.'

I rushed into the dining-room. Bernard Champion was lying on the ground, his face deadly pale, his lips bespattered with blood. His father was kneeling by him unfastening his neckcloth. 'She has killed him,' cried my uncle Geoffrey, 'she has killed my son.'

# RHYME AND RHYTHM.

BY MARTIN F. TUPPER.

EVERY one of us, man or woman, boy or girl, has heretofore so often—sinned, shall we say? or rather—done virtuously in the matter of versemaking, that this paper ought to commend itself as personally interesting to a fair tithe of British humanity, all counted; therefore, let our enterprising publisher expect a very large congregation for a sermon on so popular a text, and look to his interests accordingly. For which amongst us, O world of friendly readers, has not heretofore deliciously penned stanzas to bright eyes, or heroically blared out rifle-songs, or touched a simple hymn for the school-children, or fired up with indignation-verses about the Poles or the Pope, or greeted the beauteous Alexandra or the generous Garibaldi in “gushing” song, or committed the only blameless anonymism of a witty but good-natured Valentine on the great fourteenth? Verily, friends, we have all alike had plenty to do with versifying; and if a silent but picturesque minority in our midst is slyly pretending to plead innocent of having actively perpetrated rhymes, at all events the fair passives have received them, perchance with no small pleasure and affection.

So, then, I touch a theme in itself acceptable enough; and if it be but little more than touched, let the critical mind at once take notice that only touches are intended; a few suggestive thoughts, with a sprinkling of examples, are all our modest aim; and no one presumes herein to attempt anything like exhaustion of the subject. Much will be omitted that should, no doubt, have properly been said; many indignant, but otherwise excellent poets and poetesses, may complain of our silence, which does not mean contempt; and if some matters are included which others haply have said better, at all events your present scribe has neither seen their books nor heard their lectures. Nobody, then, need complain that our mere sketch is not a finished picture, nor accuse as plagiaristic what is quite spontaneous: if any rhyming treatises exist, at any rate none have been consulted; and the clumsy help of rhyming dictionaries (supposing such books to be among those “which no gentleman’s library ought to be without”) has never been invoked by your supra-signed confessor. But he has something, nevertheless, to say, believed to be quite new; he does think that independently he has tumbled upon a most curiously unnoticed fact, worth at least the small comment of this paper. And yet, while thus claiming a discovery, most obvious when made known, he cannot help suspecting that somewhere or other whole volumes may possibly exist about the philological mystery soon to be announced to you; which said unknown volumes perchance certain gentle guides of public

RHYME AND RHYTHM.

censure (occasionally mistaken in their Rhadamanthine dicta) will accuse 'this child' of having surreptitiously perused, transcribed, and hereinafter in some chief ideas appropriated! All I can say is, simply, that the matter is new to me, as I think it will be to you; and that I shall be glad to be referred to any author who has even alluded to my mystery.

Now the mystery is this; How came it to pass that rhyme was not invented till men had spoken and written, and danced and sung upon this earth for four or five thousand years? To which I will add another question; How happens it that no one has, in print, at least, so far as I know, noticed this curious philological and psychological fact, except 'the humble individual who now addresses you'?

Only consider what it amounts to: that until the Welsh bards, in their Triads of about the fifth century, and long afterwards the mediæval monks in their hymns, invented rhyme, no one ever thought of the sweet jingle, say rather exquisite music, of terminal similarities; that, so far, for instance, as Hebrew is concerned, in all the sublimities of Isaiah, the pious breathings of David, the pastoral idyls of the lesser prophets, the plaintive wailings of Ezekiel, the sententious cadences of Solomon, the war-song of Deborah, the dirge over Absalom, the love-story of Jacob, and the life-drama of Job,—in them all the sacred poetry of the Jews is unconscious of a rhyme; that every classic writer, Greek and Latin, to a man (and even, sweet Sappho! to a woman) seems to have been totally unaware of the delicacies beyond rhythm discovered ages afterwards in rhyme; that the love-songs of Catullus, the burlesques of Aristophanes, the dirges of Ovid, the elegies of Tyrtæus, the idyls of Bion, the varied measures of Horace, the pace-woven intricacies of innumerable Greek choruses, and the staider military march of Homer, Lucretius, and Virgil,—all (not apparently by intention, but because the idea does not seem once to have occurred to any one of them), have never risen or fallen, or melted, or crystallized, or stumbled, if you prefer it, into rhyme!

Was it then purposely eschewed, as so much unappreciated ear-tickling, offensive to the higher taste that revelled in pure rhythm? And yet now and then we do find an indifferent jingle quite out of place, and vexatious to the ear by its merely accidental presence. Take, as off-hand instances, these few:—At the beginning of the first chorus of Sophocles' Ajax 'amphirutou' rhymes awkwardly with 'anchialou;' the first two lines of Horace's most distinct claim to immortality,—

'Exegi monumentum ære perennius,

instance another clumsy rhyme; Ovid, in his 'Ænone Paridi' makes 'aurâ' in the next hexameter echoed by 'prorâ;' and Cicero's unlucky jingle is notorious, 'O fortunatam natam,' \&c. A few other examples of evidently like unintentional rhyming might by searching

be picked out of the vast field of the classic poets—three or four accidental daisies in all the multitudinous leagues of the Great Prairie: but how strange it is that these hints were never followed up, that the power of rhyme was as unknown to the ancients as that of steam or magnetism, and its charm as unperceived as the minute beauties under snails' tongues, revealed to us microscopically! How curious that, for instance, the smart epigrammatic quatrains of Martial, the merry drinking-songs of Anacreon, the luscious eclogues of Theocritus, the fervent utterances of Pindar, that none of these, nor any poetry of any other ancient poet, till much-despised dark-aged monkery arose and sent to heaven inspired doxologies from Gothic aisles,—that none, I say, of such were ever flavoured with rhyme as well as savoured with rhythm! And yet Horace in his 'Art of Poetry' claims as a chief characteristic of the true poet, 'artem concludere versum;' meaning thereby not, however, what we call rhyme, but mere terminating dactyls and spondees. Why should not some of his own odes have been as happy in their terminals as the Dies iræ, the Stabat Mater, or the Virgo Dei digna? Why is it that his exquisite ear failed to detect how much sweeter even sapphies might be made, by changes rung upon rhyme, added to the harmony of rhythm? Listen to the ear-contrast of these two stanzas; here is Horace's first sapphic,—

'Jam satis terris nivis atque diræ\
Grandinis misit pater, et rubente\
Dexterâ sacras jaculatus arces\
Terruit urbem:'

and here is a monastic chant in the same metre, altered into rhyme, from the 'Sarum Psalter,'—

'Nocte surgentes, imminente lunâ,\
Semper in psalmis meditemur unâ,\
Viribus totis Domino canentes,\
Esurientes.'

In this connection let honourable mention be justly repeated of Mr. Gladstone as a rhymed Latin hymnologist, whereof the first number of the _Watch Tower_ contains a magnificent specimen, 'Jesus, pro me perforatus,' rendered from Toplady's 'Rock of Ages.' Our many-sided Chancellor, of more 'polished corners' than the tetragon of Pythagoras, adorns all he touches, and achieves success in everything, no less than he deserves it.

Ivy-bound chaplets put me out of humour,\

Please to observe that no contrasts are here offered for sake of preferences; still less is great Milton pitted against a schoolboy infinitely smaller. One ear may prefer the rhythmic form, another the rhymed; but I do take occasion by this instance to say that it is most curious that Horace never has rung the change from rhythm to rhyme, never even seems to have imagined it!

Yet again; how more than strange this ancient ignorance of rhyme appears, when we regard the wonderful facilities thereto afforded by the Greek and Latin languages, wherein a profusion of cases and tenses, in all declensions and conjugations, is found to supply rhymes on all subjects to so prodigal an extent as to be almost too numerous! Was it, then, the very ease of the thing that caused it to be overlooked? Was the secret all too open to be sought for by the eye, too loudly shouted to be distinguished by the ear? A deaf man hears a whisper better than a roar, and few things are less plainly seen than what is straight before one.

I protest I don't comprehend how the poets of those dead old tongues could, on every theme and in every mood of mind, have so cleverly escaped rhyming; when so many hundreds of 'orums' and 'arums,' and 'ibus' and 'ebus,' and 'abats' and 'uits,' and all other sorts of terminations, were perpetually inviting and provoking the sonnetters and lyricists into rhyme! It is an inexplicable mystery, and, except for a guess at the end of this paper, I cannot undertake to expound it; and little less so is the fact that up to this hour no one has taken the trouble to notice it. The earliest known poems in rhyme are not 1200 years old; the whole old world having been for millenaries previously inundated (as we all know) with poems of every sort and kind of metre, not one of which terminated musically!

And now that, in a somewhat disjointed and discursive way, I fear, and too lengthily withal, the great wonder has been set before you of the comparatively modern origin of rhyme, bear patiently with your present preacher in a few more desultory thoughts and illustrations of his text, rhyme and rhythm.

RHYME AND RHYTHM.

Just as the too great ease of Greek and Latin rhyming might have suggested its neglect—for genius always exults over difficulties and avoids the level path,—so it would seem that in languages such as ours, where there are no terminal cases or tenses, and so where rhymes are necessarily fewer and more far to seek, the energy of man's mind has chosen especially to be a conqueror. Hence it is that our difficult English is one of the tongues known to be richest in rhymed poetry. To compare great things with small, Scotch gardeners similarly are pre-eminently good, as having on their 'native heath' to contend in the battle of horticulture with all manner of hardships in soil and climate. Human energy does marvels the more it has to fight against. And, if modern Italian poetry is perhaps an instance on the opposite tack, as an easily rhyming tongue and full of sonnetry and terza rima—well, let it prove our rule by standing for the exception; it is an idle and a musical people, with more delicacy of taste than energy of character. English, a tongue with fewer native rhymes than almost any that can be named, is redundant in lyrics; and the facility of her rhymesters (as we shall exemplify anon) is something astonishing, taking into account the difficulties wherewith they have to contend. We ring the few changes with as much variation as they are capable of, and by dint of pertinacity conceal the actual poverty of our resources. For example, such noble words as 'home' and 'love' (rhyming truly only to 'dome' and 'dove') are very inadequately echoed by 'come' and 'move;' yet hear how beautifully they are managed by Tennyson:—

'Could we forget the widow'd hour,\
And look on spirits breathed away,\
As on a maiden in the day\
When first she wears her orange flow'r,

'When crown'd with blessing she doth rise\
To take her latest leave of home,\
And hopes and light regrets that come\
Make April of her tender eyes;

'And doubtful joys the father move,\
And tears are on the mother's face,\
As, parting with a long embrace,\
She enters other realms of love,' \&c.

So, also, of a score of other instances; many of our best words have scarcely a true rhyme apiece to echo them, as the knightly thoughts involved in 'trumpet,' 'war,' and 'lady,' find no just equivalents to the ear, excepting as burlesquely, in 'crumpet,' 'Storr,' not star, and 'shady;' yet how well genius manages the matter even in such an apparently hopeless case as making 'battle' find a serious rhyme in 'cattle.' Hear Longfellow in that splendid 'Psalm of Life:'—

'In the world's broad field of battle,\

Perhaps the oldest rhymed poetry in the world is that of the ancient Cymry, of which a very curious collection is extant in Jones's _Bardic Museum_. It appears from this rare work (the writer fortunately possesses a copy) that the bards of old Britain, who flourished from time immemorial, had arranged twenty-four metres of vocal song, whereof five were especially selected by Taliesin; and as the latter sang and wrote as early as the end of our fifth century, and is easily chief, we may considerably antedate the 'Triads' and other early poems, particularly as most of these are only rhythmical. It would worry the patient reader, if there were paraded before his dazed eyes too much of this sort of doggrel, wholly impossible to be pronounced; but I quote the old British advisedly, and am not inventing:—

'Yn dewis eichiawg,\
Ffysg ffous ffodiawg,\
Ef dihum hunawg,\
Ef gobryn Carawg,\
Cymru carnedaewg,' \&c.

And, advisedly also, I leave off quoting what no one can anyhow read. My volume supplies a literal version, which may be thus roughly rhymed:

'In striving for the victory\
The warriors now must fight or die,\
The sleepers will awake and fly,\
For this Carawg would strive and try\
Rocky Wales to steal or buy,' \&c.

However, as this is not very interesting, I will attempt for you a better specimen, and one of some interest to the Laureate and his million readers, being a dialogue between 'Arthur Frenin,' or King Arthur, when a youth, and his afterwards _second_ wife 'Gwenhwyfar,' the familiar Guenivere of our great Idyls. It appears, by the way, from Taliesin, that 'Melmas, a prince of Alban,' stole her way from Arthur, and not 'Lanselot du Lâc,' who was father to Sir Galath, one of Arthur's three immaculate knights, and was quite an old man among the party: as in the parallel case of Merlin's alleged capture by Vivien, it may be well to throw out this word in vindication of possibly maligned Lanselot.

Here, then, is my version of the dialogue, as literal as may be, and putting one as an ode in mind of Horace's famous 'Donec gratus eram,' whereof the enthusiastic Scaliger avouched that he would rather be its author—'Vel totius Tarraconensis fuissem Rex,'—than even 'King of Arragon'!

_Arth._ “‘Gwenhwyfar, so soft of eye,

In Devon-Celwig’s baron-hall
Pouring the wine to one and all.’”

_Arth._ “‘Gwenhwyfar, in speech so fair,

Most ancient Talicsin indulges (as modern Barham does) in very hailstorms of rhyme occasionally : _e. g._—

“Gwelais wyr gorfawr
A ddygrchynt awr,
Gwelais waed ar llawr
Rhag rhuthr cleddyfawr,
Glesynt esgyll gwawr
Esgorynt yn waywawr.”

Thus suffer its rhyme in English; and the passage is a spirited one:—

“I saw the warriors fierce in might,
Shouting, rush together in fight,
I saw the ground with carnage strew’d,
And the blades of the warriors blood-bedew’d,
While the wings of the morning tinged with blue
The dead men’s faces of ashen hue!”

and signifying to its end as followeth—I have kept closer to the text than you may fancy—

In my bright days,\

Chant I my lays;\
Sorrowing tearfully\
Saddest of men,\
Can I sing cheerfully\
As I could then ?

“Many a verity\
In those glad times\
Of my prosperity\
Taught I in rhymes;\
Now from forgetfulness\
Wanders my tongue,\
Wasting in fretfulness\

Foolishly blind,\
Riches have wrought me here\

Ever as then ?\

Say such a thing,\

In 'Luther's Hymn' 'created' should not rhyme to 'seated;' and in several other of our ill-rendered psalms, 'sounds' and 'resounds,' 'acts' and 'exacts,' \&c., are echoes, where identity is a fault. However, the exigencies of our language (certainly not one for improvisatori, in spite of Theodore Hook) permit great indulgence in the way of rhyme; and we must not be too particular with our lyricists, but have mercy on the difficulties of their position. Every one of them, great and small, is, in his vocation, forced upon allowances at some time; for instance, the accurate Campbell twice or thrice in 'The Pleasures of Hope,' makes 'thought' rhyme to 'remote;' Pope, in that masterpiece of his, 'The Essay on Man,' rhymes the same 'thought' with 'fault,' evidently in his day pronounced 'faute,' as perhaps his 'tea' was 'tay,' or 'Great Anna whom three realms obey,' could never 'Sometimes counsel take and sometimes tea;' Shakspere, in 'Venus and Adonis,' rhymes 'broken' with 'open;' and Tennyson, in his magnificent 'Balaclava Charge,' is forced to make 'hundred' echoed by 'thunder'd' and 'sunder'd' and 'wonder'd,' as if it were vulgarly 'hundred;' while a much smaller 'T' was, on a recent happy occasion, severely criticized for making that 'Most welcome wanderer across the Northern water,' become manifest as 'Our England's Alexandra, her dear adopted daughter.' Would those implacable critics have been better pleased with the ill-omened, but more exact rhyme 'Cassandra,' as a preferable echo? Undoubtedly, I stand by my 'Welcome Wanderer.' In all these cases, and scores more might be added, our difficult tongue obliges us to take some licence, so as to do the work somehow fairly enough, where actual perfection is philologically impossible. Our common psalmody, which, as the offerings to heaven from multitudes, should be perfect in letter as well as in spirit, by extremity of licence sins most of all; though Roundell Palmer, and Keble, and Alford, and Heber, and some others, occur as admirable exceptions or reformers. Still, it were ever and anon much to be desired, that when the new incumbent introduces, as a matter of course, his own 'collection' (the obedient congregation insuring anyhow an edition going off), he be previously endowed with some quavers of poetry in his ear, as well as with the usual amount of doctrinal crotchets on his tongue. It seems to be tacitly agreed that piety and so-called orthodoxy of sentiment are all-in-all for psalmody; and so rhyme and rhythm, not to say grammar too, as well as prosody, go to the wall. The wretched doggrel that is wafted Sunday after Sunday heavenward from thousands of well-meaning worshippers, and often accompanied by the grandest organ power, is calculated to shame, not alone our church governors but also their educated lay flocks, into a really good authorized National hymn-book; to say less about the perversities of creed and diversities of practice, helped by the manifold

Pious feeling is one thing, but poetical fire quite another; however, as all parsons have to encourage their choirs, and as too many good folks fancy they can write verses at least as well as they can sing them, the sad consequence is a mass of well-meant rubbish, whereof, according to Dr. Johnson's thunder, 'the piety alone redeems it from contempt.'

RHYME AND RHYTHM.

gale, by the mere impetus of its own inspiration; whereas the mental travel after rhyme is a perpetual beater-up of new ideas, possibly to the enrichment of the poem. For, practically, when a rhyme is wanted (and no true poet ever even saw a rhyming dictionary), one thinks through terminations alphabetically, stumbling thereby on many fancies, analogous not only in sound but also in sense to the matter in hand; but this process involves a continual rejection of such rhymes and thoughts as would lead our main purpose too far astray, and constitutes one of the differences between a true poet and a false one. The latter is the slave of his rhymes, whereby (except in burlesque, where it is fair enough to suffer one's self to be run away with, as Barham is, _passim_) his negligence commits the too frequent fault of diffuseness from over-facility of diction. I am afraid 'Jean Ingelow,' though full of beauties, is an example in point. A real poet will never sacrifice sense to sound; self-denial is as necessary to his form of excellence as to that of all others. He must select, reject, compare, and these by the quickest intuition; every sort of knowledge becomes available, and the alembic of his kindled spirit receives and fuses together the most unlikely dissimilars into a poetic unity; and so he will ingeniously avail himself of the few rhymes in our tongue by the mingled powers of concise argument and expanded illustration.

I must now hasten on, with much omitted and still much to add; I fear discursively, but my theme is a very wide one.

'Of sweetest Shakspere, fancy's child,' what shall we say in the matter of rhymed poetry? During his lifetime he was better known, and set himself more store, by his lyrics than by his dramas; like Scott, he caught the world's ear with his rhyme before he imprisoned its heart by his rhythm. And, considered quite apart from morals, as so much merely picturesque description, the 'Venus and Adonis' and the 'Lucrece' of Shakspere are simply perfect; but, for modern taste and feeling they are too luxuriously coloured to be at all producible; a remark which may apply more or less to Byron's 'Don Juan' (one of the best sustained pieces of rhyming in our language), in a less degree to Chaucer, and in a still less degree to Spenser; but in a far greater to some of the poets of the Restoration, and to their more modern imitators; as Moore in his phase of Thomas Little. As to Shakspere's wonderful sonnets—a hundred and fifty-four on one subject (of love for a friend, man or woman, as the case may be, actual or ideal, according to your theory, sensually or spiritually considered, and whether supposed to be the poet's own experiences or written from a mere efflorescence of fancy), they are, as rhymed poems on a single theme, and that a personal one, only to be equalled (shall I not say exceeded?) by Tennyson's 'In Memoriam;' the latter having the advantage of absolute purity beyond its exquisite diction;

Ballad poetry is a mixture of rhyme and rhythm, the two generally alternating; some of its best modern specimens are to be found in Macaulay's 'Roman Lays' and Aytoun's 'Cavaliers.' Here is a stanza from each, a specimen brick from either of those great houses:

'He reel'd, and on Herminius\
He lean'd one breathing space;\
Then like a wild cat mad with wounds\
Sprang right at Astur's face:\
Through teeth, and skull, and helmet\
So fierce a thrust he sped,\
The good sword stood a handbreadth out\
Behind the Tuscan's head,' \&c.

'Open wide the vaults of Atholl,\
Where the bones of heroes rest,\
Open wide the hallow'd portals\
To receive another guest!\
Last of Scots, and last of freemen—\
Last of all that dauntless race,\
Who would rather die unsullied\
Than outlive the land's disgrace!\
O thou lion-hearted warrior,\
Reck not of the after-time,\
Honour may be deem'd dishonour,\
Loyalty be called a crime,' \&c.

Of a more antique cast, perhaps the best specimen we have is 'The Nut-brown Maid,' a ballad as old as 1400, and remarkable throughout for the accuracy of its rhyme, as well as the vigour of its rhythm; thereby being less disappointing to the ear than is the common case with ballad poetry, the mere cadences whereof barely compensate for the too frequently careless and inartistic unrhymed endings. Here is a stanza from that fine old song, rhyming in the middle of each long line:—

'Myne owne dere love, I se the prove\
That yo be kynde and true;\
Of mayde and wyfe, in all my lyfe,\
The best that ever I knewe:\
Be mery and glad, be no more sad,\
The care is chaunged newe;\
For it were ruthe that for your truthe\
Ye should have cause to rewe:\
Be not dismay'd; whatsoever I sayde\
To you, whan I began,—\
I wyll not to the grenewode go;\
I am no banysh'd man.'

RHYME AND RHYTHM.

where they did! Rhythm is the rule of syllabic quantity, rhyme of syllabic quality. The one respects arrangement, order, congruity; the other, besides these, adding thereto the harmony and music of sweet endings. The first pleases the mind by ingeniously constructed sentences; the latter gratifies the ear by recurrence of expected echoes. Hence the jarring effect of a faulty rhyme—hence the wisdom of preceding such a questionable pronunciation as “wind” by the better known “mind” if they are doomed to rhyme together, so as to prepare the hearer for a long _i_: in like manner with such indifferent commonplaces as “prove” and “love,” “home” and “come,” \&c., let the principal tone or word have priority, and so serve to govern the secondary rhyme by an indulgent intonation.

Rhythm was the great and only guide of the ancient poetry. Among the commonly-called classics, that is, the Greek and Latin poets, it was a system of the strictest rules and metres; not as with the Hebrews, and the Anglo-Saxons, and us their children, an affair of the ear only, but one more exactly to be counted on the fingers: the measures of old Rome (all derived from older Greece, without exception,—for Rome invented nothing, but appropriated all things),—those Latin measures, I say (too savagely drilled and flogged into us in boyhood), are, as most have known to their cost, matters of much stricter prosody than any English rhyme can be, to say less of the comparative freedom of English rhythm. It is not, however, my meaning now to worry patient readers with an array of hard words, familiar to all Etonians and especially to Carthusians (your present scribe was Thackeray’s schoolfellow under the fearfully prosaic but tremendously metrical Dr. Birch); still less is it my wish to parade a learning little useful in itself, and made far too much of at public schools as matter of scholarship. We can all ring the changes on dactyls and spondees, iambics and trochaics, anapæsts and tribrachs, and the rest of them; but an accurate English ear has it all by intuition, without knowledge of terms or rules: cadence is all in all with us.

Thus, like Monsieur Jourdain, who talked prose all his life without knowing it, our song-writers unconsciously adopt the ancient metres. “A southerly wind and a cloudy sky” is more or less dactylic; “Gaffer Grist, gaffer Grey, and his little jackass,” anapæstic; “Down among the dead men,” trochaic; “Scots, wha hae wi’ Wallace bled,” iambic; “Here a sheer hulk lies poor Tom Bowling,” spondaic; and so forth; in fact, there is no popular song nor poem but they all find their prototypes in the old rhythms. And some of these days, when everybody’s New Zealander (for Macaulay’s famous savage served Goldsmith, and Volney, and Walpole, and Shelley, and Kirke White, and other folks before them),—when this often plagiarized cannibal moralizes on the ruins of London, and English is a dead language, probably the then rising generation will have to scan our songs

In an extended sense all good prose writing is rhythmical; and from the days of Aristotle to those of Blair, rhetoricians have laid down rules for harmony in composition. Where Joseph Hume on the same subject would have been 'harsh and crabbed,' Gladstone can be 'musical as is Apollo's lute,' even on so hopeless a topic as a financial statement; and no proper man can read Macaulay's 'History,' or Johnson's 'Rambler,' or a Times' article aloud, without measured though irregular cadences. Again, all good rhyme is _à fortiori_ rhythmical, even to the wildest odics of Peter Pindar or Sydney Dobell—whose last ode, by the way, just contributed to Walter Severn's most beautiful of gift-books, the 'Golden Calendar,' ends with startling bathos thus:—

'Whether we be the world, or whether the fading world be 'We!''

So then, to close up the ranks a little, and not to take our specimens of rhythm from such skirmishing disorder, but within more definite lines, all blank verse compositions, a very large class, inclusive of Milton's, and Shakspeare's, and Tennyson's masterpieces, are eminently rhythmical. So are the prophets and psalms of our Bible, and the Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus of the Apocrypha; and (if it may be spoken of in such a category) so is a certain humble imitation of the writings of Sirach's son, for which the suprasigned has been long 'proverbial.' But of all these it is needless, as it would be prolix, to quote instances; one might transcribe 'elegant extracts' to any amount from such a sort of universal literature as blank verse amounts to: it is only the more special forms of rhythm which call upon us for illustration.

Take, then, a morsel in the archaic form, from the 'Persæ' of Æschylus, literally rendered, and syllable for syllable in the metre of the original:—

'O royal lady, grace of the Persians,\
Down to earth's inner halls send thy drink-offerings,\
We the while will in our anthems entreat\
The guides of the dead\
Propitious to be from beneath.\
Ye then, inviolate demons of burial,\
Earth, and Hermes, and King of the Manes,\
Send from below his soul to the light!\
For should he know any balm for adversity\
He could of mortals alone tell it out.'

And his 'Evangeline' is an equally successful attempt in an ancient metre, the hexameter—one in which Southey failed, but chiefly because he was writing to command as the then Laureate, and lacked a good thesis; for in general Southey's rhythms are at least as fair as his rhymes,—but who could make any capital out of 'King George going to judgment'?

Take, then, from 'Evangeline,' half-a-dozen lines illustrative of the suitability of our tongue to the Virgilian measure:—

'Late, with the rising moon, return'd the wains from the marshes,\
Laden with briny hay, that fill'd the air with its odour.\
Cheerily neigh'd the steeds, with dew on their manes and their fetlocks,\
While aloft on their shoulders the wooden and ponderous saddles,\
Painted with brilliant dyes, and adorn'd with tassels of crimson,\
Nodded in bright array, like hollyhocks heavy with blossoms.'

And now let the living Laureate speak to us in his 'Boadicea,' where the ancient rhythm of Catullus in his threnode of Atys is mingled with something of the barbaric dissonance of a wild old British harp, clashed by the angry queen:—

'Hear Icenian, Catieuchlanian, hear Coritanian, Trinobant!\
While I roved about the forest, long and bitterly meditating,\
There I heard them in the darkness, at the mystical ceremony:\
Loosely robed in flying raiment, sang the terrible prophetesses.'

Southey’s “Thalaba” is a triumph of rhythm, and probably on the whole the poem whereby he will longest live. The “Curse of Kehama” adds rhyme to metre, and opens thus :—

“Midnight, and yet no eye\

Behold her streets ablaze\

Housetop and balcony\

To view the funeral pomp that passes by,\
As if the mournful rite\

It is said that the rhyme for 'chimney' was a challenge one, as impossible—but 'slim knee' hit it. Similarly, in a certain _bout rimé_ duel at Oxford, I recollect how one who was defied with being unable to find a rhyme for 'peculiar' \[Juliar being barred], startlingly responded at once with—I can, _you_ liar!

And now, galloping down to our own day, we must, to save space and weariness, pass with mere notes of admiration scores of sweet lyricists, as Hemans and Sigourney, Burns and Scott, Moore, Byron, and innumerable others who have achieved greatness chiefly in rhymed poetry, taking only a few which may give occasion to gossip a new word or two about each. For example: touching upon Thomson, as very seldom a rhymester but almost exclusively rhythmical, let me remind any whom it may concern that the famous Ode (looking so very Campbellish),—

'When Britain first, at Heaven's command,

is Thomson's, in a forgotten 'Masque of Alfred:' and let me further announce that in the first edition of 'The Seasons' (1738, _penes me_), the notable Damon and Musidora 'Episode,' which for purity and propriety may be held to constitute Thomson's chief claim to poetic glory, is strangely diverse from the charming scene so popular now-a-days; forasmuch as said Damon watches _three_ nymphs, Amoret, Sacharissa, and Musidora, and not a monogamic one only; and that, though he certainly (as a converted Stoic) prefers the latter, he is Grand Turk enough to profess very warm feelings simultaneously for all the three! This new view of the most famous bit of Thomson may well surprise some of his admirers. Again, which of us does not give to Burns the well-known 'There's nae luck about the house'? It is one Macklin's. The celebrated 'Ode to Independence,' with the single fine line in it,—

'Lord of the lion-heart and eagle eye,'—

was written by the author of 'Humphrey Clinker,' who had so little feeling for his thesis, that he actually commences by requesting permission to _share_ the spirit of independence with somebody! So, too, if competitive examiners, eager for information, in their insatiate and promiscuous curiosity, ask you who wrote the _never quoted_ line,—

'Westward the tide of empire takes its way,'—

don't tell your inquisitors Pope, or Cowper, or haply Goldsmith, but

There, that's enough. Only I take occasion to remark how generally our actors, especially in burlesque declamation, utterly spoil such queer rhyming in the general, by attending more to the grammatical stops than to the rhythmic accent. There should always be a slight half-perceptible lull at the end of every line, whether rhymed or not. Some people, even professors of rhetoric, persist in murdering terminal harmonies by clumsily going on as if the matter were plain prose. Taste is required in this, and moderation; too long a stop enslaves the sense to the sound, and makes a monotonous namby-pamby of what, properly read, may well appear a good poem; but no pause at all at the end of a rhyme or rhythm is worse still. One's ear is constantly offended at theatres by this running together of metres, and sacrificing accents to commas.

Hood's "Haunted House" is a grand poem, not too well known:—

"O very, very dreary is the room,
Where love, domestic love, no longer nestles,
But, smitten by the common stroke of doom,
The corpse lies on the trestles:

"But house of woe, and hearse, and sable pall,
And narrow home of the departed mortal,
Ne'er look'd so gloomy as that ghostly hall,
With its deserted portal.

"For over all there hung a cloud of fear—
A sense of mystery the spirit daunted,
And said, as plain as whisper in the ear,
The place is haunted!"

But perhaps, of all rhymed poems, Hood's "Bridge of Sighs" is the most ingenious and remarkable, while its power and pathos are kept at the highest pitch:—

And I dare say that _one_ copy still remains unsold at Virtue's of the prettily-bound book, yclept 'Cithara,' whence this rhymed Sapphic Ode is extracted!

And now to bring matters to an end. After having sweetened our mouths with so many lumps of 'Turkish delight,' after having regaled our ears by such dulcet hints of lyrical melody, I return to my mystery. How could it have come to pass that never once in nearly 5,000 years did our world in her poets think of rhyming? that love managed to warble without its music, wit to sparkle without its sprightliness, hate to satirize without its point, piety to praise without its beauty?—and I will encourage repetition of all this, that the matter may, by hammered recapitulation, get a better chance of being heard and talked about. How did it happen, I repeat, that no ancient poet ever discovered this art (with some of us a very

RHYME AND RHYTHM.

235

nature), this charming art of Rhyme? What slyness would it not have added to erotics, what sweetness to lyrics, what stately cadence to heroic song, what witty turns to satire, what elegiac beauties to grief, what triumph to odes, what dignity to choruses! Somehow or other, everybody for five millenaries poetized in blank verse—blank verse of every sort of rhythm, elaborate as well as simple, from the strophed and anti-strophed chorus to the plain iambics of an Angelus, but in no one instance intentionally (barely in one accidentally) breaking into rhyme. Can it be that those delicately practised ears misliked the jingle? Yet its music is to us more exquisite than any mere rhythm can supply. Furthermore, if intentionally disavowed, how should Horace, in an ode especially built for immortality, have only just that once stumbled into the great fault all seem to have eschewed? I verily believe the discovery escaped them—all the more strangely, too, in such languages as Greek and Latin, where the cases of nouns and the tenses of verbs, and inflections of cognate words, are almost only too fertile in rhymes; the wonder being thus the greater that they are incessantly missed, avoided, or neglected. How is it, then \[who'll tell me?], that till the mediæval monks filled their choirs with music, till Gregory chanted and A'Kempis sung, the dignity and beauty of the rhymed Latin ode were never even suspected? and that, till troubadours arose in the crusading era, the ballad, or the serenade, or the joyous outburst of song otherwise, bacchanalian or military, seems in all countries to have escaped the terminal enchantment of rhyme? Did it all on a sudden occur to some obscure chorister, a Columbus-egg thought? and, infectious in its witchery, did it catch the world's great ears so universally and all at once, that no one appears to have considered how modern was the discovery? Is there extant any treatise on rhyme, attempting to explain the mystery of its long absence from the pages of poetry? From Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, from Anglo-Saxon, and from the earliest poems of every European tongue, it seems to have been systematically or universally excluded, either because all hated it as an easy and vulgar jingle, or none had invented such dulcet terminations to a measure. Possibly, the extreme East was the cradle, the officina, of rhymes; possibly some earliest Hindoo, or Chinese, or Japanese poetry may have been tagged with rhyme as long ago as when Job suffered, and Abram left Haran; possibly the music of rhyme went westward with the Kelti, lingering eastwardly among the Persians and Arabians until the Saracens brought rhyme to Europe with the flash of their scimitars. At all events the incursion of troubadours and trouvères, with their epidemic of sweet singing, into Europe, was simultaneous with their invasion. However considered, the thing is a mystery, and many times have I marvelled at it, seeking vainly in all sorts of books, not merely for an elucidation of the

puzzle, but for any allusion to its existence. Is, then, your present scribe (and let some pundit answer?) the only man alive to whom it ever has occurred to ask these questions?—

1. Did mankind—and why did they,—enjoy blank poetry from four to five thousand years before any one thought of putting rhymes to it?
2. Did the ancients avoid rhyming intentionally, or only miss it by an accident the more wonderful as pervading eras and nations?
3. Who was the true inventor and first maker of rhyme?
4. Is there any book or essay on the subject beside this present paper?
5. Isn't the matter a puzzle worthy to be worked out (chiefly from Eastern sources) by our modern unravellers of every labyrinthine skein, our cutters of all old Gordian knots?
6. Who'll do it?

These works, now too late to be consulted, certainly regard our present subject, and possibly anticipate much of what I may have said. I have also heard of, and have seen, Mr. Dallas's "Poetics," wherein I find no allusion to the mysterious absence of intended rhyme in classic poets. But a literary friend tells me, that in a forthcoming edition of that elaborate and exhaustive "Ars Poetica," the subject of our present writing is not unlikely to be discussed.
