Mr. Jefferson and I had been standing. The doctor stopped to talk to him for a few minutes, while I ran back to the drawing room to pour out a cup of tea, which I brought for my uncle.

'Yes, that is quite right, Miss Patty,' said Mr. Jefferson, as I carried it into the room. 'Mr. Champion will take some tea. You may be quite easy about your son, sir,' he added, turning to my uncle. 'Mr. Bernard will do very well, and will be able to attend to his duty to-morrow as well as he did yesterday.'

'That is very possible,' answered my uncle, sadly. 'Bernard is not the man to abandon his duty. I have no doubt you have done the very best that can be done for him, my dear Jefferson. But there are a few diseases that do not come within the compass of your art, and a broken heart is one of them. My son has received a blow to-night which he will never recover so long as he lives.'

My uncle was taking the cup of tea from my hands as he spoke. He looked up at me with the gentlest and tenderest expression in his eyes.

'You must not think that I shall love _you_ any the less for this, my dear,' he said, softly.

'It doesn't do to attach too much importance to a young man's trouble, my dear Mr. Champion,' said the doctor; 'young men do not, as a rule, break their hearts. A disappointment coming upon a man of your age or mine is likely to strike home, for it comes after a long course of disappointments. It is the last straw, you know, under which the camel is likely to lie down and die; but what a load the animal will carry while he is young and hopeful, and has not yet discovered that his life is to be made up of bearing other people's burdens! You need have no uneasiness about your son. With such a chest and such shoulders as he has, a man cannot die of a broken heart. He will knock under for a week or so perhaps, and then he will shake his grief away from him, as a young racehorse shakes off a gadfly, and will be all the better man for his trial.'

Mr. Jefferson and my uncle shook hands, and then the doctor left us. When the door closed upon him, I knelt at my benefactor's feet and implored him to be comforted. Even now, I thank God when I remember that evening; I thank God with all my heart, when I remember that I was permitted to afford some consolation to that dear and noble friend.

He talked to me as freely as if I had been his child, and told me how my cousin had opened the letter, and how, after reading the first page, he groaned aloud, with a strange gurgling noise in his throat, and then fell like a dead man at his father's feet. Little by little I told my uncle all the story of the past, and what I had done in my desire to separate my sister from Lawrence Annesley.

'You acted for the best, my dear,' he said; 'I do not doubt that

All that evening I sat with my dear uncle. He was very calm, but it seemed to me as if Bernard's grief was quite as much his as it was Bernard's: the stroke that had fallen so suddenly had crushed the father as well as the son.

'I loved her so dearly,' he said; 'she has been false to me as well as to him. If she had come to me—if she had trusted me, as she might have done,—I could have softened this grief for my boy. But to steal away from the house like some criminal; to let things go on so long, and then to desert my son. It has been too cruel, Patty—it has been too cruel. Heaven help me to feel as a Christian should, but it will be very difficult for me to forgive her.'

'She has been tempted away, uncle Geoffrey,' I said; 'she did not mean to go this morning. I know that, for she asked me to stay at home with her, and promised to spend all the day at home. Ah, if I had only stayed!'

'It has been the will of Providence that my son should suffer this grief,' my uncle answered gravely. 'How easy it is to recognize God's will in the stroke that afflicts us, and yet how difficult not to be angry with the instrument that works His will. Don't cry, Patty; I will try to forgive your sister. It is all the more difficult for me to forgive her because I love her so much. Let me think of her when she was a little child, with her head nestling on my breast; let me remember her as she was when I first brought her to this house.'

We sat together, sometimes talking sadly of what had happened, sometimes silent, until the usual hour for evening prayer. I rang the bell, and the servants came quietly in and took their places. It seemed to me as if they all had guessed the nature of our trouble. My sister's disappearance—the letter—these had helped them, no doubt, to solve the mystery. They were servants who had lived with us for a long time, and I believe they felt very sincerely for us in our sorrow; as servants will in households where the gulf between the parlour and the kitchen is bridged over by small kindnesses and friendly sympathy with humble pleasures and vexations.

My uncle Geoffrey read the simple evening prayer. His tones were unbroken, but the voice was low and faint, and the sound of it gave me unspeakable pain. Ah, how shall I ever forget all the sorrow of that sad night, and the bitter grief that followed it!

My uncle kissed and blest me as he bade me good night. I thank God for the inspiration that urged me to tell him at that moment what until then I had never in all my life expressed in any form of words. I told him that an orphan girl, who might have been a

His bounties were so freely given, and carried with them so little sense of obligation, that until that night I had never said even so much as this. If I had waited to say it after that night, I should have waited until it was too late.

They found my uncle Geoffrey sleeping very peacefully the next morning; but it was in the sleep of death. He had long been suffering from a heart disease, and it seemed but too probable that the shock of his son's grief had killed him. My cousin came to tell me what had happened.

'Do you remember what I said to you a long time ago, Patty,' he asked, after he had sat in silence for some time, with his face hidden by his folded arms; 'I have no Christian feeling for any one who touches my father. Sophy Champion has been the cause of his untimely death, and I will never forgive her so long as I live.'

I will not dwell upon that sad time. No words that I can write would tell how much I suffered. We suffer these things, and live through them. I think a merciful stupor comes down upon us, in which the first sharp anguish passes by—felt only in a dim, confused manner, like the pain of an operation endured under the influence of chloroform. The sorrow that comes afterwards is the worst,—the blank, dreary sorrow that takes possession of us when we are calm enough to realize how much we have lost.

My uncle Geoffrey's funeral train left the dear old home under the cold spring sunlight which was to have looked upon my sister's bridal. It was a bitter day for Bernard and for me; one of those days whose bitterness comes back to us with every recurring year, inseparable from the season and the atmosphere. As I stood by my uncle's grave I felt and knew that my youth was gone from me for ever. Oh, what a careless, happy time it seemed to have been now that it _was_ gone. The memory of every foolish tear I had ever shed reproached me like the memory of a sin. Had I ever been sufficiently grateful for so many blessings, had I ever known how many they were, until now, when they were gone.

We went home to the rectory very sorrowful. We were only guests on sufferance now in that house which had so long been our home. Bernard was to go to his new duties in a few weeks—the bright spring weeks which were to have been devoted to his wedding tour;—and for myself, I had to find some new home, to make some new plans for my future. I had made none as yet. Could I think of the future, when he who had been so dear to me in the past lay lifeless in the home he had made so happy.

My uncle's will was read by the lawyer who had made it. As

he had sheltered me from all trouble in his life-time, so he protected me after his death. He had left me an annuity of a hundred pounds, chargeable upon the small unentailed estate that had come to him from his father, and which was bequeathed to Bernard, who was residuary legatee. Nothing was left to my sister Sophy except a pretty, old-fashioned locket, set round with pearls, and containing a miniature of my uncle taken in his early youth, and his first gift to the woman he chose for his wife.

'I leave my darling Sophy only this small memorial of her adopted father,' the lawyer read sadly. 'For I fondly hope and believe that, when this my last testament is opened, she will be my son's wife, and the partaker of all that he inherits. I leave her only the half-faded picture, in which she will see some faint resemblance of her husband's face, and the shadow of her uncle's youth.'

I stole a glance at my cousin's face while this passage was being read, and my eyes were rivetted to it with a fascination I could not resist. It was a stern, implacable countenance, which darkened as the lawyer recited the dead man's tender words, and I began to wonder whether my sister would ever be forgiven; and then my mind wandered to the future, to the dreary morrow on which I was to leave that dear familiar home, a lonely, aimless creature. There was only one gleam of hope in the dismal horizon. I was quite free and independent now, and I could go to seek my sister—my foolish, erring girl, whose guilty folly had brought ruin on such a happy home, and had broken a strong man's heart.

I had received a letter from her that morning,—such a miserable letter, so blotted by tears as to be almost illegible. She had heard of my uncle's death, and the bitter anguish of remorse had taken hold of her. It is not often that retribution so swiftly follows wrong-doing; but I have always found that it comes sooner or later, even on this earth. My sister's letter was signed Sophia Annesley, and she entreated me to forgive her, and to come to her at the London address which she gave me. What had I to forgive, poor darling? Was I to set myself up as a judge of this girl? I, who had never been tempted.

After the will had been read, my cousin and I were left to ourselves. He was going to town on business the following day, and I should be left quite alone in the house which, in its dismal emptiness, would be haunted by such mournful memories, unless, indeed, I made up my mind to pack my trunks and accompany him to London. He would be glad to give me the protection of his escort I knew; but I almost feared to approach the subject, for another question was linked with it, a question I scarcely dared to ask. I wanted to win his forgiveness for my poor Sophy. But to approach her name was to torture him so cruelly, and to-day above all

While I was thinking this, my cousin raised his eyes and looked at me. We were sitting on either side of the fire, for the April day grew cold and stormy towards the evening, and the creaking branches of the trees swayed against the windows of our desolate drawing-room every now and then with a dreary, mournful sound.

'Patty,' said my cousin, 'what are you going to do? If we were each of us some fifteen years older, I should say, Come and be my housekeeper at Allingford. It seems very hard that we who are so like brother and sister must part; and yet I don't know, I may be able to fight my battle better away from you. You belong to the past.'

I knew very well what he meant by those sad words. My presence could only remind him of my sister,—and how could it be otherwise than painful to him.

'By-and-bye, when I am an old bachelor, snugly installed in a cosy old deanery perhaps, with mullioned windows and cedar panelling in my drawing-room, you must come and live with me, Patty, if you are still unmarried, and take care of my poor. What will my poor do, at Allingford, I wonder? It is a sad thing for a parish when its incumbent is a lonely, disappointed man—his teaching is so apt to take some colour from his own sorrows. There never was but one preacher who walked this troubled earth with the sunshine of His divine countenance unshadowed by His own sorrows. I think a clergyman ought to be a happy man—a happy man who has known unhappiness. My father was, to my mind, the ideal pastor. But you have not answered my question, Patty. What are you going to do?'

'I think—I—should like to go at once to London,' I answered nervously; 'may I go with you, Bernard, to-morrow?'

'With all my heart, dear. But where will you go at so short a notice. You will scarcely like to stay at an hotel, and you have no friends in London.'

'I am going to my sister.'

I said the words boldly; to speak them at all was so desperate a venture, that it mattered very little how they were spoken.

I felt rather than saw that my cousin gave a little shiver, almost as if I had struck him.

'You are going to your sister, Mrs. Annesley,' he said.

How strange it seemed to hear my pet called by that name; so terrible a sound when spoken in the coldest, hardest accents that I had ever heard fall from Bernard Champion's lips.

'I shall be very happy to take you to town,' he said, after a pause, 'and I will see that you reach your destination safely. There may be little things in this room that you may like to preserve as memo-

There was a touch of stern determination blended with the sorrow in his voice. I knew that he was thinking of my sister. I knew this, and yet even in that moment an irresistible impulse urged me to cast myself upon my knees before him and plead for her.

'Forgive her, Bernard,' I entreated; 'my uncle Geoffrey forgave her before he fell asleep, for he died with a smile upon his face. Oh, cousin, believe—believe me, you will be happier when you have forgiven her!'

'Happier!' he cried passionately; 'I tell you, Martha, she has crushed all capability of happiness out of my heart. She has done worse than this. She has rendered me unfit for the service of my God, for I can only give him half a heart. The other half is withered by her falsehood. Do you know how often I have tried to read that chapter,' he asked, pointing to the testament which lay on the table near him, open at the fifteenth chapter of St. John, 'and do you know how many times my mind has wandered away from that sacred page to brood upon the wrong your sister and my friend Lawrence Annesley have done me? Do you know that to-day, when I stood by my father's grave, while the promise of man's immortality was in my ears, and the nothingness of this lower world should have come closer home to my heart than it ever came before—do you know that even then your sister's image came between me and the mourning crowd and mocked me with a smile. Forgive her? and this was to have been our wedding-day! Forgive her? and I had hoped to see my father smiling upon his grandchildren! Forgive her? no, Patty. It is not in me to forgive her; she has broken my heart; she has shattered my life; for I must abandon my holy office. I was a Christian until the woman I loved struck the blow that has crushed me. I am a pagan now, and the worst of pagans. Dare I preach mercy to others when I cannot be merciful myself! Dare I cry Peace, when there is raging war in my heart!'

I had never seen the latent forces of my cousin's nature aroused until now; yet I had always instinctively comprehended that it was a passionate nature, with slumbering fires that only needed a spark to set them blazing. He walked out of the room and left me alone to think how utterly I had failed to win anything like pity for my erring girl, or for the man who had tempted her to break her sacred promise. I sat alone in the dusk until the parlour-maid brought the lamp, and set the tea-tray on the little table near the fire. She brought the London papers into the room at the same time—they had not yet been countermanded, and came at the usual hour. That packet of papers was a very small thing to set my tears flowing afresh; but the sight of the familiar sheets brought back so vividly the

It had remained in my possession ever since, and I was considering how best I could restore it to Bernard; for I could not help thinking that, after all, my sister's own words might be the most powerful petitioners to win her pardon.

I had read it alone in my desolate room on the dreadful night after my sister had left us. I read it again now, slowly and deliberately; for I felt that it was an appeal, not to Bernard only, but to all who had ever loved and cherished the writer. The letter began abruptly, and had evidently been written at intervals, but all in one day—the day which ended in so much sorrow. There were blots and erasures, and many stains and blisters, that I knew were the traces of tears. My tears fell on it as I read again, to-night, as they had fallen before.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### FORGIVEN.

'You can never forgive me,' wrote my sister; 'I know _that_ before I begin this miserable letter. Oh, to think that I should ever have need so to write to you—to think that I should live to do it! I can never forgive myself for my sin against you, and against all those who have loved and trusted me. But some day, when any sorrow you may feel in my loss—and you have loved me so much more than I deserve, that I know you will be sorry,—when all that has worn quite away, and you look back and remember what a worthless thing I was—a weak, vacillating, helpless creature, with no power to hold firmly by the right,—then, perhaps, you will have mercy on me, and forgive me. When you read this I shall have left my dear old home for ever. I shall have left you close upon the eve of our appointed wedding-day, to become the wife of Lawrence Annesley.

'When was it that I first loved him? I think it began by my being so sorry for him—so sorry for his wasted powers, his useless talents: and then I found out that he was unhappy. I scarcely know how I came to be aware of his unhappiness: unless it was by random words that he let drop now and then, and by the hopeless, absent manner that took the place of his old joyousness. For a long, long time I set no check upon my thoughts, believing implicitly that I felt for Lawrence only as I had a right to feel for the friend of my betrothed husband. It made me very happy to picture a future in

which he was only a secondary figure. I fancied him in our home, Bernard—our friend and guest,—and then all at once I found that figure blotting out all the rest of the picture, until your image melted away, and I knew that I was a false and wicked creature, unworthy of your generous love and trust.

'If you could know how I struggled with my own weak heart; if you could know how desperately I tried to cling to the right, and how I prayed for strength to do so, I think you would pity me, Bernard; the strong should have some compassion for the weak. Sometimes I felt myself wondering about Lawrence Annesley's unhappiness; and then I found myself guessing the reason of his altered manner; and a wicked joy thrilled through my heart as I fancied it was for my sake he was so changed. Oh, despise me, Bernard! I bare my whole heart before you, with all its wicked weakness. I can support your scorn better than I can endure the thought that you should mistake me for something nobler than I am, and be sorry for the loss of a creature who never existed. From my frivolous childhood until this day of my guilt and treachery, I have never been worthy of the love you have given me. I have tried to deserve your affection, but I am not the kind of woman to make you happy all your life. It is better that I should be false to you now, than that I should be a burden to you hereafter. Try to remember this, Bernard, when you think of my wickedness.

'When he told me one day that he loved me, I do not think I was surprised by what he said. But oh! how wicked I must be, for as I stood listening to his passionate words, I felt a joy such as I had never known before, a joy which seemed to lift me away from this earth and all its troubles. Oh, Bernard, forgive me! forgive me! In that moment I forgot that you had ever asked me to be your wife,—that there was a sacred tie between us, to break which would be dishonour. I forgot everything. In all the world there was only Lawrence Annesley and my own wildly beating heart.

'It was not a long treason, Bernard. That unconsciousness of sin, of broken faith, of everything in the world except my love, endured only until I heard my sister's dress rustling along the grass, and awoke to real life once more. No word of mine told Lawrence that his love was returned. My intention, at least, was pure, and I was resolved to do my duty and to keep my promise. Oh, Bernard! it seemed strange to me that, knowing your goodness and your superiority to all other men I had ever met, I yet loved a man whom I knew to be so much your inferior. Love does not always go along with respect; love does not always bow down before the noblest thing it knows; the brightest flowers do not crown nature's grandest spots; and the loftiest mountains are always the loneliest. I fancy sometimes, Bernard, that you are too great a man to be loved.

'How shall I write this letter? How can I explain to you what I

'One day—one fatal day—only a week ago, when I believed that the battle was fought and won, when I fancied him far away from me, forgetful of me perhaps, he came upon me suddenly as I was walking alone on the outskirts of the town, and, at the sight of him, I knew all at once that I could never be your wife. I loved him still. All my struggles, all my fancied victories were nothing. They might have never been, for all the trace they had left behind them now, when the sound of his voice had power to raise such a tumult in my heart. I loved him better than I had ever loved him—better for that weary time of trial and temptation—better for the long, dreary separation in which I had striven so hard to forget him. There could be no treason against you so base as the treason involved in my keeping the letter of a promise which I could not keep in the spirit. Lawrence told me how he too had tried to do his duty, and how miserably he had failed. I dare not plead for him, Bernard. The day may come—when you have won a wife worthier of you than ever I could have been,—I trust in Heaven the day will come when you will hear my poor boy plead for himself, and forgive him. There is so much in life for you; so noble a career open to you, and he has _nothing_ but the love of one foolish woman. I think you can afford to forgive him.

'During this week I have seen him every day. I cannot tell you what arguments he has used to induce me to break my faith. Nothing he could have said, no prayers of his, however passionate, could have pushed me towards this step, if my own heart had not told me that there was no deeper wrong I could do you than to become your wife.

“My first impulse was to come to you and tell you all the truth. I think, Bernard, if I had dared to speak unreservedly, if you had heard my confession and seen my tears you would have forgiven me. I know what a depth of pity and tenderness there is in your heart, and I do believe that I might have won your pardon. But I am a coward. I dare not see your face when the knowledge of my falsehood first comes upon you. I can only write this letter, which you will read after I have stolen like a guilty creature from the home that has sheltered me so long.

“I can say no more. If you cannot forgive me, do not stand between me and my uncle Geoffrey’s forgiveness—do not shut me out for ever from my sister’s love. Ah, pardon me for asking this, for the entreaty is almost an insult! I know that you are a Christian, and that you can never be less than a Christian. How often I have heard you read that tender story of the erring woman whose tearful worship was not rejected. I remember the very tones of your voice, and I cannot think that you will be otherwise than merciful to me.”

Here the letter ended; the last few lines had been rendered almost illegible by my sister’s tears. My own fell very fast as I read them.

“And I too think he must forgive her,” I mused, as I folded Sophy’s letter; and then I rang for the servant to remove the tea. I ascertained that my cousin was alone in his study. Before I went upstairs to begin my packing, which would be a weary business, lasting through the whole night perhaps, I was determined to place my sister’s letter in Bernard’s hands.

I went to the study door and knocked. After a little pause the door was opened, and my cousin stood before me.

“Do you want to speak to me, Patty?” he asked kindly; and then he added, with a sigh, “I am very tired to-night. It will keep till to-morrow, I dare say, what you want to say. Let it be said to-morrow, dear.”

“I have nothing to say, Bernard; I only want to give you this.” I offered him my sister’s letter; his hand advanced to meet it, and then recoiled, as if the thing I pressed upon him had been a serpent.

“I do not wish to read any communication from Mrs. Annesley,” he said.

“But you will read this, Bernard. It is an erring creature’s appeal to your compassion.”

He took the letter.

“I will read it, if you like, Patty,” he answered sadly. “If the reading of it can change my heart, so much the better. I have prayed to God that my heart may be changed.”

“Good-night, Bernard.”

“Good-night, dear.”

My packing lasted nearly all that night. It was close upon day-break when I laid down to take an hour's sleep—to sleep for the last time under that roof. At eight o'clock I was breakfasting with my cousin Bernard in the dining-room where so many social gatherings had been held, and would be held, no doubt, again, but with some familiar faces missing from the circle. A deep, dreary feeling came over me as I thought of that room with new furniture, and wondered how it would look. I had not imposed upon Bernard's kindness in my selection from the things that had belonged to my uncle; I had only taken a few of his favourite books, and an old-fashioned desk on which he had been in the habit of writing.

My cousin said very little to me as we sat opposite to each other that miserable morning, making such a poor pretence of taking meat and drink, for which neither of us had the faintest inclination. He said only what was absolutely necessary as we prepared for our departure, and waited for the vehicle which was to take us to the inn whence the London coach started.

It was a sad journey. I saw the familiar places gliding by me, and fancied that I had perhaps looked on them for the last time. And then we went on into the strange world beyond the narrow boundary of my lost home, and I felt what a lonely creature I was. It was a fatiguing journey. People got in and out of the coach, and ate and drank, and laughed and talked boisterously, until the dull aching of my head grew to a distracting pain. It seemed a very long journey, for my mind went wearily over and over the same ground, while the sound of the rolling wheels jarred upon my ear, while the prim hedgerows crept by me under a misty rain.

Oh, what a miserable place London seemed as the coach blundered and jolted into its stony streets in the chilly dusk! What a heartless, pitiless place it seemed, in which every living creature pushed and struggled on his own account, reckless of his neighbour! Was this the wonderful city of whose brilliant 'season' I had heard the banker's daughters speak in such raptures! We came to the coach office at last, and Bernard helped me to alight upon a muddy pavement, amongst a crowd of noisy, struggling people, who all seemed in a state of alarm about their personal property, and rather vengefully disposed towards one another. When my luggage had been gathered together somehow or other, my cousin put me into a hackney coach. He had spoken to me with all his old kindness during our journey, but he had spoken very seldom. He had sat with his head leaning back in a corner of the coach and his face in shadow. But when I had taken my place in the vehicle that was to convey me to my sister's address, Bernard lingered at the door, and I could see that he had something to say to me.

'Patty,' he said presently, as he stretched out his hand to take mine in a parting grasp, 'my heart was hardened against your sister

I could not answer him. I could only press the hand that held mine.

'God bless you, my dear! You have been my sister in the past, I hope you may be my sister again in the future. 'I will, Bernard.'

'Once more, God bless you, and good bye. Stop, your sister's address is—'

'21, Great Morland Street, Bloomsbury.'

My cousin told the coachman where to drive, and the ponderous equipage lumbered off in the dreary drizzle. I looked my last at my cousin standing in the rain, with his hat lifted, and his dark, handsome face turned towards me with a brother's protecting smile.

'And she did not love him!' I thought. 'Strange mystery of a woman's heart; she could not love this man who, to my mind, seems the very ideal of perfect manhood.'

## CHAPTER IX.

### SOPHY'S NEW LIFE.

AFTER jolting through a great many dreary streets the coach stopped in one which had an air of emptiness, and an absence of life and light which, even to my inexperience, was associated with extreme respectability. I alighted before a handsome-looking doorway, with a very dim light shining through the glass above it. Gas was not very general in those days, and the hall into which I was admitted was feebly illuminated by means of an oil-lamp with a struggling wick. The servant stared at my black dress and at me when I asked for Mrs. Annesley; and she left me standing in the hall while she assisted the coachman with my luggage. Bernard had paid the fare, so I was not exposed to the small misery of a dispute with the coachman.

A person who was not quite a lady, but who was dressed more smartly than any lady in my uncle's parish, came out of the parlour while my trunks were being brought in, and gave me a frosty kind of welcome.

'The young lady whom Mrs. Annesley expected, I suppose,' she said. 'Ah, to be sure. It's on the second floor, miss. Mary, take care the man doesn't scratch the paint with those trunks; and be as quick as you can about it, for the drawing-room tea has been rung for.'

I understood from this speech that my sister and her husband were only second-floor lodgers, and must expect only second-class civility. It all seemed very cold and strange to me, after the home faces and the home comforts. But the thought that I was near my sister blotted out all other thoughts, as I followed the servant up two dreary flights of stairs.

Sophy was sitting alone by the fire when I went in, but she sprang to her feet and ran to meet me. In another moment she was sobbing on my breast.

'My uncle Geoffrey,' she said, between her sobs. 'Oh, what a cruel blow it was, Patty! It seemed so like a judgment upon me.'

She helped me to take off my things, and threw them carelessly on a sofa. I could see that the room was shabbily furnished, and rather untidy.

'I want you to tell me how it happened, Patty,' she said, as we sat down by the fire, she in her old attitude, with her head resting on my shoulder. 'But first let me thank you for coming to me; it is very good of you to come, dear. I thought you would desert me, perhaps, for my wickedness.'

'Desert you, Sophy! You can know very little of me if you thought that.'

'Well, darling, perhaps I did not think it. I may have only feared it. Oh, Patty, do you believe my cousin Bernard will ever forgive me?'

'He has forgiven you, dear. He told me to tell you so. But this disappointment has been a very bitter blow for him, Sophy. Heaven only knows when he will recover from the shock.'

'He is very sorry, then?'

'Very sorry.'

After that I told her how Bernard had forgiven her; and then we were able to talk more calmly. I heard all about the hasty flight, the hurried wedding; not celebrated in a pretty village church, not sanctified by the solemn words that call Heaven's blessing on a happy union, but huddled over in the dingy office of a district registrar, with the lodging-house maid-servant for a witness.

'I love him dearly,' my sister said, speaking of Lawrence, 'and I think I could be happy in the knowledge of his love and truth even if we were wandering on some desolate island, with the consciousness that death was waiting for us, turn which way we would. But oh,

I felt this a bitter reproach against myself, though Sophy had no thought of my part in the sad mistake which had caused so much misery. It was I who had temporized—it was I who had hoped against hope. I told my sister this; but she would not accept any comfort in her grief.

'Martha,' she said, looking at me with indescribable sorrow in her face, 'do you think that my conduct to Bernard had anything to do with my uncle's death.'

How could I answer her? I knew what my cousin had felt upon this subject; and yet people suffering from my uncle's disease have died at the very moment when their lives seemed happiest and most tranquil. I told Sophy this, and I could see that she was comforted in some measure by my words. And then, after a long silence, during which her face had been half hidden on my breast, she began to talk to me about Lawrence.

He was so good, she told me—so devoted, so gentle; and if it had not been for the great sorrow of the last week, they would have been so happy together; even in that dingy lodging, with a snappish landlady, and a maid who never answered a bell until it had been rung three times. She told me how anxious her young husband was about the future; to earn a living for his darling; to scrape together enough money for the furnishing of a pretty house in the suburbs.

'London is so dreadful,' Sophy said, with a shudder; 'but Lawrence says that in London there is always a chance of making money. And you know he is so clever, Patty; and there are so many things in which he may succeed, if he is only fortunate. He is trying to find some pupils for drawing and painting. You know what a wonderful talent he has, or he could even teach music or languages. He has advertised in the papers, and has walked miles from place to place answering other people's advertisements; and he has some hope of a school at Clapham, where the principal was very much pleased with his sketches. You who have seen Lawrence so frivolous and unstable would never believe how determined he can be when there is a real necessity for resolution and perseverance. If he gets employed by the Clapham schoolmaster, it will be something to begin with; but in the mean time we are very poor,—but not too

poor to find a hearty welcome for you, dearest,' cried my sister, fearful lest I should fancy myself an intruder.

I told her how my uncle had provided for me. She opened her eyes to their widest extent as she heard of my modest little income. She had been happily placed all her life, knowing neither the want of money nor the possession of it, except in the most limited degree, and to her a hundred pounds seemed a very large sum. She thought of it as a child thinks of a crown piece,—something that would buy all the pretty things in the world; but she had no idea of it in relation to the petty daily wants, to supply which money dribbles ignominiously away.

I was grieved to find from my sister's lips that Lawrence had no positive income whatever. He was the spoiled child of extravagant and impoverished parents, and he had nothing in the world but what they could afford to allow him until he could establish himself in a professional position. Of this there seemed no chance now. A great deal of money had been spent upon him; but all the expense of the past had been fruitless. He was highly educated and accomplished; but his versatile talents were calculated to distinguish him in a drawing-room, and not to advance him in life. Already I began to understand that the men who make their names heard in the world are very rarely the men who shine in drawing-rooms. Lawrence himself had some idea of this, and alluded to it that night as we lingered over the tea-table. I took the caddy out of my sister's hands, for I saw she had very vague ideas as to the number of spoonfuls of tea, or the management of the teapot; and from that moment I was established in the post of housekeeper which it was my destiny to hold so long.

'The school at Clapham will be fifty pounds a year,' he said, 'and fifty pounds a year is a pound a week, or would be, if the weeks in the year were a more convenient number. I am taking my tea on a gentle slope at this moment. I told them that it would be my happiness to make their dreary London lodging as much like a home as I could, and I told them what I fancy I had scarcely need to tell them, for surely they must have known it without any words from me,—I told them that whatever I possessed in the world should be freely shared with them, that my last sixpence as well as my most willing service should be devoted to their comfort. We sat talking together till late into the night, and from that hour I felt every grief or joy of Lawrence Annesley's as much a part of my own life as if he had been indeed my brother.

I went out early the next morning and wandered all alone in the strange London streets. I was glad to get clear of the dismal streets and squares of the respectable neighbourhood into the brightness and life of the crowded thoroughfares, in which I felt myself such a helpless country-bred wanderer. But I contrived to make my way to the shops I wanted, somehow or other. I wanted some birds and flowers for my sister's windows, and after some inquiry I found a very miserable-looking neighbourhood in which all the singing birds of the metropolis seemed to have colonized, and where I bought two canaries. And then, as if by a kind of rustic instinct which took me to all that was most countrified in this stony-hearted London, I pushed my way almost unaided to Covent Garden, whence I went back to Great Morland Street in a coach, laden with my two birdcages, and with a collection of stocks and geraniums, balsams and carnations, all simple inexpensive flowers, for the ornamentation of my darling's dingy parlour.

After arranging my purchases to Sophy's delight, I went down-stairs to make friends with the snappish landlady. It seemed rather an impracticable task at first, but when she found that my sister and her husband were likely to be permanent lodgers, and that I meant to retain the little bedroom that had been taken for me, she softened considerably, and made several little concessions for the comfort of the two children who were playing at housekeeping in her second floor. I found that Lawrence had been rather unconscionable in the matter of ringing the bell, and that his university notions, with regard to the service of a scout, had been very trying to the temper of the overworked lodging-house servant. these little matters, and I went up-stairs very well pleased with the result of my mission.

Lawrence had started off to Clapham immediately after breakfast. Sophy was childishly pleased with the idea of the pleasure he would feel at the altered aspect of the room. It is a noticeable thing how much brighter the dullest room may be made to look by a little neatness of arrangement, a few cut flowers in a glass, a stand of geraniums, and a couple of birdcages. I had found the room a chaos—Sophy's needles and reels of cotton scattered amongst her husband's palettes and colours, Lawrence's books and papers heaped pell-mell on all the tables, and I amused myself by classifying all these possessions, making a little library in one corner, a nook for Sophy's needlework in another, a tidy little arrangement of a table and chair for Lawrence's painting in another. I had good reason to be thankful for the occupation, however trivial, which saved me from brooding on the sorrow that was still so new to us; but every now and then, at every little pause in my work, or even when I was busiest, the thought of my old home and my lost guardian came back to me in all its bitterness. I knew that my sister was thinking of the same sorrowful subject, for I stopped sometimes to look at her pensive face as she sat idle at an open window, watching for her husband's return.

He was delighted with the improvement of the rooms when he came back late in the afternoon; and he brought good news. The Clapham schoolmaster had accepted his services, and the fifty pounds a year were at least secure. He had written to his mother, informing her of his marriage, only the day before, he told me, as we sat talking after tea, and he was sure of help from her; but for the present this imprudent union was to be kept a secret from Sir John Annesley, who was an invalid, and who was by no means on the best terms with his son.

Looking back at that far-away time, I find myself wondering how I slipped so easily into my new life, and accepted Lawrence Annesley as my sister's husband almost as contentedly as if no cloud of sorrow had darkened their runaway union.

They were such children, and they were so fond of me. They trusted so implicitly in my superior wisdom, and leaned with such confidence upon my love. Knowing this as I did, could I be angry with them? could I remember even Bernard's wrongs, when my bright-haired darling sat with her hand clasped in mine, and poor, tender-hearted, sweet-tempered, frivolous Lawrence called me sister? And then Bernard had forgiven his cousin. The noble soul had conquered in the terrible strife. His letter to me, one of the kindest letters that ever brother wrote to sister, contained a friendly message for poor penitent Sophy, a word of friendliness even for Lawrence.

My tears fell thick and fast upon that noble letter, for the calm resignation which was breathed in every sentence told me more plainly than the most passionate lamentations could have done, that the writer's heart was broken. That phrase seems only a sentimental hyperbole, perhaps; and yet hearts have been broken. I knew that the one brief romance of my cousin's life was closed for ever; that no woman, however worthy, could be to him what Sophy had been; and that, in bidding his calm farewell to her, he parted for ever with his youth.

All Sophy's possessions, her girlish treasures, and the trousseau which had occupied so great a place in my thoughts, were sent to her within the week after my journey to London. The labels of the trunks were addressed in Bernard's hand; and in my sister's boxes I found many little things—books and prints, simple, old-fashioned knickknacks, that had been scattered about the rectory drawing-room—which had not belonged to her, but which she had admired or used; and I knew that only Bernard could have selected these things.

Sophy knew it too, and the sight of the household treasures moved her deeply.

'How good he is! how generous to remember me so tenderly!' she whispered, as she took up a little paper-knife which my uncle Geoffrey had used, and pressed it gently to her lips.

The time went by with us. Our lives were very simple, very tranquil; and I am compelled to confess we were very poor. I own this reluctantly, for I know that there was some imprudence in our little household, which I, who was trusted so entirely, ought to have prevented. Lawrence received money from his mother, my little income was advanced to me by Bernard, and the Clapham school-master paid monthly. But two children suddenly left to administer their own affairs could scarcely have been more childish than Lawrence and Sophy. My darling missed her piano, and her devoted young husband hired an expensive instrument the next day from the nearest place where such things could be hired. If Lawrence passed through Covent Garden in his daily peregrinations, he bought his wife a bouquet; if he saw anything in a shop window which he fancied she would like to have, he went into the shop and bought it. We had hothouse flowers and new music sometimes when we had no dinner; and I was obliged to make myself very disagreeable in my capacity of housekeeper, in order to bring about a little better management of our funds. But then we took life so lightly, that our worst difficulties in the way of money matters were only something to laugh at.

We were very happy; the bitter grief for my uncle's death softened into a calm and holy sorrow, which had its own place in my

life, and was no cloud upon my quiet happiness with the sister I loved so dearly.

I scarcely know how the days slipped by us; but I know that I had been living with my sister and her husband between four and five months, and it was very close upon the end of August, when our carelessly happy life was brought to a terrible close, as suddenly as some dream of departed friends and a lost home, from which we awake to find ourselves lonely and desolate.

It was nearly the end of August, and people told us that there was no one in town; but as I found myself jostled by just as many passengers, and pushed about quite as much as ever when I emerged from the quiet of Great Morland Street into any of the bustling thoroughfares, I was unable to realize the emptiness of London about which Londoners complained so bitterly. When the days were very hot, and the street especially dusty, Sophy and I, sitting at our needlework by an opened window, have confessed to each other a weary yearning for yellow corn-fields, and the rich slope of uplands where the grass was ruffled by fresh breezes from the summer sea; but we never said as much before Lawrence, for the Clapham school kept him prisoner in London, and we knew that at a word from Sophy his good resolutions would have melted into air, and he would have insisted on running away into the country to look for the roses that had vanished from his young wife's cheeks.

Yes, the girlish bloom had perished. The tender heart had suffered very bitterly from the pain of an enduring remorse. Even when most childishly happy with the husband of her choice, Sophy never forgot the wrong she had done Bernard Champion. She thought of it more and more, day by day, I believe, as her nature became sublimated by a diviner tenderness under the most sacred influence of womanhood. I had now to superintend the preparation of something even more interesting than a trousseau. My big covered work-basket was a repository of tiny morsels of delicate lawn and muslin; and when Sophy and I sat together in the sunny window looking out upon a prospect of slated roofs and blackened chimney-pots, we beguiled ourselves by fond talk of a happy future to be spent in a suburban cottage, a little bower nestling amongst lilacs and laburnums, with a tiny grass plat just big enough for the most enchanting infant in creation to roll upon.

One day, when the weather was particularly lovely, and that yearning for the breath of a fresh breeze and the beauty of a rural landscape possessed us more completely than usual, Lawrence proposed a holiday. He had just received a remittance from his mother and was in very high spirits.

'There's a university race at Henley-on-Thames, to-morrow,' he said; 'and there's a coach that starts from the White Horse Cellar

this afternoon. We'll go down; put up at an inn; see the race to-morrow; and come home by the night mail. There'll be a lot of fellows whom I know at Henley, and we shall have a glorious time of it, if you think you can manage the journey, Sophy darling, without fatigue.'

Of course my pet declared that there was no possibility of her being tired by any happy holiday spent with her husband. As for his sake she had broken her solemn engagement to Bernard, so to give him pleasure she would have made any sacrifice of her own inclination; but in this case there was no sacrifice. We were both delighted at the prospect of a day by the delicious river about which Lawrence was so eloquent; and I fancied that a change from the stifling atmosphere of London would bring new brightness to my sister's faded face.

The next day dawned upon us pleasantly in pretty country rooms, where the pure white hangings were almost as fragrant as the perfumed air that blew across so many gardens before it came in at our open windows. We breakfasted very early; and the simple country breakfast—the home-made loaf and yellow cream, the fruit and honey, and pinkly tinted new laid eggs—seemed a repast such as one reads of in a fairy tale.

Never had I seen Lawrence Annesley in such high spirits. Bright always, to-day he brightened with every flash of sunlight that flitted across his face, with every glancing ripple of the river which flowed under our window as we sat at breakfast.

The inn at which we stopped was close to the bridge, and there was a balcony outside our window which commanded a superb view of the river. Here Sophy and I were to watch the race, while Lawrence wandered freely in the meadows along the shore, finding old friends and making new acquaintance at every turn. He had been very popular among his set at the university, and his set had been a very large one. He left us almost immediately after breakfast, promising to return in an hour or two. If we grew tired of the balcony, there was a lawn below, a lovely slope of velvet grass, whose outermost fringe was ruffled by the river as it rippled by; and there was a tent under some trees. Gaily dressed people were already beginning to assemble in this river-side garden.

I think Lawrence must have come back to us at least half a dozen times during the hour in which he first left us, so anxious was he that we should be comfortable and happy, and feel no sense of loneliness in his absence. Let me recall the last time of all, when he came back flushed and dusty, delighted with his encounters with old companions, pleased with himself and all the universe, but above all things devotedly in love with his wife.

'There are such lots of fellows I know about the place,' he said,

I knew, as well as I knew anything in this world, that my sister was never “quite happy” in her husband’s absence, and I knew that she would not mar his pleasure by confessing as much just now. A picture of them rises before me as I write this, and I can see Lawrence and my sister as I saw them that day, more distinctly than I can see the pictures on the wall before me, for _they_ seem blurred and dim across a mist of tears. I see them standing side by side in the open window, while I sit out in the balcony and look back towards them. I see my sister’s face lifted to her husband’s, with unspeakable affection in its tender smile; the little hand laid lightly on his arm, so fondly tempted to detain him, so unselfishly anxious to let him go. And looking down at her I can see the bright boyish countenance, the sunny hazel eyes, which I saw first amidst the lonely ruins of Rixmount.

“Oh, darling, you must go,” she cried, pushing him from her with a pretty playful gesture; “your old friends are waiting for you. Come back to me, dear,—but not too soon.”

But not too soon! Ah, how those words rang in my ears after that day—commonplace words, that were afterwards to assume so terrible a significance!

He went away at last—after more affectionate demonstration than some people would have made on parting with their families preparatory to sailing for Australia. I am glad to think he lingered so long that morning, and that the kiss which he always pressed upon his wife’s forehead when he bade her good-bye was even more tender than usual. There are people who think all these demonstrations—these kisses and farewells before every brief separation between those who love each other—an unnecessary waste of words. But I have wondered sometimes whether the wife who scarcely looks up from the morning paper when her husband goes away to his daily duty, ever thinks, when the hall door bangs behind him, that he may never cross its threshold again with any consciousness of coming back to her—with any sense of the wailing cry that is uttered above his coffin. “Oh, if I had loved you better! Lawrence left us, and my sister, a little tired with her journey, and with the excitement of the morning, lay down upon the old-fashioned white dimity-covered sofa, and fell into a placid slumber.

'The time will seem so much shorter if I sleep,' she murmured.

I sat and watched her for a little as she slept, with my hand clasped lovingly in hers. I sat looking down at the fair pale face upon the white pillow, with the loose golden hair scattered round it; and when the hand loosened I crept softly away, and went out upon the balcony.

There were voices sounding merrily in every direction; there were gay dresses making spots of vivid colour against a cool background of green; and over all the sun was shining; and through all the gay confusion of voices and laughter I heard the eternal ripple of the river, and the rustling of the sedges on its brink.

I looked back at my sister sleeping as sweetly as an infant, with her lips a little parted, and one loose tress of pale golden hair faintly ruffled by her breath.

Oh, Heaven have mercy upon all human love and human loss, as He had compassion on the widow of Nain! All the old agony comes back to me when I think of my sister's sleep, and remember her awakening.

# OUR EMINENT LIVING DIVINES.

BY THE AUTHOR OF “THE LIFE OF SOUTHEY,” “ASTRELLO,” ETC.

## ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

THE Church of England may well be proud of her episcopal guardians and counsellors. If we search her muster-roll of bishops, past or present—those who have laboured diligently and faithfully, and have long since gone to their reward, or those who are actively labouring amongst us now,—we shall find names synonymous with primitive purity of life and jealous devotion to her interests. Throughout every page of her history we meet with men whose piety and zeal, no less than their learning and talents, have been an adornment to the holy calling to which they had bound themselves in a willing bondage. She can point to heroes, valiant for the faith, defying chains and death for the love they bore her. She can claim not a few who have joined the noble army of martyrs, and are now rejoicing in the ranks of the blessed that they have been found worthy to suffer. In no age has she been without her faithful witnesses, her zealous champions. Ridley and Latimer, Cranmer and Hooper, stand in the front and vanguard, and in their deaths kindled, as they trusted in God they would, such a light as has not yet, and never will be put out. From that day to this she has never wanted watchmen to warn her against enemies, and to reprove her false friends, though, happily, they have not been called upon to pass through the fiery ordeal, or to seal their devotion by their blood. What nobler spectacle can be afforded than that of Abbott raising his voice against the corruption and profligacy of the Stuart Court? What better service could have been rendered to religion than that magnificent labour of love, the translation of the Bible, which is indeed the Vulgate, circulating, as it does, into millions of homes, and throughout every quarter of the world? When threatened with illegal violence, who so bold and intrepid as her champions Ken and his mitred brethren? To heal the wounds of civil discord and sectarian differences, who so apt as the gentle, eloquent Tillotson? and to resist the presumptuous reasonings of intellectual scepticism, who so lucid, deep, and crushing as Butler?

We might without difficulty enlarge the list indefinitely, and show how our bishops have really been the pillars of the Church. We might cite a host of names from the days of the Reformation downward, whose very mention would kindle a glow of gratitude, pleasure, and

admiration in the hearts of all true Churchmen; but the past is not now for us, though such a review would be only a fitting preface, did our space permit it, to the work which we have taken in hand in all diffidence and charity. We propose to give, monthly, a biographical sketch of one of our more eminent living bishops, not in a captious, critical spirit, but with a view to estimate the great work they are performing, and to show that we have amongst us prelates zealous, active, and enlightened, working for the Church's welfare—men mindful of their ordination vow, and exciting within themselves the gift of grace, not in the spirit of fear, but of strength of love and of discipline. They are indeed the salt of the Church, as their humbler brethren are the salt of the earth. To them is entrusted the government of the Church; and accordingly as they discharge their duty does that Church prosper or decay, suffer or thrive. The influence they wield is vast, and in proportion to its vastness ought it to be used with judgment and discrimination, truth and prayer. They are the exemplars, in a very emphatic degree, of the Christian church, and when they fail in attaining the high standard of faith, purity, and zeal expected from them, their weakness entails no slight injury and disparagement upon the communion to which they are linked by the holiest and most privileged of bonds.

At the head of our list naturally stands—for he is there _ex officio_—the Archbishop of Canterbury; but were it otherwise, it is in no merely complimentary sense that we say the present tenant of Lambeth Palace might deservedly occupy that honourable position.

Dr. Charles Thomas Longley, Primate of all England, and Metropolitan, the subject of our present memoir, was born in London in the year 1794. His father for some time enjoyed the honourable post of Recorder of Rochester, and subsequently sat on the magisterial bench at the Thames Police Court. He was also known in his day as a political writer, and gave to the world two treatises, one on 'Trial by Jury,' the other on 'The Complete Representation of the People.' The mention of these works, however, is intended to serve no other purpose than to show that the family of the present archbishop can claim one man, at least, of culture and learning—a man who evidently took an absorbing interest in the public questions of his time. Charles Longley was sent to Westminster School, and there educated on the foundation. Little is recorded of his early school days; so we may suppose that he pursued there the even tenor of his way like the mass of his fellow-students. But one incident may be recalled, as it illustrates a custom which will probably soon become entirely obsolete, owing to tyrannous abuses it was open to. We allude to the system of fagging. Dr. Vowles Short, now Bishop of St. Asaph, was the conventional master of young Longley, and, notwithstanding the service exacted

in those juvenile hours, a friendship sprang up between them which has steadily increased with years; for certainly nothing can be more affectionate than have been the relations of these two divines ever since they left Westminster. Dr. Longley, whose name may still be seen carved on the oaken walls of the dormitory, retains a fond regard for his old school, and is rarely absent from the annual dinner, at which, when he attends, he is warmly welcomed and cheered by the Queen's scholars as he passes up the hall. He is, moreover, one of the Busby trustees.

From Westminster young Longley went to Christ Church, Oxford, as student, and took a first class in _literis humanioribus_ in the Michaelmas Term of 1815, graduating M.A. in 1818. He was appointed Censor—that is, Tutor—of his House, and Public Examiner in Classics in 1825, having for his colleagues the late Dr. Cardwell, the present Regius Professor of Pastoral Theology at Oxford, Dr. Ogilvie, and Dr. Jelf, Principal of King's College, London. This scholastic honour was repeated in Michaelmas Term of the same year, and again in Easter Term, 1826.

In 1828 Dr. Longley had joined to his tutorial duties the clerical duties of the pretty little rural village of Cowley, a village of a very small population, and without either a resident squire or a local gentry, but remarkable for the beauty and repose of its situation, it being embosomed in woods in the midst of fertile meadows. It is also a curious fact that this little village obtained in succession as its pastors three men who have subsequently become bishops of the Church of England. In 1827 Dr. Longley abandoned his academic career, and committed himself more thoroughly to the ministry by accepting the rectory of West Tytherley, in Hampshire, where he performed the duties of his office with exemplary zeal, winning the esteem and affection of those over whom he was spiritually placed by his earnest attention for their welfare, and his general courtesy and kindness of manner. This parish he retained only two years, being towards the end of 1829 appointed to the high and responsible post of Head Master of Harrow School.

The history of this celebrated nursery of knowledge deserves a slight mention here. The free school of Harrow owes its origin to that strong educational movement which stirred up the people of England during the reigns of Edward the Sixth and Queen Elizabeth,—excited, doubtless, by gratitude for the great blessings of the Reformation, and fear lest ignorance should lead the nation to relapse into the ancient superstitions which were still fresh in the minds of all. It was founded in 1590 by the piety of John Lyon, a wealthy yeoman of the hamlet of Preston in that parish, who, in the year 1571, procured letters-patent and a royal charter recognizing the foundation which he proposed, and empowering him to draw up certain statutes for the

regulation of the establishment. Nineteen years after the issue of this charter John Lyon promulgated his 'Orders, Statutes, and Rules for the Government of the School,' a very curious document indeed. The sum of £300 was to be expended on the building of a school, with houses for the master and usher, who were to be elected by the governors, the former 'to be on no account below the degree of Master of Arts,' nor the latter 'under that of Bachelor of Arts.' The stipends were at the same time fixed at £26 13s. 4d. for the master, with the addition of £3 6s. 8d. for his fuel! For the usher £13 6s. 8d., with a provision for fuel similar to that of his superior. The rules ordered to be observed in the government of the school are drawn up with the most singular precision; the number of forms, with the books to be used in each, are specified; the hours of attending school, and the vacations and holidays appointed; and the amusements directed to be confined to 'driving a top, tossing a hand-ball, and running and shooting.' The latter appears to have been considered an essential part of education, as all parents were required to furnish their sons with 'bowstrings, shafts, and braces, to exercise shooting.' It is also directed that the number of scholars should be educated freely; but at the same time the master is allowed to receive, over and above children of the inhabitants of the parish, 'so many foreigners as the whole number may be well taught and applied, and the place can conveniently contain, by the judgment and discretion of the governors,'—a proof that, even in the infancy of his foundation, John Lyon was not without hopes that others would eventually be attracted from a distance to share the advantages of his liberality, besides those benefited by a gratuitous education. Other provisions were made to the effect that '_no girls_ shall be received to be taught in the same school,' and that 'the masters must in all cases be unmarried men.' To the foregoing statutes five articles were added, which the master is required to recite to all persons bringing their sons:—'1. You shall submit your child in all things to be ordered according to the discretion of schoolmaster and usher. 2. You shall find your child sufficient paper, ink, pens, books, candles for winter, and all other things at any time requisite for the maintenance of his study. 3. You shall allow your child, at all times, bow-shafts, bowstrings, and a brace. 4. You shall see diligently, from time to time, that your child shall keep duly the ordinary hours in coming to school, and in diligently keeping and continuing his study. 5. You shall be content to receive your child and put him to some profitable occupation if, after one year's experience, he shall be found unapt to the learning of grammar. If your child shall use, at sundry times, to be absent from school, unless by reason of sickness, he shall be utterly banished from the school.' The school, for a considerable time after its foundation, appears not to have attracted

Under the auspices of Dr. Drury, amongst whose pupils are to be found the illustrious names of Lord Byron and the late Sir Robert Peel, the school reached an eminence it had never before known, the number of scholars at one time exceeding 350. Under Dr. Butler, his successor, the highest number was 295. To Dr. Butler succeeded Dr. Longley in 1829, who found on his entrance 115 boys in the school, and on his resignation, seven years after, left 165, having during that time directed the studies and moral training of 473 youths. Amongst his distinguished pupils may be mentioned Sir Benjamin C. Brodie, F.R.S., professor at Oxford, the lamented Archdeacon Henry Drury, the present Sir Robert Peel, Mr. Beresford Hope, W. H. Gregory, M.P., Lord Gifford, Lord Cantilupe, the Hon. Messrs. Grimston and Egerton, and J. B. Blackett, M.P.

Throughout his active and arduous career at Harrow, Dr. Longley was distinguished not more for the ability and firmness of his rule than for his modest bearing, his unaffected manner, his kindness and gentleness, his true piety and open-handed generosity.

He remained there till 1836, when he was called away to a higher sphere of usefulness, having been appointed to the newly created bishopric of Ripon. A farewell sermon which he preached on 1st Thessalonians, 4th chapter, 1st verse, exhibited not only his character, but the outlines of the faith that was in him. In it he reviewed the great truths of the gospel, the scheme of salvation, the atonement, justification by faith, sanctification, the power of baptism, and the nature of the Holy Sacrament. We refer to this sermon because it was published at the earnest request of the scholars, whom it deeply affected. Another proof how tenderly the name of Dr. Longley was cherished at Harrow is the fact, that at the speeches of that year affectionate allusion was made to his leaving, and Mr. F. R. Mills, who delivered the Latin oration, warmly eulogized the bishop for his ability, liberality, prudence, and amenity. 'They loved him,' said the speaker, 'present; they deplored him absent.' Nevertheless, he congratulated his lordship on the gratifying honour that had been conferred upon him.

Whilst at Harrow Dr. Longley violated one of the strictest rules of the founder—it is true he had numerous precedents to justify the amiable offence—by marrying the eldest daughter of the first Lord Congleton.

The selection of Dr. Longley for the new see of Ripon was, in every respect, a judicious one; though the acceptance of the office by him was not without its embarrassments and annoyances. A large class of the people had expressed a very strong feeling against Lord Melbourne's bill for creating new bishoprics, and in the House of Commons the Radicals voted against it to a man. It was therefore no very enviable position that of first bishop, since the occupant of the episcopal throne might feel sure the public would note and criticize his conduct with more than ordinary severity. Truly might Dr. Longley subscribe to the declaration, _Nolo episcopari_. However, having accepted the high and venerable office, he discharged its duties with exemplary zeal. For twenty years he assiduously laboured in his young diocese with the ever-present consciousness of one who felt that there were souls to be saved in that densely crowded vineyard. Cheerfully he bore the heat and burthen of that long day of toil and responsibility, and great was his reward. Immediately upon his consecration he set to work to establish a Diocesan Church Extension Fund, by means of which several hundreds of churches were erected in the large and populous towns of the north. No better instance, however, can be given of his genuine benevolence and active charity—charity in the true sense of the word—than his conduct during the great calamity at Holmfirth, which occurred on the night of the 5th February, 1852. From the succession of rainy weather, which had continued, with slight intervals, for five or six days, all the watercourses, streamlets, and rivers of Yorkshire had been filled with water, and many of them overflowed their banks, doing considerable injury. A large reservoir, especially, situated on a high moorland, above the valley of the Holme, became overcharged, and burst about one o'clock in the morning of the 5th of February, the flood carrying destruction and death in its course. The roar of the water in its fatal career down the sides of the hills and through the valley was terrific. In its mad rage the torrent inundated mills and cottages, overwhelming by one fell swoop, not only the buildings, but the inhabitants, nearly all of whom were asleep in their beds, in one fearful doom. Not less than sixty persons were drowned on that awful night. With characteristic promptitude the good bishop hastened, like a true Christian shepherd, to the scene of the catastrophe, and personally exerted himself to alleviate the sudden and dreadful distress of the sufferers. He went from house to house offering the consolations of religion to the afflicted and bereaved; he preached in various pulpits, to excite the sympathies and liberality of the public, and from his own resources largely contributed to their relief, supplying both money and clothing. In a word, he acted the _rôle_ of a true Samaritan, and much of the mitigation of that calamity is due to the watchful interest he took

His indefatigable zeal and kindly concern in the minutest as well as the most important matters of his diocese naturally won him the love and esteem of all classes, those even who opposed the idea of episcopal extension; and on his removal to a wider sphere of usefulness and activity, addresses were presented to him, not only by the clergy of the Archdeaconries of Craven and Richmond, but by the Corporation of Ripon, and from the congregation of Holmfirth. In reply, the bishop, deeply moved, thanked God that, in going in and out among them, he had secured their favourable regard as the result of his constant endeavour to identify himself with them for their good. He considered it, he said, a plain duty to appear among them in their houses of affliction, as he had pledged himself at consecration to 'uphold the weak, heal the sick, bind up the broken;' and so, with an assurance of his prayers and of his fatherly regard, he bade them farewell.

It is not, however, in deeds of active goodness and charity only that a bishop has to prove his Christian zeal and sincerity. He has to reprove the lukewarm, and to uphold the religion of Christ as revealed in the Holy Scriptures. At his last visitation at Leeds Dr. Longley could not help observing that Churchmen had not done so much as Dissenters in the way of church building, and energetically denounced the glaring desecration of the sabbath. In 1850 the judgment of the Privy Council was pronounced in the Gorham case. This case had excited a vast amount of interest, and, unfortunately, given rise to much bitter and acrimonious discussion in the Church. Now this was especially the time for a bishop to exercise his influence, and maintain peace in his diocese. Addresses, embracing the theological views of the subscribers, and calling for a bold expression of opinion, were presented to him from Leeds, Wakefield, Ripon, the Deanery of North Craven, and the Archdeaconry of Richmond. To these he gave a clear and unequivocal reply. He objected, he said, to Mr. Gorham and the Court of Privy Council which acquitted him, and delivered an elaborate argument in favour of baptismal regeneration; he, however, advised, above all things, quietness and peace. He was always firm, but never unkind, and in his dealings with the High Church clergy of St. Saviour's, Leeds, who, with Dr. Hook at their head, openly defied him, was patient and forbearing. His aim was not to stir up strife, but to pour oil on the troubled waters.

In 1856, Dr. Maltby, the venerable Bishop of Durham, the last of a long line of prelatic princes, resigned his see, owing to the increasing infirmities of age, which incapacitated him from performing the duties of his office. This was a novel step,—the only other instance of resignation being that of Nicholas de Farnham, who ruled the diocese from 1240 to 1249. With universal approval, Dr. Longley was translated to Durham. At his primary visitation in

1857 he made graceful allusion to the liberal and high-minded princes and prelates who had wielded the temporal and spiritual crosier of this northern See before him, and spoke in eloquent terms of his immediate predecessor. He declared that he was resolved to counsel and advise clergy and laity alike in the spirit and with the affection of a father; that he would support the brethren, encourage the timid, arbitrate fairly and affectionately in all differences that might be referred to him, and constantly so preach the gospel as to let the poor see that, besides their own minister, the chief pastor of the diocese cared for them and their children. Such, he declared, was the picture of a model Christian bishop; such he would endeavour to be.

For four years he laboured diligently and faithfully in this northern vineyard, when he was translated to York, and became Primate of England and Metropolitan, the highest post in the Church save one. To this post—the Archbishopric of Canterbury—he was elevated two years later, on the death of Dr. Sumner. Several names were put forward at the time as the probable successor of Dr. Sumner, and amongst them that of the Bishop of London; but the choice of the Crown fell on one who had long been tried, and whose qualifications for the supreme office were universally acknowledged. Indeed, no man could have been more judiciously selected by Lord Palmerston. To fill this high—in fact, this highest of holy functions, a man of even temper, practised moderation, large experience, and extensive knowledge is required. A proud and vain, a meddling and ambitious, a world-seeking and selfish, an irritable and domineering spirit, might work consummate mischief to the Church, by sowing divisions within her pale, and bringing the clergy and sacred things into contempt. From the days of Laud it has been, as a rule, thought expedient to search out for the archiepiscopal throne men remarkable for sound doctrine, deep piety, and eminent learning, rather than men of brilliant abilities and dazzling attainments; above all, it has been found desirable to nominate men who have not thrust themselves forward in the world of politics, and been conspicuous by their partisanship in the theological discussions of the day. St. Paul particularly enjoins that a bishop should be blameless,—that is, that his life should have been, and should be, so pure and virtuous, that the finger of detraction could not point to a blot or stain on his escutcheon—so pure and virtuous that the breath of suspicion could not tarnish it.

The prize—for a prize it is, and worthy the honest and humble ambition of any true minister of Christ who faithfully believes that by adding to the area of his duties he can extend his opportunities of doing good—is a prize of no small value. Whether we regard it historically, or as placing its occupant in a high social position, or giving immense influence and patronage, and therefore power for

weal or woe, for good or evil, it is equally a great prize. The archiepiscopal see of Canterbury is the oldest in England, and was founded so far back as the time of St. Augustine, who converted Ethelbert, King of Kent, to Christianity, if not by that monk himself. Many of the archbishops have been men of eminence, and conspicuous, if not always for their piety, at least for their ability and learning. Examining the rolls of this venerable diocese we find, before the Reformation, the names of Lanfranc, Bishop of Caen; Anselm, Bishop of Bec, Cardinal Stafford, Kemp, Bouchier, and Morton; and since the Reformation, Cranmer, Bancroft, Laud, Juxton, Tillotson, and Tenison. Moreover, the See has furnished eighteen saints to the Church of Rome, nine cardinals, twelve Chancellors, four Lord Treasurers, and one Lord Chief Justice. The diocese itself consists of the county of Kent, with the exception of the city and deanery of Rochester and some London parishes. It possessed at one time some peculiar prerogatives. For example, it was an old privilege that wherever the archbishops had manors or advowsons, they should be exempt from the jurisdiction of the ordinary. This was in existence so recently as 1846, when it was abolished by Act of Parliament. The archbishop alone styles himself called _Diviná Providentiá_, the rest of the bishops adopting simply the phrase _Diviná Permissione_. Wherever the Court may be, the King and Queen are his parishioners. The Bishop of London is his dean, the Bishop of Winchester his sub-dean, the Bishop of Lincoln his chancellor, and the Bishop of Rochester his chaplain. He ranks next to the princes of the blood royal, and before the Lord Chancellor. He is the patron of a hundred and eighty-three livings, not a few of them very valuable, many of them ranging from £500 to £900 a year; some from £1,000 and upwards, such as Aldington and Wrotham, each worth a thousand a year; Lydd, £1,200; Cliffe-at-Hoo, £1,300. He has also in his gift the archdeaconries of Maidstone and Canterbury, with a prebendal stall to each; and he enjoys the appointment of the six preacherships in the cathedral.

Since the elevation of Dr. Longley to the archbishopric, the chief theological discussions which have agitated the Church have turned upon inspiration and the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures. The judgment of the Privy Council in the case of the 'Essays and Reviews' had profoundly disquieted and distressed a very large portion of the nation, upon whom the new doctrines—not new, by the way, but only newly imported into the bosom of the Anglican Church—came with a very painful surprise. It was then naturally asked what were the views and opinions of the Primate; and to this inquiry he replied, March 14th, 1864, by a pastoral which was in every respect reassuring. He declared that he differed from the judgment of the Privy Council, though it would be unbecoming in
