The challenge to the priests of Baal, the exquisite irony of Elijah, his prayer, its answer in the appearance of the cloud “like a man’s hand,”\* the “sound of abundance of rain,”† and “the heavens black with clouds and wind,” altogether furnish a description which for graphic power is perhaps not exceeded by anything even in the inspired Volume itself.

We shall conclude these notices with a few observations on the conversion of Saul of Tarsus. The entirely miraculous character of that event is calculated to exclude from our ideas the possibility of a natural agency having been employed. Yet the whole narrative seems to indicate that electrical action was made use of as an instrument. The “light at mid-day, above the brightness of the sun,” Saul struck to the earth, the sound heard by his companions, yet the words undistinguishable to all but himself (comp. Acts ix. 7 with xxii. 9), the blindness which followed, all suggest almost irresistibly the idea of electrical phenomena having been employed as instruments in this case. It is, we know, a favourite theory with many that the infirmity to which the apostle makes such frequent although vague allusion was a defect of vision, the _remains_ of the total blindness inflicted near the gate of Damascus. We must own that this idea has always appeared to us objectionable on many accounts. Sight was restored to Saul _by miracle_, and if we suppose the cure to have been but partial and imperfect, we must suppose this miracle to have differed in a most essential particular from every other on record. Where conjecture is our only resource we should at least choose the most probable conjecture, and it seems to us that _a lasting_

WEATHER.

_nervous derangement_, while it would be a natural result of the severe shock undergone (on our supposition) by the apostle, would abundantly account for everything of the kind noticed in his writings. It would furnish a satisfactory reason for his being but an indifferent scribe, and for a “large letter written by his own hand” being a thing quite remarkable;\* it would account fully for the “weakness, fear, and much trembling”† of which he speaks, and for the fact that not only was his speech derided as contemptible,‡ but that he expresses himself quite grateful for only the negative favour of _not being despised_ on account of his bodily infirmity.§ More than this, we have on this supposition the strange, startling, and otherwise quite unaccountable contrasts between the powers of St. Paul at different times most clearly explained. Was he timid, hesitating, trembling,—_nervous_, in short, so as to give to his enemies abundant materials for disparaging his person and office? His physical infirmity, which we can (without the least strain put upon the New Testament narrative) refer to the most striking circumstance accompanying his conversion, perfectly accounts for all this. Was he at other times so marvellously eloquent as to be taken on one occasion for the incarnation of the god of oratory,|| and on another to “almost persuade” Agrippa to be a Christian?—not to mention the fact that his recorded addresses are to this day admitted to be masterpieces of elocution? We have the explanation of these apparent discrepancies in a very easily understood pledge and promise of our Lord himself (see Mark xiii. 9, 11; Luke xxi. 12, 15). When do we find St. Paul nervous, timid, stammering, unable to give effectual utterance to the feelings with which his heart was full even to overflowing? When he was in circumstances which did not call for any particular exertion of mental power. When the plain statement of the gospel message was all that was required of him. But see him in a different situation, “brought before kings and rulers,” obliged to plead his cause before the Areopagus, the Sanhedrin, Felix, Festus, Agrippa,—his powers rise with the occasion, and his judges, accustomed as they must have been to witness similar efforts, are amazed, overwhelmed with astonishment and admiration.

We do not know how we can conclude better than by calling attention to the fact that when the Psalmist would set forth the divine attributes of _power_, he describes God as _Lord of the elements_, and that he appears to dwell more emphatically upon the irresistible power of _frost_ than that of any other elemental agent: “He giveth snow like wool: He scattereth the hoar-frost like ashes. He casteth forth His ice like morsels: WHO CAN STAND BEFORE HIS COLD?” (Psa. cxlvii. 16, 17).

† 1 Cor. ii. 3.

‡ 2 Cor. x. 10.

§ Gal. iv. 13, 14.

# ESOTERIC POETRY.

A GREATER contrast than that between the Laureate and Mr. Browning it is impossible to imagine. Tennyson in style is lucid; even his mannerism is a trick of over plainness, as if he would fain make himself understood by everybody; and as to power, he is calm and self-sustained, even in his wildest flights letting us feel that he has something in reserve. Hence he is the poet of this our age—an undemonstrative but by no means prosaic age, which gloats over sensation novels but does not talk sensationally, which admires reticence and practices it, which will not, at any rate, have its poetry sensational (the spasmodic school has never had many votaries). And the poetry of any age surely comes more from its heart, tells us more of its real character than its novels. Tennyson, then, is the poet of the present generation, a well-to-do “Realistic” generation, yet not without sympathies and aspirations and forebodings of something better than mere comfort: if we call him a drawing-room poet we do not use the term at all by way of reproach. There is a very great deal of good in the _habitués_ of English drawing-rooms; and very few poets can be, like Burns or Shakspere, poets of all mankind—Milton is hardly so in any degree whatsoever. The drawing-rooms have surely a right to their representative poet. Tennyson is this, though of course he is infinitely more than this; and his being so, the very points which fit him to be the poet of the “_jeunesse dorée_,” must always hinder him from being _popular_, i.e., the property of the masses, in the same sense in which Burns is in Scotland, or Beranger in France. His office is not so much to act directly on the people, as on those who help to form the people’s thoughts. If he is purer, nobler, more truly Christian than Byron, we may be sure the “lower walks of literature” among us will be all the cleaner for his influence. That influence might, however, be brought to act far more directly on the half educated than it has hitherto done. The vast numbers of “Readings in Poetry,” “Selections,” “Garlands,” “Friendship’s Offerings,” and the like, which the publishers find profitable, bear witness to a strong, unreasoning liking for “verse” among people of all classes. What meagre hide-bound productions most of these are! Several that have come in our way lately are more than half filled with long pieces from third-rate American “poets.” From Tenny-

ESOTERIC POETRY.

son there is next to nothing in any of them. The same fatal spell seems to rest on the compilers which holds hymn-book makers back from the choice of truly poetical pieces, and forces them to stuff their volumes with the driest of sacred lyrics. A great deal in Tennyson's newest volume might be safely inserted in any popular book of 'Extracts.' Much of it surely will take its place in that _cheaper edition_, the first volume of which we so gladly hail as an earnest that our Laureate means henceforth to aim at wider popularity, without forgetting the claims of 'that fit audience though few' who have been with him throughout. He has, in the last twenty years, gradually conquered his way, from being the beloved of a small clique to being the foremost poet for all our educated classes, and now he means to win '_the many_;' and we are sure, too, that he will do it. We should like to see these new volumes, 'his own selection,' on the shelves of every mechanics' institute, every people's reading-room, through the land. We want to have him read at penny readings. Much more of him is fit for such work than some of us imagine. The very highest poetry commends itself to educated and uneducated alike. Of course, the educated feel it more, and see more in it; but still the others feel it too. Take 'Northern Farmer,' for instance. He would be sure to be a general favourite at a Reading; and we do not even despair of 'Boadicea,' the wild Catullian metre is so perfect, and such an echo of the sense, that it would carry safely over the harder lines—such as, 'Hear Icenian, Catyewchlanian; hear Coritanian Trinobant,'—many who have never even read a word of Cæsar. The 'Tropical Island,' too, and the lovely tale of Edith's visiting among her cottages (in 'Aylmer's Field'),—surely pieces like these, even without their context, would _tell_ on the general reader, just as the Virgin's head in the Sistine Madonna would still entrance us, even if it were cut out and laid here on the library table. But of course much of Tennyson is written for the educated and refined. He is often quite Greek in his suggestiveness; an epithet implies a whole book full. How true this is of 'In Memoriam,' where we have, as has been said, in a few pregnant lines, 'all the latest results of modern philosophy.' Every time we read it again we mark some word, perhaps unnoticed before, which betokens a thorough acquaintance with scientific controversies. Naturally, your half-educated reader does not love suggestive poetry, or suggestive anything. He likes to have it all down at full length, penny-a-liner fashion; his powers are exhausted with 'business,' and he likes to roll easily on from page to page without ruts or jolting. Tennyson, as a whole, will never be very widely read. His greatest works, 'Maud,' and 'In Memoriam,' will never be generally appreciated beyond a certain line of culture. Far less will Browning ever be a people's poet. His style is jerky—not so much terse as hopelessly obscure.

ESOTERIC POETRY.

375

Carlyle, in his most oracular fit, is nothing to him. Michelet even, most Carlylian of Frenchmen, is easy reading compared to him. At times he seems to have inherited the mantle of some of those Greek poets of the Later Empire, the cuttle-fishes of literature, who, striving after archaisms, attained the renown of incomprehensibility. And his power, unquestionably great, is not equable, like Tennyson's; it works by spurts. You shall have a page of mistiness, redeemed by a flash of genius, gleaming through four or five exquisite lines. A great deal of 'Mr. Sludge, the medium,' in his last volume, 'Dramatis Personæ,' is mere prose; a very clever satire on the absurd folly of spiritualism, but not _poetry_, except by fits and starts. For the Laureate we may say the muse is a demure, well-ordered maiden; for Mr. Browning she is a wanton, passing fair, with features too voluptuous to be looked on, one who, by a look or a sigh, loves at times to make her worshipper do all sorts of strange things, not out of firm will, but out of wilfulness.

The difference between the two poets is well seen by comparing 'In Memoriam' with 'Caliban upon Setebos; or, Theology in the Island.' If we accept 'In Memoriam' as the exponent of the Laureate's theology, we may not, perhaps, hold him strictly orthodox; but we shall assuredly account him Christian in the highest sense of the word. He has unwavering faith in God's goodness, and in the future of humanity.

'Thou wilt not leave us in the dust:\
Thou madest man he knows not why;\
He thinks he was not made to die,—\
_And Thou hast made him, Thou art just._'

Though at times 'his faith is dry,' and he seems to see nought but himself projected upon the vast void of the future, though—

'Nature, red in tooth and claw,\
With raving shrieks against his creed—\
The creed that God is love indeed,\
And love creation's final law,'—

and though he feels he is but 'an infant crying for the light,'

'And with no language but a cry,'

still he will never give up his trust in Him, the

'Strong Son of God, Immortal Love:'

nor will any vague pantheistic absorption theory satisfy him. He is thoroughly clear as to our identity in the spirit world—

The eternal soul from all beside.'

ESOTERIC POETRY.

Indeed we always rise from reading 'In Memoriam' with a feeling of calm thankfulness. All that wonderful series of 'geological sonnets,' though some of them seem less hopeful than others, is summed up in the assurance that progress is the law of humanity as it is of creation.

'Contemplate all this work of time;\
The giant labouring in his youth,\
Nor dream of human love and truth\
As dying nature's earth and lime;\
But trust that those we call the dead\
Are dwellers in an ampler day,\
For ever nobler ends. . . .'

And the ethical teaching of the whole is gathered into those grand lines, wherein, by-and-bye (when Tennyson shall be our Dante), expositors will possibly find the joint working of the three persons of the Trinity unmistakably traced out:—

'O living Will, that shalt endure\
When all that seems shall suffer shock,\
Rise in the spiritual rock,\
Flow through our deeds and make them pure;\
That we may lift from out the dust\
A cry as unto One that hears—\
A cry above the conquered years\
To One that with us works; and trust\
With faith, that comes of self-control,\
The truths that never can be proved\
Until we closed with all we loved,\
And all we flow from, soul in soul.'

We quote freely, because we fear 'In Memoriam' is like Milton, more talked about than known. But it deserves to be well known, for there is much in it which meets the wants of the day—wants which, call them intellectual or spiritual, are certainly general and deep-seated. And now take Mr. Browning by way of contrast. At once we lose the calm earnestness which in the Laureate encouraged us to do what his own much loved friend did, 'fight our doubts and gather strength.' Mr. Browning often seems to be mocking us. Tennyson never does that; he is genial, sympathetic, never cynical. The theological element is particularly strong in this new volume of Mr. Browning. Those who know 'Saul' and 'Rabbi ben Ezra,' and others of his former poems, will remember that he has always been fond of long discussions on sacred subjects, as well as of the somewhat irreverent allusions, which come out so constantly in 'Pippa Passes,' for instance. 'Christmas Eve' at once occurs to the mind as full of Mr. Browning's 'views.' Probably it is far the most beautiful, as a work of art, of all his productions. We know no piece of word-painting so glorious as the description of St. Peter's at Rome during the grand ceremony. And yet it is full of crude

ESOTERIC POETRY.

377

notions, of unkindly hits at English nonconformists, striving to gain a little light in their own way in their mean little chapel, because they think the parson, their “authorized light,” hides his candles (if he has any) under a bushel. “Christmas Eve” is marred by its theology. But in the present volume Mr. Browning is much more orthodox; he sets out with the intention of being so; and, as we shall see, some of his reasonings in “A Death in the Desert” are unimpeachable, while his attack on the pantheist fools and astute schemers who, between them, constitute the class of spiritualists, is clever and utterly destructive. But the greatest poem, to our mind, in the volume, and that which deals more with eschatology than even “St. John’s Death in the Desert,” is “Caliban upon Setebos.” It is not comfortable reading. Of all the bitter satires on human littleness which ever were written, perhaps these uneasy maunderings of Shakspere’s “most delicate monster” form the bitterest. “Gulliver’s Travels” are good fun. We forget, in the comical narrative, the grim truths which the unhappy writer meant to convey. But here there is no possibility of forgetting. Caliban gives us his thoughts on God and Providence and the “Future;” and straightway rises up before us all we have ever read or heard about the different forms of _Effera relligio_—all the bloody propitiations, all the hatred, checked by fear, with which men have looked on the gods: Amasis, his ring, Louis XI., his hat-band full of leaden saints—here Prospero’s drudge is giving us the germ of them all. And philosophy, too—read Ritter through, and learn what each successive sage said about God and the world, and veritably you will find that this “most sagacious monster” has just as firm a grip of the root of the matter as the very best of them. “Thou thoughtest that I am such an one as thyself;” that is Caliban’s error; but then in that very error there is a certain germ of truth, if, as every one agrees, every religion which man can conceive of must be anthropomorphic. We try by abstraction to get an idea of the Godhead conformable to what our Article says, “without body, parts, or passions,” but we do not very often succeed. Mr. Browning seems, as we said, to be mocking us; he holds, we fancy, Mr. Mansel’s view of the Great Unconditioned, and seems to dare us to speculate on such matters, under penalty of being sure to err as crassly as his own Caliban does.

But we must give our readers an idea of the whole piece. It is very plain reading—for Mr. Browning. Fortunately for us the monster does not affect the jerky, disjointed style which the more human _personæ_ of the “drama” mostly use: it is worked out, moreover, with exquisite care, illustrated from the rich stores of a full knowledge of nature in her more hidden workings, which puts it in the same relation to the “tropical island scene” in “Enoch Arden” that a walk with Mr. Bates in a Brazilian forest would hold

ESOTERIC POETRY.

to a seat in the pit when the closing tableau of an extravaganza was being lighted up with Bengalfire.

'The monster,\
Sprawling, now that the heat of day is best,\
Flat on his belly in the pit's much mire,\
With elbows wide, fists clenched to prop his chin,'

maunders on to himself—

“Touching _that other_ whom his dam called God.”

Not that he cares about the question in the abstract, but _for him to think and talk_ he believes vexes Prospero. Here, at the very outset, is an unpleasant alternative; the relation of Prospero and Caliban either shows the necessary degradation which slavery brings on the slave, or it is an instance of what the New Zealand settlers would fain establish—the unimprovableness of savage races. Anyhow, the conclusions at which the monster arrives show how man’s idea of God first gets debased, and then reacts on and debases the man still more. Caliban is no atheist, has no notion of an “eternal sequence;” he makes up his mind that there is a God very near him, interested, in a certain way, in what he does—a God, who, “being cold and ill-at-ease, made sun and moon; but not the stars, the stars came otherwise” (is not this, by the way, a little too acute—too fine a distinction, even for such a most sagacious monster?), and whose whim is law over what He hath made. You cannot predicate good or evil of Him—simply power.

'He is strong, and, Lord,\
Am strong myself, compared to yonder crabs\
That march now from the mountain to the sea;\
Let twenty pass and stone the twenty first;\
Loving not, hating not, just choosing so.\
Say the first straggler that boasts purple spots,\
Shall join the file, one pinner twisted off;\
Say this bruised fellow shall receive a worm,\
And two worms he whose nippers end in red;\
As it likes me, each time I do—so He.'

But this God does feel envy; for He often _makes things better than himself_, just as I, Caliban, can cut an elder pipe, that shall imitate the jay’s screaming so well as to cheat the small birds. But if my pipe were to boast that it made the cry which drew the birds, why I should crush it under foot—so _He_. Be sure He spites all that tries to be self-asserting, that pretends to independence—though sometimes ridiculous boldness in a feeble creature will amuse Him, and so will get forgiveness,—even as I laugh at and let off the squirrel who steals nuts from under my thumb, and bites when I threaten it. Envious spite, then, or mere whim being His “rules,” the question is, how to please Him?

“The best way to escape His ire is not to seem too happy.”

ESOTERIC POETRY.

379

Caliban's dam had given him some notion of immortality; but he discards the idea, preferring to hold, that 'with the life the pain shall stop.' And so we must rub through life as best we can,—' _Dancing on dark nights; moaning in the sun, but getting under holes to laugh._' And if Setebos overhears us, and asks, 'What chucklest at?' vowing to cut off a finger, or burn the best of those three kids, or let these toothsome apples rot on tree,—penance, propitiation, that is the way to disarm the spite of One who works His work—

_'By no means for the love of what is worked.'_

After all, Setebos is not all in all. Beyond him is _that Other_ ('_Quiet_,' the old dam used to call It), who perhaps made Setebos, and one day may catch and conquer Him, if It does not first 'doze off—as good as die.' Whilst he is thus speculating a storm comes on, and the terrified monster, thinking his God has overheard him, cries,—

Lo! lieth flat and '_loveth Setebos_,'—

and vows he '_won't touch one little mess of whelks for a month, so he may 'scape._' . . . In all this we have no charge of obscurity to make against Mr. Browning. He is terribly and cynically plain. We are merely showing why his circle of admirers will, even amongst educated people, be always a limited one. Men do not care to be made needlessly uncomfortable. If you go in for a metaphysical treatise of doubtful orthodoxy, you must expect speculations which will not put the world in its relation to God in the pleasantest light; but why have them in poetry? Ought not poetical justice to suggest, at least, a winding up with something consoling? No; Mr. Browning will never be popular, not even (as the Laureate is) with the great mass of well-taught readers, who possess a certain modicum of poetical taste. '_Il les froisse._' He must be content to rank with caviare and olives, and other questionable dainties, comforted by the feeling, that (as with olives, \&c.), those who do like him, like him intensely; he becomes a sort of passion for them. Well, it is his own fault; he is hard to understand in many, especially of his shorter, pieces. He ought not to be above playing at times explanatory Euripidean chorus to himself, instead of dropping us plump into the middle of a conversation of choice spirits, hyper-æsthetics, great at enigmatical repartee, and wonderfully rich in allusion to we cannot, for the life of us, make out what. That is his way in a great many of his shorter pieces. Where he is plain, as in Caliban aforesaid, he is too fond of sounding the abyss of human doubt. When we read 'Natural Theology in the Island,' we feel we must put our hands before our eyes and rush away, rather than encounter the

ESOTERIC POETRY.

By the way, that title “Natural Theology,” is a suspicious one. _Reactionists_ are labouring hard to show that Morality has no independent basis; that, apart from Revelation, it cannot properly be said to exist at all. Can it be that Mr. Browning, who is so orthodox in a “A Death in the Desert,” means to hint that, without revelation, and the witness of the Spirit to keep that revelation living in men’s hearts (for Caliban may be said to have had a revelation—Sycorax’s revelation, to wit—only he had not Sycorax’s spirit to work with it), men must sink to Caliban’s views of God and goodness? Whatever its ethical aim, the poem is by far the most remarkable in Mr. Browning’s last volume; and yet it will not add to his popularity. “Enoch Arden,” on the other hand, will become a household word with hundreds who would be puzzled to explain even the plain allusions in “Tithonus.” “In Memoriam” will yearly have a larger number of readers and admirers; but “Caliban upon Setebos,” though as full, in its way, of philosophic speculation as “In Memoriam” itself, will always continue among our strictly esoteric poems.
